Maggots appeared only in the open jars, where flies could lay eggs, giving empirical support to the view that living things come from other living things.

words.definition: To imitate in an effort to equal or surpass.
examples: Young players emulate their heroes.

sat.passage: Young painters in Renaissance Florence often trained by copying the works of established masters. By studying how a celebrated artist handled light, color, and perspective, apprentices hoped to emulate his achievements and, ideally, someday surpass them with masterpieces of their own.

words.definition: To make a bill into law; to put into practice; to act out.
words.usage: Most often for laws and policies.
examples: The city enacted a ban on single-use plastic bags.

sat.passage: After a series of deadly factory fires, public pressure on state legislators grew intense. Within two years, lawmakers had debated and passed more than thirty new statutes requiring fire exits, sprinklers, and regular inspections. Reformers celebrated the decision to enact these measures as a turning point for workplace safety.

words.definition: To include comprehensively; to surround.
examples: The park encompasses three lakes.

sat.passage: The new national park is far larger than its predecessor. Its boundaries encompass three mountain ranges, more than forty lakes, and the entire watershed of the river that flows through the valley, giving migrating elk room to move between their summer and winter grazing grounds.

words.definition: To meet unexpectedly; to face a difficulty.
words.usage: Used for people, problems, and animals.
examples: The explorers encountered fierce storms.

sat.passage: Setting out across the plains in late summer, the expedition expected an easy crossing of the mountains. Instead, the party would encounter early blizzards, waist-deep snow, and dwindling food supplies, hardships that nearly forced the travelers to turn back before they reached the western rivers.

words.definition: Native to or regularly found in a certain area.
examples: The lemur is endemic to Madagascar.

sat.passage: Madagascar separated from the African mainland more than 150 million years ago, and its plants and animals evolved in isolation. As a result, about ninety percent of the island's species, including every kind of lemur, are endemic and occur nowhere else on Earth.

words.definition: To declare public approval or support of.
words.usage: Used for candidates, products, and ideas.
examples: Several scientists endorsed the new guidelines.

sat.passage: When the city council proposed converting an abandoned rail line into a walking trail, the plan faced little opposition. The local hiking club publicly praised it, the chamber of commerce predicted it would attract tourists, and the mayor announced that she would endorse the project in her annual address.

words.definition: Continuing or long-lasting.
words.usage: Describes legacies, influence, popularity, and friendships.
examples: The novel's enduring popularity surprised even its publisher.

sat.passage: When it was first published in 1813, the novel sold modestly and received only a handful of reviews. Yet more than two centuries later, it remains in print in dozens of languages and is adapted for film and television almost every decade, a testament to its enduring appeal.

words.definition: To make sure a law or rule is obeyed.
examples: Police enforced the new speed limit.

sat.passage: The fishing law had been on the books for years, but with only one warden assigned to the entire coastline, illegal catches went largely unpunished. Only after the state hired additional officers and equipped patrol boats with tracking systems were authorities able to enforce the limits effectively.

words.definition: To give the right to vote.
examples: The amendment enfranchised women.

sat.passage: Through the early 1900s, women in many countries could own property and pay taxes but could not cast a ballot. Suffragists marched, petitioned, and lobbied for decades before governments finally passed laws to enfranchise them, granting women the same voting rights men had long held.

words.definition: To improve the quality or value of.
words.usage: Used for performance, flavor, and images.
examples: Spices enhance the flavor of the soup.

sat.passage: Astronomers rarely use raw telescope images in their research. Instead, they apply software that reduces background noise, sharpens blurred edges, and boosts faint colors. These techniques enhance the images so that dim galaxies and fine structures become visible.

words.definition: Mysterious and difficult to understand.
examples: The Mona Lisa's enigmatic smile fascinates viewers.

sat.passage: Carved into the hillside more than two thousand years ago, the giant figures have puzzled researchers for generations. No written records explain who made them or why, and their strange shapes match no known symbols from the region. The purpose of these enigmatic carvings is still debated.

words.definition: Very large.
examples: The project had an enormous impact on the city.

sat.passage: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived. Adults can reach thirty meters in length and weigh as much as two hundred tons, and even a newborn calf weighs more than a full-grown elephant. Such enormous creatures survive by eating up to four tons of tiny krill each day.

words.definition: A thing with distinct and independent existence.
words.usage: Used for organizations, beings, and concepts.
examples: The company became a separate legal entity.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: For decades the research station was run as a department of the university, sharing its budget and staff. In 2005, however, it was reorganized as an independent entity, with its own board of directors, its own funding sources, and the legal authority to sign contracts in its own name.

words.definition: Firmly established and difficult to change.
examples: The habits were deeply entrenched.

sat.passage: When railroads first proposed standard time zones in the 1880s, many towns resisted. Each community had set its clocks by the local sun for generations, and residents viewed the custom as part of their identity. Because such entrenched habits were hard to overturn, it took decades for the new system to win full acceptance.

words.definition: To list one by one.
examples: The article enumerates five causes of the war.

sat.passage: The engineers' report on the bridge collapse does not offer a single explanation. Instead, it goes on to enumerate seven separate factors, listing each in turn, from corroded support cables and outdated design standards to heavier-than-expected traffic and years of delayed maintenance.

words.definition: To picture something in the mind as a future possibility.
examples: The architect envisioned a park where the parking lot once stood.

sat.passage: When the landscape architect first walked through the abandoned rail yard, she saw more than rusted tracks and weeds. She began to envision a park filled with wildflower meadows, shaded walking paths, and an outdoor amphitheater, and she spent the next decade turning that picture into reality.

words.definition: Lasting for a very short time.
examples: The beauty of the cherry blossoms is ephemeral.

sat.passage: Mayflies spend up to two years as aquatic larvae in streams and ponds. Once they mature and take to the air, however, their adult lives are remarkably ephemeral: most survive only a single day, just long enough to mate and lay eggs before dying.

words.definition: To be a perfect example of something.
words.usage: Used when one person or thing represents a quality or type completely.
examples: Her careful, patient research epitomizes the scientific method.

sat.passage: Built in 1931, the skyscraper's sleek setbacks, geometric ornaments, and gleaming metal spire contain nearly every feature associated with Art Deco design. Architecture students are often taken there because the building is said to epitomize the style more completely than any other.

words.definition: A particular period of time in history or geology.
examples: The invention marked a new epoch in medicine.

sat.passage: Some geologists argue that human activity has altered Earth so profoundly that the planet has entered a new epoch. Layers of plastic, concrete, and radioactive particles now appear in sediments worldwide, and they propose that this period, beginning in the mid-twentieth century, be named the Anthropocene.

words.definition: Calmness, especially in difficult situations.
examples: She accepted the news with equanimity.

sat.passage: The pilot's voice over the intercom remained steady as she explained that one engine had failed and the plane would return to the airport. Passengers later said that her equanimity in the face of danger kept the cabin calm, and the aircraft landed safely twenty minutes later.

words.definition: To consider or treat as the same or equal.
examples: Critics warned against equating wealth with happiness.

sat.passage: Many early economists measured a nation's well-being almost entirely by its total output of goods. Later scholars objected that this approach tended to equate wealth with happiness, ignoring factors such as health, leisure, and community ties that surveys show matter greatly to people's satisfaction with their lives.

words.definition: A state in which opposing forces are balanced.
words.usage: Used in science, economics, and emotions.
examples: The ecosystem reached a new equilibrium after the wolves returned.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: When wolves were reintroduced to the park, elk numbers fell sharply and willow saplings that the elk had been eating began to recover. Over the next two decades, however, the swings grew smaller, and populations of wolves, elk, and willows settled into a new equilibrium in which none changed dramatically from year to year.

words.definition: To supply with the necessary items or skills.
examples: The course equips students to manage their own money.

sat.passage: The community college's new program is designed for adults returning to the workforce. Over twelve weeks, participants learn to build spreadsheets, write professional emails, and manage project schedules. Organizers hope the course will equip graduates with the practical skills employers increasingly expect.

words.definition: Fair and impartial.
examples: The plan ensures an equitable division of funds.

sat.passage: When three neighboring towns agreed to share water from a single reservoir, they argued for months over how to divide it. The final agreement assigns each town a share based on its population and farmland, so that no community receives more than its fair portion. Residents of all three towns praised the arrangement as equitable.

words.definition: Equal in value, meaning, or effect.
examples: A mile is roughly equivalent to 1.6 kilometers.

sat.passage: Comparing ancient and modern prices is difficult. Historians estimate that in parts of the Roman Empire, a soldier's daily wage could buy about ten loaves of bread; by that measure, his pay was roughly equivalent to what a worker earning sixty dollars a day could purchase today.

words.definition: To wear away gradually.
examples: Waves slowly eroded the cliffs.
Repeated delays eroded public trust.

sat.passage: The city's new transit line was promised for 2015, then 2018, then 2021. Each delay was accompanied by a larger budget and a fresh set of assurances from officials. Surveys show that these repeated broken promises have continued to erode residents' confidence in the transit agency.

words.definition: Not even or regular; unpredictable.
examples: The moth's erratic flight confuses predators.

sat.passage: Unlike many insects that fly in straight paths, the moth zigzags, loops, and abruptly changes direction several times per second. Biologists believe this erratic flight helps it escape bats, because a predator cannot easily predict where its prey will be a moment later.

words.definition: Wrong or based on a mistake.
examples: The erroneous report caused a brief panic in the markets.

sat.passage: For decades, textbooks claimed that different regions of the tongue detect different tastes, with sweetness sensed at the tip and bitterness at the back. Later experiments showed that taste receptors for every flavor are spread across the entire tongue, revealing the old map to be erroneous.

words.definition: The fundamental nature or most important quality of something.
words.usage: Often 'the essence of' something; 'in essence' means basically.
examples: Kindness is the essence of her character.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The poet rewrote the short poem more than forty times, cutting it from thirty lines to just six. She explained that she had removed every image and phrase that was merely decorative, keeping only what was necessary to express the poem's essence: the quiet grief of a mother watching her son leave home.

words.definition: Respect and admiration; (v.) to respect and admire.
examples: The architect was held in high esteem by her peers.

sat.passage: Although she never sought publicity, the botanist was consulted by researchers from around the world, and her field guides became standard references. When she retired, dozens of former students and colleagues traveled to honor her, a sign of the high esteem in which she was held.

words.definition: Relating to moral principles; morally right.
words.usage: Used for decisions, research, and business.
examples: The study raised ethical questions about privacy.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the 1970s, investigators learned that some medical studies had been conducted on patients who were never told the risks or asked for permission. In response, universities created review boards to examine proposed research and ensure that it met ethical standards, including informed consent and protection from unnecessary harm.

words.definition: A mild word used in place of a harsh one.
examples: 'Downsizing' is a euphemism for firing workers.

sat.passage: In the company's annual report, the layoff of nearly two thousand employees appeared only as a "workforce adjustment." Labor advocates criticized the phrase as a classic euphemism designed to soften an announcement that, put plainly, meant thousands of people had lost their jobs.

words.definition: To judge or assess the value, quality, or importance of something.
words.usage: Neutral academic verb for assessing evidence or work.
examples: Researchers evaluated the effectiveness of three teaching methods.

sat.passage: To determine which of three reading programs best helped struggling third graders, the school district assigned each program to a different group of schools. At the end of the year, researchers will evaluate the programs by comparing students' test scores, attendance, and teachers' reports of their progress.

words.definition: Occurring at the end of a process.
examples: The eventual winner was a newcomer.

sat.passage: In the early rounds of the chess tournament, few spectators paid attention to the seventeen-year-old from a small town. She lost her first game and barely advanced to the second week. Yet she won her next eight matches in a row, and the crowd that gathered for the final watched her become the eventual champion.

words.definition: Clearly seen or understood; obvious.
examples: Her joy was evident in her smile.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The rescued sea turtle had refused food for weeks. When she finally snapped up a piece of squid, the veterinary team's relief was evident: technicians cheered, the lead veterinarian broke into a wide grin, and someone ran to tell the volunteers waiting outside.

words.definition: To bring a feeling or memory to mind.
words.usage: Common in literature and art questions.
examples: The smell of pine evoked memories of camp.

sat.passage: The novelist rarely tells readers directly what her characters feel. Instead, she relies on small sensory details, such as the smell of wet wool or the creak of a porch swing, to evoke a sense of the narrator's lost childhood and the longing she feels for it.

words.definition: To develop gradually.
words.usage: Used for species, ideas, and technologies.
examples: Her style evolved over decades.

sat.passage: The painter's earliest canvases were realistic landscapes, faithful to every leaf and cloud. Over the next three decades, his style would gradually evolve: shapes grew simpler, colors bolder, and by the end of his career his works consisted of a few blocks of pure color.

words.definition: To make a problem, situation, or feeling worse.
words.usage: Negative; used for conditions, conflicts, and symptoms.
examples: Rising temperatures exacerbated the water shortage.

sat.passage: The region was already suffering from a two-year drought when an unusually hot summer arrived. Soaring temperatures increased evaporation from reservoirs and drove residents to water their lawns more often, both of which served only to exacerbate the existing water shortage.

words.definition: A statement that represents something as better, worse, or larger than it really is.
words.usage: Used for overstatements; often signals a claim is not literally true.
examples: Calling the hill a mountain is an exaggeration.

sat.passage: In his letters home, the young sailor described waves "as tall as church steeples" during a storm off Cape Horn. Weather records for that week, however, show swells of only about four meters, suggesting that his account was an exaggeration meant to impress his family.

words.definition: To irritate intensely.
examples: The constant delays exasperated passengers.

sat.passage: The renovation of the museum was supposed to take six months. Two years later, the entrance was still blocked by scaffolding, galleries were closed without notice, and the reopening date had been postponed four times. These repeated delays began to exasperate even the museum's most loyal members.

words.definition: To be greater than; to go beyond.
examples: Sales exceeded the company's forecast.

sat.passage: Organizers of the community book drive had hoped to collect five thousand books for local schools. By the end of the month, donations had poured in from businesses, churches, and families across the county, and the total came to more than twelve thousand, far enough to exceed the original goal.

words.definition: To deny access to; to leave out.
examples: The study excluded participants under 18.

sat.passage: In designing their study of a new allergy medication, the researchers decided to exclude anyone who was already taking other allergy drugs. Including such participants, they reasoned, would make it impossible to tell whether any improvement came from the new medication or from the treatments the patients were already using.

words.definition: To carry out a plan or task; to put to death.
examples: The team executed the plan flawlessly.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The rescue of the trapped miners required weeks of careful planning. Engineers designed a narrow capsule, drillers bored a shaft more than six hundred meters deep, and medical teams prepared for every possible emergency. When the moment came, the crews were able to execute the plan flawlessly, lifting every miner to the surface within a single day.

words.definition: Serving as a perfect example; excellent.
examples: Her exemplary work earned her a promotion.

sat.passage: During her twelve years at the hospital, the nurse never missed a shift, trained dozens of new staff members, and was repeatedly praised by patients for her patience and skill. The administration presented her with its highest award, citing her exemplary service as a model for others.

words.definition: To be a typical example of.
examples: The building exemplifies the city's early modern architecture.

sat.passage: The town's main street is lined with brick storefronts built in the 1890s, each featuring tall arched windows, decorative iron cornices, and painted signs above the doors. Preservationists say these buildings exemplify the commercial architecture of small midwestern railroad towns of that era.

words.definition: Including or considering all elements or aspects; thorough.
words.usage: Describes searches, studies, and lists that leave nothing out.
examples: After an exhaustive search of the archives, she found the missing letter.

sat.passage: The historian spent four years tracking down the missing letter. She examined every box in three national archives, read thousands of pages of diplomatic correspondence, and contacted the descendants of everyone the writer was known to have met. Only after this exhaustive search did she finally locate it in a private collection.

words.definition: To show or display; (n.) a public display.
examples: The patients exhibited similar symptoms.

sat.passage: Doctors at the rural clinic grew concerned when patients from the same village began arriving with fevers, joint pain, and a distinctive rash. Because so many of them would exhibit identical symptoms within a single week, investigators suspected a shared source, which they soon traced to a contaminated well.

words.definition: A mass departure.
words.usage: Used for people leaving a place.
examples: The drought caused an exodus from rural areas.

sat.passage: Between 1916 and 1970, roughly six million Black Americans left the rural South for cities in the North and West, seeking factory jobs and escape from segregation laws. This vast exodus reshaped the nation's cities, transforming their politics, music, and neighborhoods.

words.definition: To clear of blame.
examples: DNA evidence exonerated the prisoner.

sat.passage: The man had spent eighteen years in prison for a robbery he insisted he had not committed. When new DNA testing of evidence from the crime scene revealed that the genetic material belonged to someone else, the results helped exonerate him, and a judge ordered his immediate release.

words.definition: To speed up a process.
examples: Extra staff expedited the review.

sat.passage: During the outbreak, the usual process for approving new diagnostic tests could take more than a year. To expedite the review, regulators hired temporary staff, allowed companies to submit data in stages, and met with developers weekly, reducing the waiting time to just a few months.

words.definition: Expert skill or knowledge in a particular field.
examples: Her expertise in ancient languages helped decode the text.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The ancient manuscript was written in a script that few living scholars could read. Researchers therefore turned to a retired linguist who had spent fifty years studying the region's lost languages. Her expertise allowed the team to translate passages that had baffled others for decades.

words.definition: The end of the period during which something is valid.
words.usage: Used for contracts, licenses, and food dates.
examples: The lease's expiration forced the store to move.

sat.passage: The family bookstore had occupied the same corner for forty years, renting its space under a series of long-term leases. When the building's new owner announced that rent would triple, the store had no choice but to relocate upon the expiration of its current lease that spring.

words.definition: To explain in detail.
examples: The teacher explicated the poem line by line.

sat.passage: In the seminar, the professor spent an entire class period on a single fourteen-line sonnet. Working slowly, she would explicate each line in turn, pointing out double meanings, tracing the source of each image, and showing how the poem's rhyme scheme reinforced its argument.

words.definition: Stated clearly and in detail, leaving no room for confusion.
examples: The instructions were explicit about the deadline.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Earlier versions of the contest rules had only hinted that entries must be the applicant's own work, leading to disputes when some contestants submitted group projects. The revised guidelines are explicit, stating in bold type that each submission must be created entirely by a single student without outside help.

words.definition: To make full use of a resource or opportunity; to use unfairly for one's own advantage.
words.usage: Can be neutral (exploit a weakness in a design) or negative (exploit workers).
examples: The vine exploits gaps in the forest canopy to reach sunlight.

sat.passage: In the dense rainforest, little sunlight reaches the ground. Rather than growing a thick trunk of its own, the strangler fig sends its roots down around a host tree and climbs toward the canopy. The plant is thus able to exploit the height of its host to reach the light it needs.

words.definition: To uncover; to make vulnerable; to reveal wrongdoing.
words.usage: Exposed to sunlight; exposed a scandal.
examples: The reporter exposed corruption in the city council.

sat.passage: For months, a team of reporters examined city contracts, interviewed former employees, and tracked payments between officials and construction firms. Their investigation helped expose a bribery scheme in which council members had steered millions of dollars in projects to companies owned by their relatives.

words.definition: Covering a large area or including a great deal.
words.usage: Used for research, damage, knowledge, and collections.
examples: The museum's collection of maps is extensive.

sat.passage: The hurricane's winds and flooding damaged nearly every structure along a forty-kilometer stretch of coastline. Roads were washed away, power lines were downed across three counties, and thousands of homes were left uninhabitable. Officials said repairing such extensive damage could take several years.

words.definition: The degree to which something is true; the area covered.
words.usage: 'To some extent'; 'the full extent of the damage.'
examples: Scientists are still measuring the extent of the oil spill.

sat.passage: Days after the tanker ran aground, oil had been spotted along beaches more than a hundred kilometers apart. Using aircraft and satellite images, scientists are still trying to map the full extent of the spill, which may have spread far beyond what was first reported.

words.definition: Belonging to or coming from outside.
examples: External pressures forced the company to change.

sat.passage: Some educators argue that grades and prizes are poor long-term motivators. In their view, students who work only for external rewards often lose interest once those rewards are removed, whereas students driven by their own curiosity tend to keep learning on their own.

words.definition: Irrelevant or unrelated to the subject at hand.
words.usage: Describes details or information that should be removed.
examples: The editor cut extraneous details to keep the article short.

sat.passage: The editor returned the draft of the article with dozens of sentences crossed out. In her note, she explained that the writer's anecdotes about his travel arrangements and the history of the hotel, while entertaining, were extraneous to the story's real subject: the city's struggle to rebuild after the flood.

words.definition: To invent falsely; to construct.
examples: The witness fabricated the story.

sat.passage: The journalist's articles were praised for their vivid quotations until editors tried to contact some of the people he had interviewed. Several of them could not be found, and others said they had never spoken to him. An investigation concluded that he had chosen to fabricate entire conversations.

words.definition: One side or aspect of something.
words.usage: Used for problems, personalities, and gems.
examples: The book explores every facet of the explorer's life.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The biography does not limit itself to the inventor's laboratory work. Its chapters also examine his troubled childhood, his long friendship with a rival scientist, his lifelong love of opera, and his failed run for public office. The author explores nearly every facet of this complicated life.

words.definition: To make an action or process easier.
words.usage: Used for discussions, trade, and learning.
examples: The new bridge facilitated trade between the towns.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Before the bridge was built, merchants in the two river towns had to wait hours for a slow ferry, and goods often spoiled on the way. The new crossing allowed wagons to move freely between the towns in minutes, which helped facilitate trade and contributed to both towns' rapid growth.

words.definition: A small group within a larger one, often in disagreement.
examples: The party split into rival factions.

sat.passage: As the debate over the new constitution dragged on, the reform party could no longer present a united front. One faction demanded immediate, sweeping changes to the voting system, while the rest of the party favored gradual reforms, and the two groups eventually began holding separate meetings.

words.definition: A mistaken belief; a flaw in reasoning.
examples: It's a fallacy that cold weather causes colds.

sat.passage: Many people believe that going outside with wet hair in cold weather causes colds. Medical researchers point out that colds are caused by viruses, not by low temperatures, and that people catch more colds in winter mainly because they spend more time indoors together. The popular belief is, in short, a fallacy.

words.definition: Very attentive to detail and cleanliness.
examples: The fastidious chef inspected every plate.

sat.passage: Before a single plate left her kitchen, the chef examined it under a bright lamp, wiped away stray drops of sauce with a cloth, and adjusted each garnish with tweezers. Some of her staff found this fastidious attention to detail exhausting, but diners said it made every dish look like a painting.

words.definition: Extreme tiredness; weakness in materials from repeated stress.
examples: Long shifts cause fatigue among nurses.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Engineers examining the cracked aircraft wing found no sign of a single sudden impact. Instead, the metal had weakened gradually after thousands of cycles of bending during takeoffs and landings, until tiny cracks formed and spread. Their report attributed the failure to metal fatigue.

words.definition: Possible and practical to do.
examples: Building the bridge was not feasible without federal funds.

sat.passage: The town council liked the idea of building a light-rail line to the regional airport. After engineers estimated the cost at more than four times the town's annual budget, however, and state officials declined to provide funding, council members concluded that the project was not feasible.

words.definition: Having or showing passionate intensity.
examples: She was a fervent advocate for clean water.

sat.passage: She had grown up beside a river polluted by factory waste, and as an adult she devoted her life to cleaning it up. She organized protests, testified before lawmakers dozens of times, and even moved her family to a riverside cabin to monitor the water herself. Friends described her as a fervent advocate for clean water.

words.definition: Relating to the medieval system in which vassals held land from lords in exchange for service.
examples: Peasants in the feudal system worked the lord's land.

sat.passage: In medieval Europe, most peasants worked land they did not own. Under the feudal system, a lord granted estates to vassals, who in return pledged military service and a share of each harvest. This web of obligations bound together kings, nobles, and farmers for centuries.
sat.meaning: Based on land granted for service

words.definition: Having limits; not infinite.
examples: Fossil fuels are a finite resource.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Groundwater in many desert aquifers accumulated over thousands of years and is replenished only slowly by rain. Because this supply is finite, hydrologists warn that pumping it faster than it refills will eventually leave wells dry.

words.definition: To grow or develop successfully; to thrive.
examples: Art flourished during the city's golden age.

sat.passage: After a dam was removed from the river, salmon returned to spawning grounds they had not reached in decades. Within a few years, the fish began to flourish, and the eagles and bears that feed on them grew more numerous as well.

words.definition: To rise and fall irregularly.
words.usage: Used for prices, temperatures, and moods.
examples: Gas prices fluctuate with the seasons.

sat.passage: Desert temperatures can fluctuate dramatically within a single day: a sandy plain that reaches 45°C by mid-afternoon may drop close to freezing before dawn. Animals living there must cope with both extremes.

words.definition: An irregular rising and falling in number or amount.
words.usage: Used for prices, temperatures, and populations.
examples: Small fluctuations in temperature can affect seed germination.

sat.passage: Economists tracking the price of coffee beans noticed a sharp fluctuation last year. Prices nearly doubled in the spring after a frost damaged crops, then fell back to their earlier level by autumn once new harvests arrived.

words.definition: Continuous change or flow.
examples: The job market is in constant flux.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: During the early years of the internet, the rules of the music business were in flux. Record labels, artists, and new online services were all experimenting with different ways to sell songs, and no one could predict which model would last.

words.definition: To create or shape with effort; to make a fake copy.
words.usage: Context decides: 'forge a bond' versus 'forge a signature'.
examples: The two nations forged a lasting alliance after the war.

sat.passage: Facing a common rival, the two small kingdoms worked to forge an alliance. Their rulers arranged a marriage between their families, exchanged ambassadors, and agreed to defend each other's borders, creating a partnership that lasted more than a century.

words.definition: Inspiring fear or respect through size, power, or skill.
examples: The champion was a formidable opponent.

sat.passage: Early mountaineers regarded the peak's north face as truly formidable. Its sheer walls of ice rose nearly two kilometers, and sudden storms had turned back every team that attempted it for thirty years.

words.definition: To abandon or give up.
examples: He refused to forsake his principles.

sat.passage: In the novel, Elena is offered a comfortable position in the city if she will forsake the struggling village school she founded. She refuses, telling the messenger that she would rather teach by candlelight than leave her students without a teacher.

words.definition: About to happen; willing to share information.
words.usage: A forthcoming book; she was not forthcoming.
examples: The witness was not forthcoming about what she saw.

sat.passage: When reporters asked the mayor's office how the contract had been awarded, officials were not forthcoming. They declined to release the bidding documents and referred all questions to a lawyer, who also refused to comment.

words.definition: To strengthen against attack or weakness.
examples: Settlers fortified the village with a tall wooden wall.

sat.passage: To protect the harbor from naval raids, colonial engineers worked to fortify its entrance. They built thick stone walls along both shores, mounted cannons on the cliffs, and stretched a heavy chain across the channel that could be raised to block approaching ships.

words.definition: Courage in pain or adversity.
examples: She endured the illness with fortitude.

sat.passage: Recovering from a spinal injury, the young violinist spent eighteen months relearning how to hold her bow. Her teachers marveled at her fortitude: despite constant pain and slow progress, she practiced every day without complaint and returned to the stage within two years.

words.definition: Happening by chance, often luckily.
examples: A fortuitous error led to the discovery of penicillin.

sat.passage: The discovery of the cave paintings was entirely fortuitous. Four teenagers chasing a runaway dog stumbled into a narrow opening in the hillside and found walls covered with images of horses and bison that had gone unseen for thousands of years.

words.definition: To encourage the development of.
words.usage: Used for growth, ideas, cooperation, and talent.
examples: The program fosters creativity in young students.

sat.passage: Hoping to foster cooperation among residents, the city converted several empty lots into community gardens. Neighbors who had never spoken began sharing tools, trading seeds, and organizing harvest dinners together.

words.definition: Forming the necessary base or core of something.
words.usage: Describes ideas, texts, or skills that others build on.
examples: Her research was foundational to the field of genetics.

sat.passage: For centuries, students of geometry began with the same ancient textbook. Its definitions and proofs were foundational, providing the basic principles on which later mathematicians built entire new fields, from trigonometry to the study of curved surfaces.

words.definition: Easily broken or damaged; delicate.
words.usage: Used for objects, ecosystems, and situations.
examples: Coral reefs are fragile ecosystems sensitive to warming water.

sat.passage: Coral reefs are fragile ecosystems. A rise in water temperature of just one or two degrees can cause corals to expel the algae that feed them, and a single careless anchor drop can destroy colonies that took centuries to grow.

words.definition: The outer edge; a group with extreme or unusual views.
words.usage: Used for edges and for ideas outside the mainstream.
examples: The theory was once dismissed as a fringe idea.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: For decades, the idea that continents drift across Earth's surface was a fringe theory, dismissed by most geologists as fanciful. Only in the 1960s, when maps of the ocean floor revealed spreading ridges, did the idea move into the scientific mainstream.

words.definition: Not having serious purpose or value.
examples: The judge dismissed the frivolous lawsuit.

sat.passage: The museum's board rejected the proposal for a gold-plated entrance sign. Members called the expense frivolous at a time when the roof leaked and several galleries lacked the climate control needed to protect old paintings.

words.definition: Economical with money or food.
examples: Her frugal habits helped her save for college.

sat.passage: Living on a teacher's small salary, my grandmother was famously frugal. She reused wrapping paper, mended her clothes instead of replacing them, and grew most of the vegetables her family ate, yet she still saved enough to pay for three children's college tuition.

words.definition: Forming a necessary base; essential.
words.usage: Describes principles, rights, and changes; adverb 'fundamentally'.
examples: Freedom of speech is a fundamental right.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Some discoveries refine existing theories; others require a fundamental change in how scientists think. When researchers learned that some microbes live without sunlight, near volcanic vents on the ocean floor, they had to rethink basic assumptions about where life can exist.

words.definition: Incapable of producing any useful result; pointless.
words.usage: Describes efforts that are bound to fail.
examples: Trying to argue with the storm's timing was futile.

sat.passage: Engineers spent years trying to keep the desert highway clear by plowing away drifting sand, but the effort proved futile: each storm buried the road again within hours. Eventually, they planted rows of shrubs to slow the wind, which finally kept the dunes in place.

words.definition: To shock or excite into action.
examples: The speech galvanized the volunteers.

sat.passage: The collapse of a poorly maintained bridge in one Midwestern city helped galvanize public support for national inspection standards. Within months, citizens who had rarely thought about infrastructure were writing to legislators, and new safety laws passed with broad backing.

words.definition: To gather or collect, especially support or praise.
examples: The proposal garnered wide support.

sat.passage: The documentary was made on a tiny budget by two first-time filmmakers, yet it managed to garner widespread praise. Critics called it the most moving film of the year, and it went on to win awards at festivals on three continents.

words.definition: To estimate or judge, often by measuring.
words.usage: The noun is a measuring instrument.
examples: Teachers use short quizzes to gauge how well students understand the unit.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Before launching a new line of sneakers nationwide, the company released a small batch in three cities to gauge customer interest. Sales data from those stores would show whether the design was popular enough to justify mass production.

words.definition: To make a broad statement based on specific cases.
words.usage: Often a warning: you can't generalize from one example.
examples: The results of one small study cannot be generalized to all students.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The study surveyed only college students in a single city, so the authors cautioned readers not to generalize its results to all adults. People of different ages and backgrounds, they noted, might respond very differently to the same questions.

words.definition: To produce or create.
words.usage: Used for energy, ideas, and interest.
examples: Wind turbines generate electricity.

sat.passage: Wind turbines along the coast now generate about a third of the region's electricity. On especially gusty days, the turbines produce more power than local homes can use, and the surplus is sent to neighboring states.

words.definition: Truly what something is said to be; sincere.
examples: Experts confirmed that the signature was genuine.

sat.passage: Appraisers were skeptical when a farmer brought in a painting he claimed was a lost work by a famous seventeenth-century artist. After chemical tests showed that its pigments and canvas matched those of the period, however, experts agreed that the painting was genuine.

words.definition: To gather information or facts bit by bit.
examples: Historians gleaned details about daily life from old account books.

sat.passage: Because few written records survive from the town's early years, historians have had to glean details about daily life from scattered sources: tax receipts, shipping logs, a handful of letters, and household objects found in old wells. From these fragments, a surprisingly detailed picture of the town has emerged.

words.definition: To struggle to deal with a difficult problem or to wrestle.
examples: Scientists continue to grapple with the question of how life began.

sat.passage: Coastal cities are still trying to grapple with the effects of rising sea levels. Planners must decide whether to build seawalls, raise roads, or move entire neighborhoods inland, and each option is expensive and controversial.

words.definition: To seize firmly; to understand fully.
examples: It took time for students to grasp the idea of negative numbers.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: At first, the apprentice could follow the master carpenter's instructions but could not grasp why each joint had to be cut at a particular angle. Only after a poorly fitted chair collapsed beneath him did he see how the angles distributed weight.

words.definition: Fond of company; sociable.
words.usage: People and animals that live in groups.
examples: Starlings are gregarious birds that flock in thousands.

sat.passage: Unlike solitary leopards, lions are gregarious animals. They live in prides of up to thirty individuals, hunt cooperatively, and spend much of the day resting together in the shade.

words.definition: A real or imagined cause for complaint.
examples: The workers presented a list of grievances.

sat.passage: The workers' chief grievance was the factory's twelve-hour shift, which left them exhausted and, they argued, more likely to suffer accidents. After months of petitions went unanswered, they organized a strike demanding an eight-hour day.

words.definition: To promise with certainty.
examples: Hard work does not guarantee success.

sat.passage: Because rainfall in the region varies so much from year to year, no amount of careful planting can guarantee a good harvest. Farmers therefore grow several different crops, hoping that at least some will thrive whatever the weather.

words.definition: The natural home of a plant or animal.
examples: Wetlands provide habitat for many migrating birds.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The giant panda's habitat is limited to a few mountain ranges in central China, where cool, damp bamboo forests provide nearly all of the animal's food. As roads and farms have divided these forests, conservationists have worked to reconnect them with wildlife corridors.

words.definition: Overused and unoriginal.
words.usage: Similar to banal; describes phrases and plots.
examples: The story relied on hackneyed clichés.

sat.passage: The novel's critics found little to praise in its plot, which relied on hackneyed devices: a long-lost twin, a mysterious letter that arrives at the perfect moment, and a villain who explains his scheme just before being caught. Several reviewers complained that they had seen every twist coming.

words.definition: A sign of something to come.
examples: Robins are a harbinger of spring.

sat.passage: In many northern towns, the first red-winged blackbirds of the year are treated as a harbinger of spring. The males arrive in late winter, often while snow still covers the ground, and their calls signal that warmer weather will soon follow.

words.definition: Done with excessive speed or urgency; hurried.
words.usage: Often implies carelessness (a hasty decision); adverb 'hastily'.
examples: The hasty repairs failed within a week.

sat.passage: The committee's hasty decision to close the library branch drew criticism from residents. Members had voted after only ten minutes of discussion, without reviewing usage data or asking the public for comment.

words.definition: To pay attention to.
examples: The sailors failed to heed the storm warnings.

sat.passage: Hikers who heed the rangers' warnings about afternoon thunderstorms usually start their climbs before dawn and are off the exposed summit by noon. Those who ignore the advice risk being caught above the tree line when lightning strikes.

words.definition: Dominance of one group or nation over others.
examples: The empire's hegemony lasted centuries.

sat.passage: For much of the nineteenth century, Britain's navy was larger than the next two navies combined, giving the nation a hegemony over world sea trade that few rivals dared to challenge. Its warships patrolled merchant routes from the Caribbean to the Indian Ocean.

words.definition: As a consequence; for this reason.
examples: The roads were icy; hence the delay.

sat.passage: The island's soil is thin and its rainfall unpredictable; hence, most of its food has always arrived by ship. When storms delayed deliveries, residents relied on salted fish and stored grain.

words.definition: Diverse in character or content.
examples: The class was a heterogeneous mix of ages and backgrounds.

sat.passage: The soil samples from the floodplain were remarkably heterogeneous. Within a few meters, researchers found layers of fine clay, coarse gravel, and sand rich in decaying leaves, each left by a different flood.

words.definition: A system in which people or things are ranked one above another.
words.usage: Used for organizations, societies, and animal groups.
examples: Wolf packs have a strict social hierarchy.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Within a wolf pack, a clear hierarchy determines which animals eat first after a hunt and which may breed. Subordinate wolves typically drop their heads and tails when approaching the dominant pair.

words.definition: To create difficulties that slow or delay.
examples: Heavy rain hindered the rescue efforts.

sat.passage: Heavy snowfall continued to hinder rescue efforts on the mountain. Helicopters could not fly in the low clouds, and teams on foot advanced only a few hundred meters per hour through drifts as deep as their waists.

words.definition: To gather and store away a large supply, often secretly.
words.usage: Used for animals storing food and people stockpiling goods.
examples: Squirrels hoard acorns to survive the winter.

sat.passage: As autumn days grow shorter, red squirrels hoard pinecones in large piles beneath their favorite trees. These stores, which can contain thousands of cones, allow the animals to survive winters when fresh food is scarce.

words.definition: Of the same kind; uniform.
examples: The mixture was stirred until it was homogeneous.

sat.passage: Early factories valued homogeneous materials. A batch of steel with the same composition throughout could be cut, shaped, and welded predictably, whereas metal with uneven pockets of impurities often cracked under stress.

words.definition: Bringing or deserving honor; morally upright.
examples: Returning the lost wallet was the honorable thing to do.

sat.passage: Although the general lost the battle, historians describe his conduct as honorable: he refused to abandon his wounded soldiers, treated prisoners humanely, and accepted full blame for the defeat rather than shifting it onto his officers. Even his former enemies praised his integrity.

words.definition: The line where earth and sky appear to meet; the limit of one's knowledge or experience.
examples: Travel broadened her horizons.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Living in a remote mountain village, the girl had never traveled more than twenty kilometers from home. A scholarship to a city boarding school widened her horizons: she studied astronomy, learned two new languages, and met classmates from a dozen countries.

words.definition: Unfriendly; opposed.
examples: The desert is a hostile environment for most plants.

sat.passage: The first scientific teams to winter in Antarctica faced a hostile environment. Temperatures fell below -60°C, winds reached hurricane strength, and months of darkness made even short trips outside dangerous.

words.definition: A modest view of one's own importance.
examples: Despite her fame, she showed great humility.

sat.passage: Despite winning the national science prize, the young researcher spoke with notable humility. She credited her lab partners and teachers for the discovery and insisted that she had simply been lucky enough to notice an unusual result.

words.definition: Deliberate exaggeration for effect.
examples: 'I've told you a million times' is hyperbole.

sat.passage: When the coach told reporters that his team had practiced "a million hours" before the championship, no one took the number literally. The remark was hyperbole, meant to convey how hard the players had worked rather than to state an exact figure.

words.definition: A proposed explanation that can be tested.
examples: The experiment supported the researchers' hypothesis.

sat.passage: Noticing that frogs in one pond had more limb deformities than frogs elsewhere, a biologist proposed a hypothesis: a parasite in the pond's water was disrupting the tadpoles' development. She then designed an experiment to test whether frogs raised without the parasite developed normally.

words.definition: To propose an explanation that can be tested.
examples: The team hypothesized that the birds navigate using Earth's magnetic field.

sat.passage: Because the oldest pottery fragments at the site lie beneath a layer of volcanic ash, archaeologists hypothesize that an eruption forced the original settlers to abandon the village. They plan to date the ash to see whether it matches the period when the settlement was emptied.

words.definition: Pursuing high principles, often unrealistically.
examples: The idealistic volunteers hoped to end hunger.

sat.passage: As a young lawyer, Marcus was idealistic, convinced that a single well-argued case could end unfair housing practices across the entire state. Twenty years of slow legal battles taught him that change usually came in small, hard-won steps.

words.definition: A system of ideas forming the basis of a political or economic theory.
examples: The two parties have very different ideologies.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The newspaper's editors tried to avoid tying the paper to any single political ideology. They published columns by writers on the left and the right and encouraged readers to weigh competing arguments for themselves.

words.definition: Peculiar to an individual.
examples: The writer has an idiosyncratic style.

sat.passage: The composer's notation was highly idiosyncratic. Instead of standard symbols, she used colored dots, wavy lines, and small drawings of animals to tell performers how loudly or softly to play, and musicians often needed her personal guide to interpret a score.

words.definition: Extremely happy, peaceful, or picturesque.
examples: They spent an idyllic summer by the lake.

sat.passage: The painting shows an idyllic country scene: cows graze beside a calm stream, children play under shady oaks, and a farmhouse glows in the warm light of late afternoon. Viewers at the time saw it as a peaceful escape from crowded industrial cities.

words.definition: Lacking knowledge or awareness.
words.usage: 'Ignorant of' a fact; not necessarily an insult.
examples: Early sailors were ignorant of the continent's existence.

sat.passage: Many early sailors were ignorant of the cause of scurvy. They did not know that the disease came from a lack of vitamin C, so voyages often lost large portions of their crews before anyone thought to bring citrus fruit aboard.

words.definition: To light up; to help clarify or explain.
examples: The letters illuminate the author's thinking.

sat.passage: Letters discovered in an attic help illuminate the life of a nineteenth-century mapmaker about whom little was known. In them, she describes her surveying trips, her disputes with publishers, and her methods for drawing coastlines accurately.

words.definition: A false idea or belief; something that deceives the senses.
words.usage: Optical illusions; the illusion of safety.
examples: The mirror created the illusion of a larger room.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Visitors to the exhibit see what appears to be a deep tunnel cut into the gallery wall. The effect is an illusion: the "tunnel" is painted on a flat surface, with carefully shaded lines that trick the eye into perceiving depth.

words.definition: To explain or make clear by using examples; to provide pictures for.
words.usage: Common in questions about what an example demonstrates.
examples: The author uses the story of the lost dog to illustrate the town's kindness.

sat.passage: To illustrate how quickly bacteria can multiply, the teacher placed a single grain of rice on the first square of a chessboard, two on the second, and four on the third. Students soon realized that the final squares would require more rice than exists on Earth.

words.definition: To copy the behavior or style of another.
examples: Young birds imitate the songs of adult birds.

sat.passage: Young songbirds learn their calls by listening to adult males and trying to imitate them. A zebra finch raised in isolation, without a tutor to copy, produces a song that sounds noticeably different from those of wild birds.

words.definition: About to happen very soon.
examples: Dark clouds warned of an imminent storm.

sat.passage: When seismometers detected swarms of small earthquakes beneath the volcano and the ground near its summit began to bulge, scientists concluded that an eruption was imminent. Officials ordered nearby villages evacuated within twenty-four hours.

words.definition: Protected from a disease; not affected by something.
examples: No one is immune to the effects of stress.

sat.passage: Unlike most of her competitors, the champion seemed immune to pressure. Whether she was leading comfortably or facing match point, she played each shot with the same calm focus.

words.definition: Treating all sides equally; not biased.
examples: An impartial panel reviewed the competing proposals.

sat.passage: Because both teams had accused previous referees of favoritism, the league brought in an official from another country for the final match. Fans on both sides agreed that he was impartial, applying the rules equally no matter which team committed a foul.

words.definition: A situation in which no progress is possible.
examples: Talks reached an impasse over wages.

sat.passage: After three weeks of talks, negotiators for the union and the company reached an impasse. Neither side would budge on wages, and both rejected a mediator's compromise, so the discussions were suspended indefinitely.

words.definition: Not feeling or showing emotion.
examples: The guard remained impassive as tourists joked.

sat.passage: Throughout the trial, the defendant remained impassive. Even as witnesses described the crime in vivid detail and the jury announced its verdict, his face showed neither fear nor relief.

words.definition: To delay or prevent by obstructing.
examples: Fallen trees impeded traffic on the highway.

sat.passage: Fallen trees and debris continued to impede the flow of the river after the storm. Water backed up behind the blockages, flooding nearby fields until crews could clear the channel.

words.definition: About to happen, often something unpleasant.
words.usage: Often with storms, deadlines, or crises.
examples: Birds fell silent before the impending storm.

sat.passage: Dark clouds gathered over the harbor, and the wind shifted sharply to the east. Sensing the impending storm, fishermen hauled their boats onto the beach and tied down their nets.

words.definition: Impossible to pass through or enter; impossible to understand.
examples: The legal document was written in nearly impenetrable language.

sat.passage: The insurance contract was nearly impenetrable to ordinary customers. Written in dense legal language with sentences running half a page, it left many policyholders unsure what their coverage actually included.

words.definition: Of vital importance; essential.
examples: It is imperative that we act quickly.

sat.passage: Because the vaccine must be kept below -70°C, it is imperative that clinics have specialized freezers. If the doses warm even briefly, they can lose their effectiveness and must be thrown away.

words.definition: So slight or gradual that it cannot be noticed.
words.usage: Describes very small or slow changes.
examples: The continents move at an imperceptible rate.

sat.passage: The glacier's movement is imperceptible to a person standing on it; the ice advances only a few centimeters each day. Over decades, however, that slow creep carries boulders many kilometers down the valley.

words.definition: Not seeming reasonable or probable; hard to believe.
words.usage: Opposite of plausible; describes explanations and claims.
examples: The suspect's story seemed implausible to the detectives.

sat.passage: The defendant claimed that a stranger had broken into the locked office, taken the files, and relocked the door without leaving fingerprints or appearing on any security camera. Jurors found the story implausible and quickly returned a guilty verdict.

words.definition: (v.) To put a plan or decision into effect; (n.) a tool.
words.usage: As a verb, used for policies, programs, and systems.
examples: The school implemented a new recycling program in the fall.

sat.passage: After the city council approved the new recycling program, officials had six months to implement it. They distributed bins to every household, hired additional drivers, and launched an advertising campaign to explain the new rules.

words.definition: To show to be involved in a crime or cause.
examples: The study implicated poor diet in the illness.

sat.passage: Investigators examining the warehouse fire found evidence that seemed to implicate the building's owner. Records showed he had recently tripled his insurance coverage, and a witness had seen his car parked nearby shortly before the flames appeared.

words.definition: Implied though not directly expressed.
examples: There was an implicit criticism in her polite reply.

sat.passage: Although the club's rules never stated that members had to wear formal clothing, the expectation was implicit: newcomers who arrived in jeans received disapproving glances and were rarely invited back. No one had to say a word for the message to be understood.

words.definition: To suggest without stating directly.
examples: Her silence seemed to imply disapproval.

sat.passage: The author never directly states that the narrator's father has lost his job. However, by describing how he leaves the house each morning in a suit and then spends the day sitting alone in a park, she seems to imply it.

words.definition: Importance or significance; also, a good brought in from another country.
words.usage: The SAT tests the meaning 'significance' (a discovery of great import).
examples: Few realized the import of the letter until decades later.

sat.passage: At first, few scholars recognized the import of the clay tablets uncovered in the desert. Only after linguists deciphered them, revealing the earliest known written laws of the region, did the tablets' value to historians become clear.

words.definition: To force something unwelcome on someone.
examples: The city imposed a curfew.

sat.passage: To reduce traffic in the historic center, the city decided to impose a fee on drivers entering downtown during weekday rush hours. Many shop owners objected, arguing that the charge would drive customers to suburban malls.

words.definition: Made poor; deprived of strength or quality.
examples: The program helps impoverished families.

sat.passage: Decades of growing the same crop year after year left the farmland impoverished. Stripped of nitrogen and other nutrients, the soil produced smaller harvests each season until farmers began rotating crops and planting clover.

words.definition: Lacking exactness or accuracy.
examples: Early maps of the coastline were imprecise.

sat.passage: Early clocks were notoriously imprecise; some gained or lost as much as fifteen minutes a day. Sailors who relied on them to calculate longitude could end up far off course.

words.definition: A sudden strong urge to act; a signal in a nerve.
examples: He bought the guitar on impulse.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Standing in the checkout line, Maya felt a sudden impulse to buy the glossy magazine, though she had not planned to. She resisted, reminding herself that she was saving for a new bicycle.

words.definition: Not engaging in activity; not working.
words.usage: Describes volcanoes, accounts, and organisms in dormancy.
examples: The volcano has been inactive for centuries.

sat.passage: Geologists classify the volcano as inactive: it has not erupted in more than ten thousand years and shows no signs of rising magma. Still, they continue to monitor it, since even long-quiet volcanoes occasionally reawaken.

words.definition: Lacking the quality or quantity required; insufficient.
examples: The shelter's supplies were inadequate for the number of visitors.

sat.passage: The town's water treatment plant was built for twenty thousand residents. Now that the population has tripled, the plant's capacity has become inadequate, and during dry summers officials must ask residents to limit their water use.

words.definition: Not resulting from deliberate planning; unintentional.
words.usage: Usually describes mistakes or side effects; adverb 'inadvertently' is common.
examples: The researchers inadvertently discovered a new species while studying soil samples.

sat.passage: The chemist's most famous discovery was inadvertent. While trying to make a new adhesive, she spilled a compound on her shoe and noticed that it repelled water and oil, a property that later made it valuable for stain-resistant fabrics.

words.definition: Not promising success; unlucky.
examples: The rainstorm was an inauspicious start to the parade.

sat.passage: The expedition got off to an inauspicious start. On the first day, a supply truck broke down, two members fell ill, and a storm forced the team to wait in a roadside motel for nearly a week.

words.definition: Something that motivates or encourages action.
examples: Tax credits gave homeowners an incentive to install solar panels.

sat.passage: To encourage residents to install solar panels, the state offered an incentive: homeowners who added panels could deduct a third of the installation cost from their taxes. Within five years, the number of rooftop systems had quadrupled.

words.definition: Continuing without pause.
examples: The incessant barking kept us awake.

sat.passage: For three months, the incessant hammering from the building site next door made it nearly impossible for the writer to concentrate. The noise began at seven each morning and did not stop until dusk, even on weekends.

words.definition: The occurrence or frequency of something, especially something unwanted.
words.usage: Common with disease (the incidence of flu).
examples: The incidence of asthma has risen in cities.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: After the town began adding fluoride to its drinking water, dentists reported a sharp drop in the incidence of tooth decay among children. The number of cavities per child fell by nearly half within a decade.

words.definition: An event or occurrence, often an unusual or unpleasant one.
words.usage: Neutral word for a specific happening.
examples: The incident led to new safety rules at the factory.

sat.passage: Airport officials reported a minor incident on Tuesday morning when a baggage cart rolled onto a taxiway. No one was injured, but two departing flights were delayed for about twenty minutes while crews moved the cart.

words.definition: Happening as a minor side effect; secondary.
examples: The discovery of the new species was incidental to a study of soil.

sat.passage: For the photographer, the birds in the picture were incidental; she had set up her camera to capture the old lighthouse at sunset, and the flock simply happened to fly through the frame. Critics, however, praised the birds as the image's most striking feature.

words.definition: Intelligently sharp and direct.
examples: Her incisive questions exposed the flaw in the plan.

sat.passage: The reviewer's incisive critique identified, in just a few paragraphs, the three weaknesses in the study's design that other readers had missed. The authors later thanked her for pointing them toward a more convincing experiment.

words.definition: To encourage or stir up violent or unlawful behavior.
examples: The speech incited the crowd.

sat.passage: The governor accused the pamphlet's authors of trying to incite a riot. Its pages urged readers to gather outside the courthouse armed with clubs and to "take justice into their own hands" if the verdict displeased them.

words.definition: (v.) To lean or tend toward; (n.) a slope.
words.usage: 'Inclined to' means likely to or tending to.
examples: I'm inclined to agree with your conclusion.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Because they had been treated unfairly by previous landlords, many tenants were inclined to distrust the new management company's promises. Only after the company repaired long-neglected heating systems did residents begin to believe it.

words.definition: The act of including or being included.
words.usage: Used for groups, lists, and social policy.
examples: The inclusion of new data changed the results.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The anthology's editors drew praise for their inclusion of writers who had long been overlooked, such as poets who published only in small regional magazines. Many readers encountered these voices for the first time in its pages.

words.definition: Not in harmony with its surroundings; out of place.
words.usage: Describes details, objects, or behavior that seem strangely mismatched.
examples: A modern glass building looked incongruous among the old stone cottages.

sat.passage: In the middle of the quiet nineteenth-century village stood an incongruous sight: a glass-and-steel office tower, twenty stories tall, surrounded by thatched cottages and cobblestone lanes. Visitors often stopped to photograph the odd contrast.

words.definition: Not important or significant.
words.usage: Often 'inconsequential to'. Used to dismiss minor details or effects.
examples: The error turned out to be inconsequential to the final results.

sat.passage: The editor told the young reporter to cut the paragraph describing the color of the mayor's tie. Such inconsequential details, she explained, distracted readers from the story's real subject: a budget shortfall that threatened to close two fire stations.

words.definition: To include as part of a whole.
words.usage: Used for ideas, materials, and suggestions.
examples: The architect incorporated local stone into the design.

sat.passage: When redesigning the museum, the architects chose to incorporate parts of the original 1890s structure into the new building. The old brick facade now forms one wall of the glass atrium, and iron columns from the former train shed support its roof.

words.definition: Unwilling or unable to believe something.
examples: She gave an incredulous laugh at the excuse.

sat.passage: When the young astronomer announced that she had found a comet with her backyard telescope, her colleagues were incredulous. Only after observatories around the world confirmed the sighting did they accept that an amateur instrument had made the discovery.

words.definition: (n.) The current holder of an office; (adj.) necessary as a duty.
words.usage: 'It is incumbent on you' means it is your duty.
examples: The incumbent mayor won a second term.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the city's mayoral race, the incumbent enjoyed several advantages over her challengers. Having already served two terms, she was well known to voters and could point to new parks and repaired roads completed under her leadership.

words.definition: Impossible to read or understand.
words.usage: Used for handwriting, codes, and ancient scripts.
examples: The scribe's faded notes were nearly indecipherable.

sat.passage: The letters were written in a faded, cramped script, and water damage had blurred many lines, leaving large portions indecipherable. Archivists later used infrared imaging to recover some of the missing words.

words.definition: Lack of interest, concern, or sympathy.
words.usage: Often 'indifference to'. Suggests not caring either way.
examples: The cat watched the commotion with complete indifference.

sat.passage: The scientist's warnings about the polluted river were met with indifference. Local officials neither disputed her data nor acted on it, and the factory continued releasing waste for another decade.

words.definition: Showing no interest or concern; neither good nor bad.
examples: The crowd seemed indifferent to the speaker's passionate appeal.

sat.passage: Most of the students were eager to join the field trip to the planetarium, but Theo seemed indifferent. He shrugged when asked whether he wanted to go and spent the bus ride reading a comic book without glancing out the window.

words.definition: Originating or occurring naturally in a particular place; native.
words.usage: Used for peoples, plants, and animals.
examples: The plant is indigenous to the Andes.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Ecologists restoring the prairie removed invasive grasses introduced from Europe and replanted species indigenous to the region, such as big bluestem and purple coneflower. Within a few seasons, native bees and butterflies returned.

words.definition: Angry at something perceived as unfair.
examples: She was indignant at the false accusation.

sat.passage: Residents were indignant when they learned that the council had quietly approved a landfill next to the elementary school without holding a single public hearing. Hundreds packed the next meeting to protest what they called an unfair and secretive decision.

words.definition: To bring about or cause; to persuade.
words.usage: Used in medicine and science (induce sleep).
examples: The medication can induce drowsiness.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Doctors sometimes use medication to induce sleep in patients recovering from serious head injuries. Keeping the brain at rest, they believe, can reduce swelling and give damaged tissue time to heal.

words.definition: Allowing pleasures freely; lenient.
examples: Her indulgent grandparents spoiled her.

sat.passage: The grandparents were famously indulgent with the children: they allowed second helpings of dessert, let bedtimes stretch past midnight, and rarely said no to any request. The children's parents sometimes worried that each visit undid months of careful rules.

words.definition: Hardworking.
examples: Ants are famously industrious.

sat.passage: Beavers are among the most industrious animals in North America. A single family may cut down hundreds of trees in a year, hauling branches and mud to build dams that can stretch more than a hundred meters.

words.definition: Not producing any significant or desired effect.
examples: The old pesticide became ineffective as insects developed resistance.

sat.passage: Early efforts to control an invasive water plant on a large tropical lake relied on crews cutting it by hand. The approach proved ineffective: the weed regrew faster than workers could clear it, and within months the shorelines were choked again. Only after officials released a beetle that feeds on the plant did the floating mats begin to shrink.

words.definition: Lacking skill; clumsy.
examples: The inept repairs made the leak worse.

sat.passage: In the novel's opening chapter, Marguerite takes her first job at a busy bakery and quickly proves inept in the kitchen. She drops trays of rolls, confuses customers' orders, and twice forgets to set the oven timer, leaving loaves blackened. Yet by the final chapter, she runs the shop herself.

words.definition: Difference in size, degree, or circumstances, especially unfair difference.
words.usage: Common in economics and social studies passages.
examples: The report examined income inequality across states.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Economists studying a mid-sized city found that between 1980 and 2010 the wealthiest tenth of households saw their incomes nearly double, while incomes for the poorest tenth barely changed. This widening inequality was visible in housing as well: new luxury apartments rose downtown even as families in older neighborhoods struggled to pay rent.

words.definition: Certain to happen; unavoidable.
words.usage: Describes outcomes that can't be prevented.
examples: With so much rain, flooding was inevitable.

sat.passage: The coastal town's lighthouse stood on a sandy bluff that lost several feet to erosion each year, so engineers concluded that its collapse into the sea was inevitable unless the tower was moved. In 1999 crews lifted it onto rails and rolled it nearly half a mile inland, where it still stands.

words.definition: Impossible to stop or prevent.
examples: The glacier's inexorable advance buried the valley.

sat.passage: Glaciers may appear motionless, but they advance with inexorable force, grinding down bedrock and carrying boulders the size of houses for miles. Over thousands of years, this slow but unstoppable movement carved many of the deep valleys and lakes found across northern Europe.

words.definition: Incapable of making mistakes or being wrong.
words.usage: Often used to deny something is perfect (no test is infallible).
examples: Even experienced doctors are not infallible.

sat.passage: Fingerprint analysis was long treated by courts as nearly infallible, and examiners often testified with total certainty that a print matched a suspect. Recent reviews, however, have documented cases in which skilled examiners made incorrect matches, prompting calls for clearer standards and regular testing of error rates.

words.definition: To reach a conclusion from evidence and reasoning rather than direct statement.
examples: From the faded handwriting, historians inferred that the letter was very old.

sat.passage: Archaeologists excavating an ancient settlement found no written records describing what its residents ate. From the charred barley grains, fish bones, and grinding stones scattered across the site, however, the team was able to infer that the community relied on both farming and fishing.

words.definition: A conclusion reached from evidence and reasoning.
words.usage: Key reading skill: making inferences from a text.
examples: From the muddy boots, she drew the inference that he had been outside.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The poem never states the speaker's age, but readers can draw a reasonable inference from its details: she remembers the town before its highway was built, and she describes her grandchildren visiting each summer. Together, these clues suggest that she is an older woman looking back on her life.

words.definition: Lower in rank, status, or quality.
examples: The copy was inferior to the original painting.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)
