sat.passage: When cheap imported cloth flooded the market in the 1820s, local weavers complained that it was inferior to their own: the threads were loose, the dyes faded after a few washings, and the fabric tore easily. Many buyers, however, cared more about the low price than about durability.

words.definition: Not occurring often; rare.
examples: Rainfall in the desert is infrequent but intense.

sat.passage: In the high desert, rain is infrequent, sometimes falling only a handful of times in a year. Plants there have adapted accordingly: many store water in thick stems, and some seeds can lie dormant for years, sprouting only after a rare storm soaks the ground.

words.definition: Clever, original, and inventive.
examples: She came up with an ingenious way to purify water.

sat.passage: Lacking electricity, a rural community needed a way to keep vegetables fresh during hot summers. Its solution was ingenious: two clay pots, one nested inside the other, with wet sand packed between them. As water evaporated through the outer pot, it drew heat away from the inner one, cooling the food inside.

words.definition: Existing as a permanent, essential part.
examples: There are risks inherent in any surgery.

sat.passage: Some degree of uncertainty is inherent in every method of measurement. Even the most precise laboratory scale is affected by tiny vibrations and changes in air pressure, so scientists report their results with a range of possible error rather than pretending that any measurement is perfect.

words.definition: To receive money, property, or traits from a predecessor.
words.usage: Used for genetics, family property, and problems left by others.
examples: Children inherit many physical traits from their parents.

sat.passage: When the new mayor took office, she was forced to inherit a city budget deep in debt, along with a transit system that had gone without repairs for a decade. Neither problem was of her making, but voters expected her to solve both within her first term.

words.definition: To hinder or restrain; to make someone self-conscious.
words.usage: Used for growth, reactions, and behavior.
examples: Cold temperatures inhibit bacterial growth.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Some plants release chemicals into the soil that inhibit the growth of nearby competitors. Black walnut trees, for example, produce a compound called juglone, which prevents many other species from sprouting or thriving beneath their branches.

words.definition: Existing at the beginning.
examples: Initial reactions to the film were mixed.

sat.passage: The team's initial results seemed to show that the new fertilizer doubled crop yields. When the experiment was repeated on larger plots over three growing seasons, however, the benefit shrank to only a few percent, a reminder that early findings often need confirmation.

words.definition: To cause a process or action to begin.
words.usage: Used for projects, talks, and reactions.
examples: The city initiated a program to plant more trees.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In 1955, the arrest of a Black woman who refused to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus helped initiate a citywide boycott. For more than a year, tens of thousands of residents walked or shared rides rather than use the buses, until the courts ordered the system desegregated.

words.definition: Inborn; natural rather than learned.
examples: Many birds have an innate ability to navigate.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Newly hatched sea turtles, which never see their parents, crawl toward the ocean within minutes of emerging from their nests. Because no adult teaches them this behavior, biologists regard the hatchlings' attraction to the bright horizon over the water as innate rather than learned.

words.definition: Not harmful or offensive.
words.usage: Describes substances, remarks, or actions that seem harmless (sometimes misleadingly so).
examples: The question seemed innocuous, but it upset several guests.

sat.passage: To most people, the plant looks innocuous, with its delicate white flowers and feathery leaves. Yet every part of it is highly toxic, and eating even a small amount can be fatal, which is why botanists warn hikers never to forage for plants they cannot identify with certainty.

words.definition: To introduce new methods or ideas.
examples: Companies must innovate to survive.

sat.passage: During the 1800s, the textile mills of New England faced fierce competition and were under constant pressure to innovate. Owners who adopted new power looms and reorganized their factories around faster machinery thrived, while those who clung to older methods often went out of business.

words.definition: Featuring new methods; original.
examples: The school uses innovative teaching methods.

sat.passage: The architect's design for the library was widely praised as innovative. Instead of hiding the building's heating and ventilation ducts behind walls, she painted them bright colors and left them exposed, turning machinery that is usually concealed into a striking decorative feature.

words.definition: Curious; eager to learn.
examples: The inquisitive child asked endless questions.

sat.passage: As a child, the naturalist was so inquisitive that her parents struggled to keep up with her questions about why snails leave silver trails and where swallows go in winter. She filled notebook after notebook with observations, searching for answers that adults often could not give.

words.definition: Impossible to satisfy.
examples: She had an insatiable curiosity about the stars.

sat.passage: The young printer's appetite for books was insatiable. He borrowed volumes from every friend who would lend them, read late into the night by candlelight, and, no matter how many he finished, always went looking for the next.

words.definition: Unaware of or not responding to something; unconscious.
words.usage: Often 'insensible to' (insensible to pain or criticism). Not the same as 'not sensible.'
examples: Lost in thought, he was insensible to the noise around him.

sat.passage: Exhausted after three days without sleep, the climbers were nearly insensible to the cold by the time rescuers reached them. They no longer shivered or complained about their frostbitten fingers, a sign, doctors later explained, that their bodies had begun to shut down.

words.definition: Spreading harmfully in a subtle, gradual way.
words.usage: Often describes dangers that go unnoticed.
examples: The insidious effects of erosion went unnoticed for decades.

sat.passage: Lead poisoning is especially insidious because its early symptoms, such as fatigue and irritability, are easy to mistake for ordinary stress. Children in older homes may absorb small amounts from peeling paint for years before anyone notices the damage to their health.
sat.meaning: Harmful in a gradual, hidden way

words.definition: A deep understanding of a person or thing.
examples: The diary offers insight into daily life during the war.

sat.passage: Long overlooked by historians, the diaries of ordinary factory workers offer valuable insight into daily life during industrialization. Their entries describe sixteen-hour shifts, crowded boardinghouses, and small pleasures such as Sunday walks, details rarely found in official reports.

words.definition: Showing deep understanding.
examples: The critic wrote an insightful review.

sat.passage: Critics initially dismissed the film as a simple comedy, but later reviewers found it insightful. They noted that its jokes about a family's dinner-table arguments revealed, with surprising depth, how members of different generations misunderstand one another's values.

words.definition: To look at closely to assess condition or find flaws.
words.usage: Used for buildings, products, and documents.
examples: Officials inspected the bridge after the earthquake.

sat.passage: Before a bridge is reopened after a major flood, engineers inspect its supports for damage. They look closely for cracks in the concrete, measure whether any piers have shifted, and check whether swift water has washed away the soil around the foundations.

words.definition: The state of being likely to change or fail suddenly.
words.usage: Used for governments, markets, and structures.
examples: Political instability scared away investors.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the decades after it won independence, the country experienced severe political instability, with six different governments rising and falling in just fifteen years. Frequent changes in leadership made long-term planning nearly impossible, and foreign investors hesitated to commit money to projects that a new regime might cancel.

words.definition: To bring about or initiate, often trouble.
examples: Who instigated the argument?

sat.passage: Court records from 1786 show that the farmers were charged with having helped instigate the uprising. Prosecutors argued that the men had organized meetings, drafted angry petitions, and urged their neighbors to close the courthouses by force.

words.definition: An inborn pattern of behavior; a natural tendency.
words.usage: Used for animals and gut feelings in people.
examples: Sea turtles head toward the ocean by instinct.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: A newly hatched cuckoo, laid in another bird's nest, will push its host's eggs out of the nest within hours, even though it has never seen this done. Ornithologists attribute the behavior to instinct, since the chick has had no opportunity to learn it.

words.definition: (v.) To set up or start a policy or system; (n.) an organization.
words.usage: As a verb, used for rules, programs, and reforms.
examples: The school instituted a new dress code.

sat.passage: Alarmed by a rise in drowning deaths, the town council voted to institute a new policy requiring trained lifeguards at every public beach during the summer. Within two years of the rule taking effect, the number of drownings had fallen by half.

words.definition: Necessary to make a whole complete; essential.
words.usage: Often 'integral to'. Signals that a part is central, not optional.
examples: Bees are integral to the pollination of many crops.

sat.passage: Bees are integral to almond farming: almond trees cannot produce nuts without cross-pollination, so growers rent hundreds of thousands of beehives each spring. Without the insects, an industry worth billions of dollars would collapse.

words.definition: To combine into a whole; to bring into equal membership.
examples: The new system integrates data from many sensors.

sat.passage: The curriculum's designers wanted students to integrate what they learned in different subjects rather than treat each class separately. In one project, students used math to analyze water samples, wrote reports on their findings, and studied the history of the local river.

words.definition: Honesty and strong moral principles; wholeness.
examples: The judge was known for her integrity.

sat.passage: The reporter's integrity was tested when a wealthy businessman offered her a large sum to drop a story about his company's pollution. She refused the money, published the article, and later reported the attempted bribe to her editor.

words.definition: Extreme in degree or strength; deeply felt.
words.usage: Describes heat, emotion, effort, or focus.
examples: The two teams shared an intense rivalry that lasted decades.

sat.passage: During the eruption, the heat near the volcano's vent was so intense that it melted the instruments scientists had placed nearby. Readings taken from a safer distance suggested temperatures well above 1,000 degrees Celsius.

words.definition: The quality of being strong, extreme, or concentrated.
words.usage: Used for light, emotions, and storms.
examples: The storm increased in intensity overnight.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Hurricanes are classified by the intensity of their sustained winds. A Category 1 storm has winds of at least 74 miles per hour, whereas a Category 5 storm, the most powerful, brings winds of 157 miles per hour or more.

words.definition: Done on purpose; deliberate.
examples: The author's repetition of the phrase is intentional.

sat.passage: At first, viewers assumed the cracks running across the painting's surface were damage caused by age. Conservators discovered, however, that they were intentional: the artist had mixed a special drying agent into the paint so that it would split as it dried, creating the look of an ancient fresco.

words.definition: Able to be exchanged for each other without making a difference.
words.usage: Describes parts, terms, or roles that can substitute for one another.
examples: The two words are not interchangeable, despite their similar meanings.

sat.passage: Before the early 1800s, each musket was made by hand, so a broken part had to be custom-fitted by a skilled gunsmith. Manufacturers then began producing interchangeable components, built to such exact specifications that a part from one musket could replace the same part in any other.
sat.meaning: Able to substitute for one another

words.definition: Mutually joined or related.
words.usage: Describes systems, ideas, and networks whose parts affect one another.
examples: Climate, oceans, and ecosystems are deeply interconnected.

sat.passage: Ecologists describe the forest as a deeply interconnected system. Fungi in the soil link the roots of different trees, allowing them to exchange water and nutrients, so damage to one part of the network can affect organisms far away.

words.definition: To get in the way of; to involve oneself without invitation.
examples: Noise can interfere with concentration.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Light pollution from cities can interfere with the migration of birds that navigate by the stars. On cloudy nights, flocks drawn toward brightly lit buildings sometimes circle for hours, exhausting themselves or colliding with windows.

words.definition: Coming between two things in time, place, or order.
words.usage: Used for levels, stages, and forms.
examples: The fossil shows features intermediate between fish and amphibians.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Fossils record the gradual transition of whales from land to sea. One species, which had four legs but also nostrils positioned partway up its snout, represents an intermediate stage between fully land-dwelling ancestors and modern whales, whose blowholes sit atop their heads.

words.definition: To explain the meaning of; to understand in a particular way.
words.usage: Used for data, texts, and behavior.
examples: Scientists interpret the rock layers as evidence of ancient floods.

sat.passage: Two historians reading the same letter can interpret it very differently. One may see the general's cheerful tone as a sign of confidence before the battle, while another may read it as an attempt to hide his fears from his family.

words.definition: A stretch of time or space between two events or points.
words.usage: Regular intervals means evenly spaced in time.
examples: Readings were recorded at ten-minute intervals throughout the night.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Old Faithful, a geyser in Yellowstone National Park, erupts at fairly predictable times. Rangers estimate the interval between eruptions, which typically ranges from about an hour to an hour and a half, by measuring how long the previous eruption lasted.

words.definition: To come between to prevent or alter a result.
words.usage: Used for governments, teachers, and events.
examples: The teacher intervened before the argument escalated.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: When two neighboring towns could not agree on how to share water from the river, state officials decided to intervene. They appointed an engineer to measure the river's flow and divided the water according to each town's population, ending a dispute that had lasted a decade.

words.definition: Fearless; adventurous.
examples: The intrepid explorer crossed the Arctic alone.

sat.passage: Few wildlife photographers would attempt the shot, but the intrepid Ana Ruiz was undeterred. She spent three weeks camped on a narrow ledge hundreds of feet above the ground, braving storms and freezing winds to capture images of nesting eagles.

words.definition: Very complicated or detailed.
words.usage: Used for patterns, designs, plots, and systems.
examples: The quilt featured an intricate pattern of interlocking stars.

sat.passage: Viewed under a microscope, a single snowflake reveals an intricate structure: six branching arms, each covered in smaller branches that are themselves lined with tinier crystals. No two flakes appear to share exactly the same pattern of detail.

words.definition: Arousing curiosity or interest; fascinating.
words.usage: Describes puzzles, findings, and possibilities worth exploring.
examples: The scientists found an intriguing link between sleep and memory.

sat.passage: Astronomers find Jupiter's moon Europa especially intriguing. Beneath its icy crust lies what appears to be a vast ocean of liquid water, raising the possibility that the moon could support some form of life.

words.definition: Belonging naturally; essential.
examples: The ring has little intrinsic value but great sentimental value.

sat.passage: Psychologists distinguish between rewards that come from outside, such as grades or money, and those that are intrinsic to an activity itself. A child who practices the piano simply because she enjoys making music is driven by the latter, while one who practices only to earn a prize is driven by the former.

words.definition: To flood; to overwhelm with things.
examples: The office was inundated with complaints.

sat.passage: After the newspaper published an article about the abandoned puppies, the animal shelter was inundated with calls. Its two volunteers spent the next week answering hundreds of inquiries from families eager to adopt.

words.definition: To enter forcefully as an enemy; to spread into.
words.usage: Used for armies and invasive species.
examples: Non-native plants invaded the wetlands.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Each spring, swarms of desert locusts can invade farmland across North Africa, devouring crops in a matter of hours. A single swarm may contain billions of insects and travel more than a hundred kilometers in one day.

words.definition: Not legally or logically acceptable; not true or correct.
words.usage: Invalid arguments, tickets, or results (pronounced in-VAL-id).
examples: The ticket was invalid because it had expired.

sat.passage: The researchers later discovered that their thermometer had been miscalibrated throughout the study, recording every temperature three degrees too high. As a result, they declared their conclusions invalid and repeated the experiment with new equipment.

words.definition: To carry out a systematic inquiry to discover facts.
words.usage: Used for crimes, scientific questions, and causes.
examples: The team investigated why the frogs were disappearing.

sat.passage: When dozens of residents of the town fell ill after a church picnic, public health officials set out to investigate the cause. By interviewing attendees about what they had eaten and testing leftover food, they traced the outbreak to a batch of potato salad.

words.definition: To give strength or energy to.
examples: The cold swim invigorated her.

sat.passage: After a long winter of declining attendance, the museum's directors hoped a new interactive dinosaur exhibit would invigorate public interest. The plan worked: within a month, visitor numbers had nearly doubled, and school groups were booking tours months in advance.

words.definition: To call on as support or authority; to bring to mind.
words.usage: Invoke a law, a memory, or a principle.
examples: The lawyer invoked her client's right to remain silent.

sat.passage: In their petition to the king, the colonists did not argue merely that the new tax was unwise. They chose to invoke the ancient rights of English subjects, claiming that a Parliament in which they had no representatives could not lawfully tax them.

words.definition: Done without will or conscious control.
words.usage: Describes reflexes and actions one can't help; adverb 'involuntarily'.
examples: Shivering is an involuntary response to cold.

sat.passage: Shivering is an involuntary response to cold: the muscles contract and relax rapidly without any conscious decision, generating heat that helps warm the body. Just as no one decides to blink when dust hits the eye, no one chooses to begin shivering.

words.definition: A contrast between expectation and reality; saying the opposite of what is meant.
examples: The irony is that the fire station burned down.

sat.passage: The irony of the situation was not lost on the town's residents: the fire station, built to protect the community from blazes, burned to the ground after a faulty heater caught fire one winter night. Firefighters had to call in trucks from a neighboring town to put it out.

words.definition: Not connected with or important to the matter at hand.
examples: The lawyer argued that the evidence was irrelevant.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The lawyer objected that the witness's testimony about the defendant's childhood was irrelevant to the case. The trial, she argued, concerned only whether the defendant had signed the contract in question, not the details of his upbringing.

words.definition: Showing a lack of respect for serious things.
examples: The comedian's irreverent humor mocked politicians.

sat.passage: The magazine became famous for its irreverent humor, regularly mocking politicians, celebrities, and even its own editors. Readers who expected serious commentary were sometimes offended, but younger audiences loved its playful refusal to treat anyone as untouchable.

words.definition: To set apart or separate from others; to identify a single factor.
words.usage: In science, means separating a substance or variable for study.
examples: The chemists isolated the compound responsible for the plant's scent.

sat.passage: To determine which ingredient in willow bark relieved pain, chemists needed to isolate the active compound. After separating the bark's many substances one by one and testing each, they identified salicin, a chemical later used to develop aspirin.

words.definition: Having or showing good judgment.
examples: The judicious use of water saved the crops.

sat.passage: With only a small budget for the season, the theater's director had to be judicious in her spending. She reused sets from earlier productions, borrowed costumes from a local college, and saved most of her funds for hiring experienced actors.

words.definition: The official power to make legal decisions; the area of authority.
examples: The case is outside the court's jurisdiction.

sat.passage: Because the crime occurred on a ship in international waters, local police lacked jurisdiction in the case. Instead, it was handled by authorities in the country where the ship was registered.

words.definition: A good reason for something.
words.usage: Used for decisions, claims, and actions.
examples: There was no justification for the delay.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The governor's decision to close the state's parks was widely criticized, since officials offered no justification for it. Only weeks later did they explain that the closures were meant to save money during a budget crisis.

words.definition: To show or prove to be right or reasonable.
words.usage: Used for decisions, costs, and claims.
examples: The results justified the high cost of the study.

sat.passage: Building the new highway would cost nearly two billion dollars, and critics questioned whether the expected reduction in traffic could justify such an expense. Supporters responded that shorter commutes would save drivers millions of hours each year.

words.definition: To place side by side for contrasting effect.
words.usage: Noun 'juxtaposition'; common in literature and art.
examples: The photo juxtaposes wealth and poverty.

sat.passage: In the exhibit, the curators chose to juxtapose a glittering ball gown from the 1890s with the patched work clothes of a factory seamstress from the same decade. Seen side by side, the two garments reveal the vast gap between rich and poor in that era.

words.definition: Using very few words.
examples: The laconic cowboy answered with a nod.

sat.passage: The ranch foreman was famously laconic. When a visiting reporter asked him to describe the worst blizzard he had survived, he considered the question for a long moment and answered with a single word.

words.definition: To express sorrow or regret.
examples: The author laments the loss of small farms.

sat.passage: In her letters home, the young settler would often lament the loss of the bustling city she had left behind. She wrote longingly of crowded markets and evening concerts, which seemed very far from her quiet cabin on the prairie.

words.definition: Existing but not yet developed, visible, or active.
words.usage: Describes hidden talents, potential, or dormant infections.
examples: The virus can remain latent in the body for years.

sat.passage: The virus that causes chickenpox does not leave the body after the illness ends. Instead, it remains latent in nerve cells, sometimes for decades, and may reactivate in old age as the painful condition known as shingles.

words.definition: Deserving praise.
examples: Reducing waste is a laudable goal.

sat.passage: The city's goal of planting one million trees by 2030 is laudable, and few residents oppose it. Critics point out, however, that the plan sets aside no money for watering the young trees, many of which may die before reaching maturity.

words.definition: Rich, elaborate, or generous; (v.) to give generously.
examples: The king threw a lavish feast.

sat.passage: The merchant spent his fortune on a lavish mansion with marble staircases, gilded ceilings, and gardens filled with imported statues. Neighbors who lived in plain farmhouses nearby regarded the extravagant home with a mix of envy and disapproval.

words.definition: Something handed down from the past.
examples: Her legacy includes three hospitals.

sat.passage: The architect died in 1959, but her legacy endures in the dozens of schools she designed across the region. Their wide windows and open courtyards, revolutionary at the time, still shape how many communities think about learning spaces.

words.definition: Conforming to the law or rules; able to be defended with logic; valid.
words.usage: Describes claims, concerns, and authorities that are reasonable or lawful.
examples: Residents raised legitimate concerns about traffic near the school.

sat.passage: Residents who complained that the new factory would pollute the river raised a legitimate concern: a similar plant upstream had leaked chemicals into the water just five years earlier. Officials agreed to require additional safety inspections before the factory could open.

words.definition: Sluggish and lacking energy.
examples: The heat made everyone lethargic.

sat.passage: Reptiles cannot generate much of their own body heat, so on cold mornings a lizard is often lethargic, moving slowly and reacting only weakly to threats. Only after basking in the sun for some time does it become quick enough to chase insects.

words.definition: To impose a tax or fine.
examples: The king decided to levy a tax on salt.

sat.passage: To pay off its war debts, the government decided to levy a tax on imported tea, paper, and glass. Colonial merchants protested by refusing to buy British goods, and many of the duties were eventually repealed.

words.definition: Legally responsible; likely to do something.
words.usage: 'Liable to' means likely; 'liable for' means responsible.
examples: Old bridges are liable to collapse in earthquakes.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Old wooden bridges are liable to rot where water collects in their joints, so inspectors pay special attention to these areas. Even a small patch of decay can weaken a beam enough to make the structure unsafe.

words.definition: The state of being likely; probability.
words.usage: Used in science and everyday reasoning.
examples: Exercise reduces the likelihood of heart disease.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Doctors have long known that regular exercise reduces the likelihood of heart disease. In one long-term study, adults who walked briskly for thirty minutes a day were about a third less likely to develop the condition than those who rarely exercised.

words.definition: In the same way; also.
examples: The first study found no effect; likewise, the second.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Many desert mammals, such as the kangaroo rat, rarely drink water, obtaining most of the moisture they need from the seeds they eat. Some desert birds likewise get much of their water from food, surviving for long periods without visiting a spring.

words.definition: Of imposing height; noble; haughty.
examples: The school has lofty ambitions for its students.

sat.passage: The founders of the small college had lofty ambitions: they hoped it would one day rival the great universities of Europe, attracting the world's finest scholars. For its first decade, however, the school occupied a single rented building and enrolled fewer than forty students.

words.definition: Clear and easy to understand; thinking clearly.
examples: The textbook gives a lucid explanation of gravity.

sat.passage: Although the physicist's research dealt with highly complex mathematics, her lectures for the general public were remarkably lucid. She explained difficult ideas using everyday comparisons, and listeners with no scientific training left feeling they had understood her.

words.definition: Producing a great deal of profit.
examples: The spice trade was extremely lucrative for medieval merchants.

sat.passage: In the early nineteenth century, the fur trade was so lucrative that companies competed fiercely for access to the forests of the North American interior. A single shipment of beaver pelts sold in Europe could earn enough to finance an entire expedition.

words.definition: Generous or forgiving, especially toward a rival.
examples: The winner was magnanimous toward her opponent.

sat.passage: After winning the election by a wide margin, the new president was magnanimous toward her defeated opponent. She praised his years of public service and invited him to lead a commission on education reform.

words.definition: Great size or importance; a measured size.
words.usage: Used for earthquakes, problems, and numbers.
examples: No one grasped the magnitude of the discovery.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Seismologists rank earthquakes by their magnitude, a measure of the energy released at the source. Each step up the scale represents about thirty-two times more energy, so an earthquake rated 7 releases roughly a thousand times more energy than one rated 5.

words.definition: Easily shaped; easily influenced.
examples: Gold is a highly malleable metal.

sat.passage: Gold is the most malleable of all metals: a single gram can be hammered into a sheet so thin that light passes through it. Ancient artisans took advantage of this property to cover statues and manuscripts with delicate layers of gold leaf.

words.definition: An official order; authority given by voters.
examples: The state mandated seat belts in all cars.

sat.passage: After winning nearly seventy percent of the vote, the new governor claimed a mandate to overhaul the state's tax system. Opponents argued, however, that voters had chosen her mainly for her promises on education, not taxes.

words.definition: Required by law or rules; compulsory.
examples: Attendance at the safety training is mandatory for all staff.

sat.passage: In 1918 the last U.S. state passed a law making school attendance mandatory for children. Before such laws, many children worked on farms or in factories instead of attending classes, and families faced no penalty for keeping them home.

words.definition: (v.) To show or display clearly; (adj.) clear or obvious to the eye or mind.
words.usage: Often 'manifest in' or 'manifest itself'. The SAT has tested 'manifest' meaning 'visible/evident'.
examples: Her talent for music manifested itself at an early age.

sat.passage: The coach's frustration was manifest to everyone in the stadium: he paced the sideline, threw his clipboard to the ground, and shouted at the referees after nearly every call. Even fans in the highest seats could tell he was furious.

words.definition: To handle skillfully; to control or influence unfairly.
examples: Researchers manipulated one variable at a time.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Surgeons performing delicate eye operations often use robotic arms, which can manipulate instruments far smaller than a human hand could steadily hold. Each tiny movement of the surgeon's controls is scaled down, allowing extraordinary precision.

words.definition: Minor and not important; at the edge.
words.usage: Describes small effects and groups pushed to the edges.
examples: The change had only a marginal effect on sales.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The new fertilizer produced only a marginal improvement in crop yields, increasing harvests by less than two percent. Given its high price, most farmers decided it was not worth adopting.

words.definition: To treat as unimportant or powerless.
words.usage: Used for groups pushed to society's edges.
examples: The policy marginalized rural voices.

sat.passage: Historians note that official accounts of the town's founding tended to marginalize the contributions of women, mentioning them only in passing if at all. Recently discovered letters show that women ran several of the settlement's businesses and organized its first school.

words.definition: Fully developed; (v.) to become fully developed.
examples: The trees take ten years to mature.

sat.passage: Unlike many fish, which reach adulthood within a year or two, the Greenland shark may take more than a century to mature. Because individuals reproduce so late in life, populations that are overfished are likely to recover very slowly.

words.definition: Lacking in quantity or quality.
examples: The workers survived on meager wages.

sat.passage: Despite working twelve-hour days in the mill, the family earned meager wages that barely covered rent and bread. Meat appeared on their table only on holidays, and the children wore shoes passed down from older cousins.

words.definition: A system of parts working together; a process by which something happens.
words.usage: Used for machines and for natural or social processes.
examples: Scientists are studying the mechanism by which birds sense magnetic fields.

sat.passage: For decades, scientists knew that aspirin reduced pain and fever but did not understand its mechanism. In the 1970s, researchers discovered that the drug works by blocking the production of chemicals that the body releases in response to injury.

words.definition: To help two sides reach an agreement; to bring about a result.
examples: A neutral judge mediated the dispute.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: When contract talks between the factory's owners and its workers broke down, a retired judge was brought in to mediate. Meeting separately with each side over several weeks, she helped them reach a compromise on wages and working hours.

words.definition: A deep, pensive sadness.
examples: A melancholy song drifted from the window.

sat.passage: A gentle melancholy hangs over the novel's final chapter. The aging painter returns to the seaside village of his youth, walks the empty beach where he once sketched with friends now long gone, and quietly realizes that the life he remembers can never be recovered.

words.definition: To combine into one.
words.usage: Used for companies, roads, and ideas.
examples: The two rivers merge just south of the city.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: When two rivers merge, their waters do not always mix right away. Where the dark Rio Negro meets the sandy-colored Amazon, the two flows run side by side for several kilometers before finally blending into a single stream.

words.definition: A figure of speech describing one thing as if it were another.
examples: 'Time is a thief' is a metaphor.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the poem, the speaker never directly describes her grief. Instead, she relies on a metaphor, calling her sorrow "a house with every window shuttered," which suggests that the loss has closed her off from the world.

words.definition: Done in an orderly, systematic way.
examples: The detective's methodical search found the clue.

sat.passage: The detective was methodical in her approach to every case. She examined each room in the same order, labeled every piece of evidence, and refused to form a theory until she had reviewed all the facts.

words.definition: Showing great attention to detail; very careful.
examples: Her meticulous notes made the experiment easy to repeat.

sat.passage: Before the restoration began, the conservators made meticulous records of the damaged mural, photographing every square inch and noting the precise location of each crack and missing flake of paint. These records allowed them to track every change they later made.

words.definition: To move from one region to another, often seasonally.
examples: Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of miles.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Each autumn, millions of monarch butterflies migrate from Canada and the northern United States to forests in central Mexico, a journey of up to 4,800 kilometers. No single butterfly makes the round trip; the return north is completed by its descendants over several generations.

words.definition: To imitate the appearance, sound, or behavior of something.
words.usage: Common in biology (mimicry) and descriptions of copying.
examples: Some harmless snakes mimic the colors of venomous ones.

sat.passage: The harmless scarlet kingsnake has red, black, and yellow bands similar to those of the venomous coral snake. Because predators avoid the coral snake, the kingsnake's resemblance protects it, an example of how one species can mimic another to survive.

words.definition: Of the least possible amount; very small.
examples: The storm caused minimal damage.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Because the earthquake struck a sparsely populated region far from any major city, the damage was minimal: a few barns lost their roofs, and several roads cracked. Officials reported no serious injuries.

words.definition: Disliking or distrusting people in general.
words.usage: Describes characters or attitudes that avoid or scorn humanity.
examples: The misanthropic old man rarely left his cabin.

sat.passage: In the novel, the old lighthouse keeper is thoroughly misanthropic. He refuses visitors, leaves letters from his family unopened, and tells the one sailor who seeks shelter in a storm that he prefers the company of gulls to that of people.

words.definition: To interpret wrongly.
words.usage: Used for words, intentions, and actions that are misunderstood.
examples: Readers misconstrued the satire as a serious proposal.

sat.passage: When the scientist told reporters that the new drug "showed promise," some headlines misconstrued her remark as an announcement of a cure. In fact, she had meant only that early tests justified further study.

words.definition: To make less severe or painful.
words.usage: Common in environmental and policy passages.
examples: Planting trees can mitigate the effects of urban heat.

sat.passage: Planting trees along city streets can help mitigate the effects of extreme heat. The shade they provide lowers sidewalk temperatures by several degrees, and the water evaporating from their leaves cools the surrounding air.

words.definition: The ability to move freely; the ability to change social or economic status.
examples: Education is often linked to social mobility.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the nineteenth century, the expansion of public schooling increased social mobility. Children of farmers and laborers who learned to read and write could pursue careers as clerks, teachers, or engineers, rising to positions their parents could never have reached.

words.definition: The avoidance of extremes; restraint.
words.usage: Often 'in moderation'. Also the act of making something less extreme.
examples: The doctor said coffee is fine in moderation.

sat.passage: The doctor advised her patients to enjoy sweets in moderation rather than banning them entirely. Eating an occasional dessert, she explained, is unlikely to cause harm, but consuming sugary foods at every meal can lead to serious health problems.

words.definition: To make partial changes to.
words.usage: Used for plans, designs, and genes.
examples: The team modified the design after testing.

sat.passage: To help crops survive drought, plant scientists sometimes modify the genes that control how quickly leaves lose water. Small changes to a single gene can allow a plant to close its pores more efficiently, conserving moisture during dry spells.

words.definition: The force gained by motion; the impetus of a developing process.
words.usage: Used in physics and for movements gaining strength.
examples: The campaign gained momentum after the debate.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The campaign to protect the wetland began with a handful of local birdwatchers, but it gained momentum as news of the plan to drain the marsh spread. Within a year, thousands of residents had signed petitions, and the state agreed to make the area a protected reserve.

words.definition: Exclusive control of a supply or trade.
examples: The company held a monopoly on salt.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: For nearly two centuries, a single trading company held a monopoly in the nutmeg trade, punishing any grower on the islands who tried to sell to rival merchants. Because no competitor could legally buy the spice, the company was free to set prices as high as it wished.

words.definition: Principles concerning right and wrong behavior.
examples: The novel questions conventional morality.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In many of her novels, the author refuses to divide characters neatly into heroes and villains. Instead, she places ordinary people in situations where honesty and loyalty conflict, inviting readers to question their own assumptions about morality and to consider whether a lie told to protect a friend can ever be right.

words.definition: A recurring theme, image, or pattern.
words.usage: Used in literature, art, and music.
examples: Light and darkness are a recurring motif in the poem.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Throughout the composer's symphony, a short four-note figure returns again and again: first played softly by the flutes, later thundered by the brass, and finally whispered by a solo violin in the closing bars. This motif ties the work's contrasting movements together.

words.definition: A reason for doing something.
examples: Her motive for writing the book was to honor her grandmother.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Detectives investigating the theft were puzzled at first. The stolen painting was nearly worthless, and the thief had ignored far more valuable works hanging nearby. Only when they learned that the painting depicted the suspect's grandmother did the motive for the crime become clear: the thief had wanted to reclaim a family memory.

words.definition: Ordinary and dull.
examples: She found beauty in mundane objects.

sat.passage: The diaries of the eighteenth-century lighthouse keeper disappoint readers hoping for tales of shipwrecks and storms. Most entries record mundane chores such as trimming wicks, polishing lenses, and noting the weather. Yet historians value these routine details for what they reveal about daily life on the coast.

words.definition: A change in genetic material; a change in form.
examples: A single mutation made the bacteria resistant.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Most pale-colored moths in the region are easily spotted by birds against dark tree bark. A small population, however, carries a mutation that darkens the insects' wings. Because these darker moths are harder for predators to see, the altered gene has become increasingly common over several generations.

words.definition: Shared by two or more parties.
examples: The partnership was based on mutual trust.

sat.passage: When the two rival bakeries on Elm Street finally agreed to share a single delivery van, both owners benefited: each cut fuel costs nearly in half, and neither had to hire a second driver. The arrangement, built on mutual interest rather than friendship, lasted for more than a decade.

words.definition: Countless; a great number.
examples: The reef supports myriad species.

sat.passage: The coral reef supports myriad species, from tiny shrimp that clean the teeth of larger fish to sea turtles that graze on its algae. Divers who survey a single square meter of the reef often record dozens of different organisms.

words.definition: A traditional story; a widely held but false belief.
examples: It's a myth that lightning never strikes the same place twice.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Many people believe that goldfish can remember things for only three seconds. Experiments have shown, however, that goldfish can be trained to push levers for food and can recall the task months later, revealing this popular claim to be a myth.

words.definition: Lacking experience or judgment; innocent.
examples: It was naive to think the project would be easy.

sat.passage: Fresh from the countryside, the young clerk in the novel trusts everyone he meets in the city. He lends his savings to a stranger who promises to double them and believes a landlord's claim that rent will never rise. Only after losing nearly everything does he recognize how naive he had been.

words.definition: Just beginning to develop.
examples: The nascent movement grew quickly.

sat.passage: In the 1890s, the automobile industry was still nascent: only a handful of workshops built cars, mostly by hand, and many people doubted the noisy machines would ever replace horses. Within three decades, however, factories were producing millions of vehicles a year.

words.definition: The fact of being required; something essential.
words.usage: 'Out of necessity' means because it was needed.
examples: Water is a necessity for all life.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: During the long winter siege of 1709, residents of the walled town ran out of firewood. They burned furniture, fence posts, and even old books, not out of carelessness but out of necessity, since no other fuel remained.

words.definition: To cancel out the effect of; to deny.
examples: The cost of shipping negated any savings.

sat.passage: The new seawall was meant to protect the harbor town from flooding. Engineers later discovered, however, that the wall redirected waves toward a nearby beach, speeding erosion there so much that the damage threatened to negate the benefits the barrier provided to the town.

words.definition: To fail to care for or pay attention to.
words.usage: Used for duties, buildings, and people left without care.
examples: Years of neglect left the historic theater in ruins.

sat.passage: After the family that owned the estate moved abroad, its formal gardens fell into ruin. For decades, no one pruned the hedges or cleared the fountains, and by the time preservationists arrived, years of neglect had allowed ivy to swallow entire statues.

words.definition: So small or unimportant as to be not worth considering.
examples: The difference in price was negligible.

sat.passage: Critics of the proposed wind farm warned that its turbines would kill large numbers of migrating birds. A two-year study of a similar site found the effect to be negligible: fewer than five birds were struck in that time, a number far smaller than those killed by nearby traffic.

words.definition: Not supporting either side; having no strong characteristics.
examples: The reporter tried to keep a neutral tone.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Throughout the war, the small alpine nation remained neutral, refusing to send troops or supplies to either alliance. Its banks and hotels instead became meeting places where diplomats from both sides could negotiate in secret.

words.definition: In spite of that.
examples: It was raining; nevertheless, the game went on.

sat.passage: The early steam locomotive was slow, noisy, and prone to breakdowns, and many observers dismissed it as a passing novelty. Investors, nevertheless, poured money into new rail lines, convinced that the machines would soon transform travel and trade.

words.definition: A specialized role or position; a shallow recess.
examples: Each finch species occupies a different ecological niche.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the rain forests of Madagascar, the aye-aye fills an unusual niche. Like a woodpecker, it taps on tree bark to locate hollow tunnels made by insect larvae, then uses its long, thin middle finger to pull the grubs out, a role that woodpeckers occupy elsewhere but that no bird plays on the island.

words.definition: Having high moral qualities; belonging to the aristocracy.
words.usage: Describes character, goals, and social rank.
examples: Feeding the hungry is a noble cause.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Although the expedition failed to reach the pole, newspapers praised its leader for a noble decision. Rather than abandon two injured companions, he turned the entire team back, sacrificing his own chance at fame to bring everyone home alive.

words.definition: Moving from place to place without a permanent home.
examples: Nomadic herders follow the grass across the steppe.

sat.passage: For centuries, many herding peoples of the Central Asian steppe have lived nomadic lives, moving their felt tents several times a year so that their sheep and horses can reach fresh pasture as the seasons change. Their homes can be taken down and packed onto animals in only a few hours.

words.definition: In name only; very small.
words.usage: A nominal leader has no real power; a nominal fee is tiny.
examples: The museum charges only a nominal fee.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Although the young king officially ruled the country, his authority was nominal: his uncle controlled the army, signed every law, and decided which advisers the king could even meet. Foreign ambassadors soon learned to bring their requests directly to the uncle.

words.definition: Calm and relaxed; seeming unconcerned.
examples: He was nonchalant about the big test.

sat.passage: While the other contestants paced backstage and rehearsed their lines under their breath, Mira sat with her feet propped on a chair, idly flipping through a magazine. Her nonchalant manner surprised the stage crew, who knew this was the first competition she had ever entered.

words.definition: In spite of that; nevertheless.
examples: The task was difficult; nonetheless, they finished on time.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The village's first schoolhouse had a leaking roof, a single wood stove, and only a dozen donated books. Parents, nonetheless, sent their children there eagerly, believing that even this modest education would open doors that had been closed to them.

words.definition: Something usual or standard; an accepted standard of behavior.
words.usage: Social norms; deviations from the norm.
examples: Remote work has become the norm for many companies.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the nineteenth century, it was the norm for wealthy families in the region to hire private tutors rather than send their children to public schools. Today, by contrast, nearly all children there attend public schools, and home tutoring is relatively uncommon.

words.definition: A sentimental longing for the past.
examples: The old songs filled her with nostalgia.

sat.passage: Years after leaving the fishing village where she grew up, the narrator finds herself thinking fondly of its crooked docks and the smell of salt and diesel. She knows that life there was hard, but nostalgia softens her memories, making even the cold winters seem cozy in hindsight.

words.definition: An idea or belief.
examples: The study challenges the notion that older adults can't learn new skills.

sat.passage: For centuries, many physicians accepted the notion that diseases were caused by "bad air" rising from swamps and garbage. Only in the late nineteenth century did experiments showing that microbes cause infection lead doctors to abandon this belief.

words.definition: Famous for something bad.
examples: The road is notorious for accidents.

sat.passage: The stretch of rocky coast near the old fishing town is notorious among sailors. Shifting sandbars, hidden reefs, and sudden storms have wrecked hundreds of ships there, and captains have long dreaded the passage.

words.definition: In spite of.
words.usage: Formal; can come before or after a noun.
examples: Notwithstanding the bad weather, the event was a success.

sat.passage: The museum's new wing, which opened last spring, has drawn record crowds. The city council, notwithstanding the project's high construction costs, now considers the wing one of its best investments, since ticket sales have already repaid nearly half the expense.

words.definition: New or unusual in an interesting way.
words.usage: The SAT often tests this adjective meaning, not 'a book'.
examples: The team proposed a novel method for cleaning oil spills.

sat.passage: Rather than relying on fences, which elephants easily knock down, a group of farmers tested a novel solution: they hung beehives along the borders of their fields. Elephants, which avoid bees, largely stayed away, and the farmers earned extra income by selling honey.

words.definition: A person new to an activity; a beginner.
examples: The course is designed for novices with no experience.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The sailing club pairs each novice with an experienced member during her first season on the water. Because newcomers often panic when the boat tips in a gust, these mentors teach them how to shift their weight and stay calm.

words.definition: Characterized by subtle shades of meaning or expression.
words.usage: Describes arguments and portrayals that avoid oversimplifying.
examples: The documentary offers a nuanced view of the conflict.

sat.passage: Earlier biographies portrayed the general either as a flawless hero or as a ruthless tyrant. The new biography offers a more nuanced portrait, acknowledging his military brilliance while also examining the harsh policies he imposed on conquered towns.

words.definition: To make legally void; to cancel out the effect of.
words.usage: Used for laws, contracts, and effects that are canceled.
examples: A single error can nullify the results of the experiment.

sat.passage: In 1832, legislators in one state declared that a federal tariff would have no force within their borders, claiming that states had the power to nullify national laws they considered unconstitutional. The president rejected this claim and threatened to send troops to collect the tax.

words.definition: To care for and encourage growth.
examples: Good teachers nurture curiosity.

sat.passage: In the greenhouse, volunteers nurture seedlings of rare native wildflowers, watering them daily and shielding them from frost until the young plants are strong enough to be moved to the restored prairie. Last year, more than two thousand plants were transplanted outdoors.

words.definition: An expression of disapproval or opposition.
examples: The main objection to the plan was its cost.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: When the town proposed replacing the old library with a parking garage, residents voiced a strong objection at the council meeting. More than two hundred people signed a petition, and several speakers argued that the building was a landmark worth preserving.

words.definition: (adj.) Not influenced by personal feelings; (n.) a goal.
examples: Scientists try to remain objective.

sat.passage: To keep the study objective, the researchers who rated the children's drawings were not told which children had attended the art program and which had not. That way, their expectations could not influence the scores they assigned.

words.definition: Not aware of what is happening.
examples: He was oblivious to the danger.

sat.passage: Absorbed in her sketchbook, the art student was oblivious to the storm gathering outside the café window. She did not look up until thunder rattled the glass and the other customers had already hurried home.

words.definition: (adj.) Not well known or hard to understand; (v.) to hide or make unclear.
words.usage: Both meanings are tested: an obscure poet; clouds obscure the moon.
examples: The scholar rescued an obscure poet's work from neglect.
Fog obscured the view of the bridge.

sat.passage: The poet published only a single slim volume during her lifetime, and for nearly a century she remained obscure, her work known to just a few scholars. Interest in her poems revived only after a collection of her letters was discovered in an attic.

words.definition: Able to be noticed or perceived.
words.usage: Science term for things that can be measured or seen.
examples: The effect is observable only under a microscope.

sat.passage: Dark matter cannot be seen directly, because it neither emits nor reflects light. Astronomers infer its existence instead from its observable effects, such as the way galaxies rotate faster at their edges than visible matter alone could explain.

words.definition: Quick to notice things; also, following rules or customs closely.
words.usage: Usually describes people who notice details.
examples: An observant hiker spotted the rare orchid beside the trail.

sat.passage: Because she was unusually observant, the young naturalist noticed that the beetles in the meadow emerged only after the morning dew had dried. Her careful notes later helped entomologists understand how the insects avoid drowning.

words.definition: No longer produced or used; out of date.
examples: Typewriters became obsolete with the rise of computers.

sat.passage: When digital cameras became cheap and widespread in the early 2000s, film rapidly became obsolete for most consumers. Photo labs that had once lined shopping streets closed by the thousands, and only a few companies continued to manufacture rolls of film.

words.definition: Stubbornly refusing to change.
examples: The obstinate mule refused to move.

sat.passage: The mule in the folktale is famously obstinate: no matter how the farmer pleads, bribes, or pushes, it refuses to cross the bridge. Only when the farmer walks away in frustration does the animal, entirely on its own, trot across.

words.definition: To block or get in the way of.
words.usage: Used for paths, views, and processes.
examples: A fallen tree obstructed the road.

sat.passage: After the earthquake, landslides obstructed the only road into the mountain village. Rescuers had to deliver food and medicine by helicopter until crews could clear away the rocks and mud. In the meantime, families on the far side of the slide were cut off from the nearest hospital.

words.definition: To get or acquire, often through effort.
examples: Researchers obtained permission to study the artifacts.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: To study the chemistry of the deep ocean floor, researchers needed to obtain samples of mud from nearly four kilometers below the surface. They lowered a weighted tube on a cable, drove it into the sediment, and hauled it back to the ship.

words.definition: An incident or event; the fact of something happening.
examples: Snow in April is a rare occurrence here.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In most of the country, snowfall is a rare occurrence. So when several centimeters fell on the coastal city one January morning, schools closed and residents rushed outdoors to photograph palm trees dusted with white.

words.definition: A strange or peculiar thing or trait.
words.usage: Describes something unusual, sometimes a curiosity.
examples: The two-headed turtle was treated as an oddity at the aquarium.

sat.passage: In the 1790s, a preserved animal with a duck's bill, a beaver's tail, and webbed feet arrived in Britain from Australia. Many naturalists considered the specimen a mere oddity, possibly a fake stitched together by a prankster, and only later accepted the platypus as a genuine species.

words.definition: Casual or careless; done without preparation.
words.usage: Describes remarks or manners that seem unplanned or indifferent.
examples: His offhand comment about the budget caused an uproar.

sat.passage: The director's offhand remark about the lead actor's accent, made casually while he was adjusting the lights, ended up shaping the entire production. The actor spent the next six weeks perfecting a new dialect.

words.definition: To counterbalance or compensate for.
examples: Higher prices were offset by better quality.

sat.passage: To offset the carbon dioxide released by its delivery trucks, the company funds the planting of thousands of trees each year. The trees absorb the gas as they grow, balancing out some of the emissions.

words.definition: A person's children or an animal's young.
examples: The bird feeds its offspring insects.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Female sea turtles crawl onto beaches to bury their eggs in the sand, then return to the ocean. Their offspring hatch weeks later and must scramble to the water on their own, guided by the brightness of the horizon.

words.definition: Giving the impression something bad will happen.
examples: Dark, ominous clouds gathered.

sat.passage: As the hikers neared the summit, the sky darkened, and ominous rumbles echoed across the valley. Remembering the ranger's warning about afternoon lightning, they turned back immediately. Within twenty minutes, a fierce storm had swept over the very ridge where they had planned to eat lunch.

words.definition: Continuing; still in progress.
examples: The investigation is ongoing.

sat.passage: The excavation at the ancient palace is ongoing: each summer, teams uncover new rooms, and researchers expect the work to continue for at least another decade. Findings so far include painted pottery and carved stone seals.

words.definition: The beginning of something, especially something unpleasant.
words.usage: The onset of winter, of symptoms.
examples: Birds fly south at the onset of winter.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Many songbirds leave their northern breeding grounds as early as August. By departing well before the onset of winter, they avoid the hard frosts that make insects and seeds scarce. Birds that linger too long in the north may find little to eat once the ground freezes.

words.definition: Not able to be seen through; hard to understand.
examples: The company's finances were opaque.

sat.passage: Readers have long found the philosopher's later writings opaque. Her sentences stretch across entire pages, she invents terms without defining them, and even specialists disagree about what her central argument is. Some readers have joked that her books need a translator even for native speakers.

words.definition: Functioning; in effect; most relevant.
words.usage: Phrase 'the operative word' means the key word; also describes laws or systems in effect.
examples: The old rules remain operative until the new policy is approved.

sat.passage: The lease allowed the tenant to leave early only if the building became "unsafe," and in the dispute that followed, that was the operative word. Lawyers for both sides spent weeks arguing over whether a broken heating system made an apartment unsafe.

words.definition: Unjustly harsh; weighing heavily.
examples: The oppressive heat kept people indoors.

sat.passage: The summer heat in the valley was oppressive. Temperatures stayed above forty degrees Celsius for weeks, and farmworkers could labor only in the early morning, before the air became too heavy to breathe comfortably.

words.definition: Best or most favorable.
examples: Tomatoes grow best at an optimal temperature of about 75°F.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Tomato seeds sprout fastest when the soil is between 24 and 29 degrees Celsius. Gardeners in cool climates therefore often start seeds indoors on heating mats, keeping the soil within this optimal range until the seedlings are ready to be transplanted.

words.definition: Hopefulness about the future.
examples: The good news filled the town with optimism.

sat.passage: Despite three failed launches, the engineers greeted each setback with optimism, convinced that every explosion taught them something that would make the next rocket succeed. Their confidence proved justified when the fourth attempt reached orbit.

words.definition: Available to be chosen but not required.
examples: The second essay on the application is optional.

sat.passage: Students in the course must complete four laboratory reports, but the field trip to the river delta is optional. Those who cannot attend may instead read an article about wetland ecosystems and write a short response.

words.definition: To align or position relative to something; to familiarize.
examples: Sunflowers orient themselves toward the sun.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Before beginning a hike in unfamiliar terrain, experienced backpackers orient their maps so that the northern edge points toward true north. Aligning the map in this way makes it easier to match drawn features with the hills and streams in view.

words.definition: The ability to think independently and creatively; being new.
examples: Judges praised the originality of her design.

sat.passage: Judges at the design competition praised the winning chair less for its comfort than for its originality: no one had ever before built furniture from woven strips of recycled bicycle tires. The designer said the idea came to her while repairing a flat.

words.definition: Serving to decorate rather than to be useful.
words.usage: Describes plants, details, and features that are decorative.
examples: The ornamental columns support nothing; they are purely decorative.

sat.passage: Some of the trees on the estate were grown for fruit or timber, but the cherry trees lining the drive were purely ornamental. They produced no edible fruit and had been planted only for their spectacular spring blossoms.

words.definition: Showy; designed to impress.
examples: Their ostentatious mansion had three fountains.

sat.passage: Eager to display his newfound wealth, the merchant filled his mansion with gold-plated railings, marble fountains, and portraits of himself in jeweled frames. Neighbors found the house's ostentatious decor tasteless, a sharp contrast to the simple homes around it.

words.definition: To exclude from a group.
examples: The villagers ostracized the newcomer.

sat.passage: In some ancient Greek cities, citizens could vote once a year to ostracize a politician they considered dangerous, sending him into exile for ten years. Voters scratched the person's name on a piece of broken pottery.

words.definition: Friendly and socially confident; leaving a position.
words.usage: Describes personalities, or officials about to leave office.
examples: The outgoing mayor gave a farewell speech.

sat.passage: In her final speech, the outgoing mayor thanked the city workers she had served alongside for twelve years. She also wished her successor, who would take office the following week, every success. Many residents came to hear her farewell, and several of her longtime staff members wept openly.

words.definition: Old-fashioned; no longer in use or accepted.
words.usage: Describes ideas, technologies, and methods replaced by newer ones.
examples: Researchers abandoned the outmoded theory once better data appeared.

sat.passage: By the 1960s, many hospitals had stopped using the iron lung, a large metal chamber that helped polio patients breathe. Vaccines and smaller ventilators had made the bulky machines outmoded, though a few patients continued to rely on them for decades.

words.definition: To exceed or move faster than; to surpass.
examples: Demand for the vaccine quickly outstripped supply.

sat.passage: In the early 1800s, demand for cotton began to outstrip supply as new textile mills opened across northern England. Prices rose sharply, and merchants searched desperately for new sources of the fiber. Some planters responded by clearing new land as fast as they could.

words.definition: To extend over and partly cover; to have parts in common.
words.usage: Used for areas, ideas, and time periods.
examples: The two species' ranges overlap in the valley.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The breeding ranges of the two warbler species overlap only in a narrow band of forest along the river. There, where both birds nest side by side, ornithologists have recorded occasional hybrids. Elsewhere, the species are separated by hundreds of kilometers and never meet.

words.definition: To fail to notice; to ignore; to have a view from above.
words.usage: Several meanings are tested: overlook a mistake; a house overlooks the sea.
examples: Early researchers overlooked the role of fungi in forest health.

sat.passage: The first team to study the fossil overlooked a tiny bone near the animal's jaw, assuming it was a fragment of rock. Decades later, a graduate student examining the specimen under a microscope recognized it as part of the creature's inner ear.

words.definition: Done or shown openly; not hidden.
examples: The letter contained no overt threat, but its tone was menacing.

sat.passage: Rather than openly criticizing the king, which could have led to imprisonment, the playwright hid his political commentary in a fable about quarreling animals. Audiences understood the message, but because the criticism was never overt, censors could find no grounds to ban the play.

words.definition: To overpower with emotion, force, or quantity.
words.usage: Used for feelings, systems, and defenses.
examples: The sudden flood of orders overwhelmed the small bakery.

sat.passage: During the 1918 influenza pandemic, the number of patients threatened to overwhelm city hospitals. Some converted gymnasiums and schools into temporary wards after every bed had been filled. Nurses worked double shifts, and volunteers with no medical training were recruited to help care for the sick.

words.definition: To calm or soothe; to bring peace.
examples: She tried to pacify the crying child.

sat.passage: The crying infant in the story cannot be soothed by toys or songs. Finally, her grandfather manages to pacify her by carrying her outside, where the steady rustle of the wind in the trees lulls her to sleep.

words.definition: So intense as to be almost touchable; obvious.
examples: The tension in the room was palpable.

sat.passage: As the final contestant stepped up to the microphone, the tension in the auditorium was palpable. No one whispered, programs stopped rustling, and several audience members leaned forward and gripped their armrests. When the contestant finally began to sing, the crowd released a collective breath.

words.definition: A typical model or pattern; a framework of ideas.
words.usage: 'Paradigm shift' means a fundamental change in approach.
examples: Einstein's theory caused a paradigm shift in physics.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: For more than a thousand years, most astronomers worked within a paradigm that placed Earth motionless at the center of the universe, interpreting every observation in light of that assumption. The shift to a sun-centered model required not just new data but an entirely new way of thinking about the heavens.

words.definition: A seemingly contradictory statement or situation that may be true.
words.usage: Common in literary and scientific discussions.
examples: It's a paradox that the more choices we have, the harder it is to decide.

sat.passage: One famous paradox in biology concerns plankton: hundreds of species coexist in the open ocean, competing for the same few nutrients, even though ecological theory predicts that a single best competitor should drive the others to extinction. Researchers are still debating how so many species manage to survive.

words.definition: Side by side and equally distant; similar.
examples: The author draws a parallel between the two revolutions.

sat.passage: In her essay, one historian draws a parallel between the canal-building boom of the 1820s and the rush to lay fiber-optic cable in the 1990s. In both cases, she argues, investors poured money into new networks faster than demand could justify, and many lost fortunes.

words.definition: More important than anything else.
examples: Student safety is paramount.

sat.passage: For the engineers designing the children's playground, safety was paramount. They chose rubber surfaces over gravel, rounded every corner, and rejected a tall slide that children loved in testing but that posed a risk of serious falls.

words.definition: Not complete; favoring one side.
words.usage: 'Partial to' means having a liking for.
examples: The data offer only a partial picture.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Only a partial skeleton of the dinosaur was recovered from the hillside. Researchers found the skull, several ribs, and one leg, but the tail and both arms were missing, likely washed away long ago.

words.definition: Strongly supporting a party or cause, often with bias.
examples: The debate became bitterly partisan.

sat.passage: Unlike the newspapers of the 1800s, many of which openly served one political party and attacked its rivals, the new journal promised readers coverage free of partisan bias. Its editors invited writers from across the political spectrum and printed their arguments side by side.

words.definition: Accepting what happens without active response.
examples: Viewers are often passive consumers of advertising.

sat.passage: In the experiment, some students actively quizzed themselves on the material, while others took a more passive approach, simply rereading their notes several times. On the final test, the students who had quizzed themselves scored significantly higher.

words.definition: Relating to idealized country life.
words.usage: Pastoral scenes in art and literature.
examples: The painting shows a pastoral scene of sheep and hills.

sat.passage: The painter's early landscapes depict pastoral scenes of shepherds resting beneath oak trees and cows grazing beside quiet streams. Her later work, by contrast, captures the smoke and crowded streets of the industrial city where she eventually settled.

words.definition: A quality that evokes pity or sadness.
examples: The speech used pathos to move the audience.

sat.passage: The documentary avoids dry statistics about the drought, relying instead on pathos. It lingers, for example, on a farmer silently watching his last cattle being loaded onto a truck to be sold. No narrator explains the scene; the camera simply holds on his face as the truck pulls away.

words.definition: Support given by a patron, such as funding for the arts.
words.usage: Historical arts funding; also political favors.
examples: Renaissance artists depended on the patronage of wealthy families.

sat.passage: During the Renaissance, many painters depended on the patronage of wealthy families, who paid for altarpieces and portraits and often housed artists in their palaces. Without such support, few artists could have afforded expensive pigments or years of training.

words.definition: Engaged in deep thought.
examples: She grew pensive as she read the letter.

sat.passage: After reading the letter from her estranged brother, Lena sat by the window for a long time in a pensive mood, turning over his words and wondering whether she should reply. She did not speak again until dinner.

words.definition: To become aware of through the senses; to understand in a particular way.
examples: Dogs perceive sounds humans cannot hear.

sat.passage: Honeybees perceive ultraviolet light, which is invisible to humans. Many flowers that look plain yellow to us display striking ultraviolet patterns that the bees can see, guiding them straight to the nectar. To a bee, a field of flowers is covered with bright signs that humans cannot detect.

words.definition: Able to be seen, noticed, or felt.
words.usage: Often about small but noticeable changes; opposite of imperceptible.
examples: There was a perceptible drop in temperature after sunset.
