sat.passage: The change in the glacier's position from one day to the next is barely perceptible, amounting to only a few centimeters. Over decades, however, those small daily movements add up, and photographs show the ice retreating nearly a kilometer.

words.definition: On the edge; of secondary importance.
words.usage: Describes locations (peripheral vision) and minor issues.
examples: The budget debate was peripheral to the main purpose of the meeting.

sat.passage: At the town meeting, residents spent nearly an hour debating the color of the new park benches. It was a peripheral question compared with the project's central problem: the park's budget had already run out.

words.definition: Lasting or intended to last indefinitely.
examples: The museum added the sculpture to its permanent collection.

sat.passage: Unlike the traveling exhibition, which will leave the museum in March, the dinosaur hall is permanent. Its skeletons have been on display since the building opened in 1921, and they will remain for the foreseeable future.

words.definition: Having a harmful effect, especially gradually.
examples: Rumors had a pernicious effect on morale.

sat.passage: The invasive vine is especially pernicious because its damage is slow and easy to miss. It climbs gradually over native trees, blocking their sunlight for years until the weakened trunks finally collapse. By the time the problem is obvious to visitors, much of the forest may already be lost.

words.definition: Never ending or changing; continuing indefinitely.
words.usage: Describes cycles, states, and complaints that seem endless.
examples: The polar region lives in perpetual darkness for part of the winter.

sat.passage: Residents of the floodplain live in perpetual fear of the river. Every spring the water rises, and even in dry years they keep sandbags stacked beside their doors. Older residents can describe each major flood in detail, from the year the church filled with water to the night the bridge washed away.

words.definition: To confuse completely.
examples: The results perplexed the scientists.

sat.passage: The ancient stone map continues to perplex archaeologists. Its carved lines match no known rivers or roads, and its symbols resemble no writing system yet discovered. Some researchers suspect it depicts the night sky rather than the land, but no theory has yet explained all of its features.

words.definition: Persistence in doing something despite difficulty.
examples: Her perseverance paid off when she won the race.

sat.passage: The inventor tested more than two thousand materials for the filament of his electric lamp, many of which burned out within seconds. Colleagues credited his eventual success less to genius than to perseverance, noting that he never stopped trying new fibers despite repeated failure.

words.definition: To continue firmly despite difficulty; to continue to exist.
examples: The myth persists despite evidence against it.

sat.passage: Some pesticides break down within a few weeks of being sprayed. Others, however, persist in the soil for decades, poisoning earthworms and accumulating in the bodies of the birds that eat them. Because they remain in the environment for so long, many of these chemicals have been banned.

words.definition: Continuing firmly despite difficulty; lasting a long time.
examples: A persistent cough sent her to the doctor.

sat.passage: Doctors advise patients to seek care for a persistent cough, one that lasts more than three weeks. A cough that will not go away can signal a more serious illness than a common cold.

words.definition: A particular way of viewing things; a point of view.
words.usage: Common in questions about narrators and authors.
examples: The story is told from the perspective of a child.

sat.passage: The novel is told from the perspective of a young servant in a wealthy household. As a result, readers learn about the family's secrets only as she overhears them through closed doors and while serving at the dinner table.

words.definition: Spreading widely throughout.
examples: Smartphones have a pervasive influence on daily life.

sat.passage: By the early twenty-first century, plastic pollution had become pervasive in the oceans. Researchers found microscopic fragments in Arctic sea ice, in the deepest ocean trenches, and in the stomachs of seabirds on remote islands.

words.definition: Remarkable; extraordinary.
examples: The app enjoyed phenomenal growth.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The small bakery's growth has been phenomenal. In five years, it expanded from a single counter to forty locations across the region, and its sourdough now sells in supermarkets nationwide. Industry analysts, who had predicted the business would struggle to survive its first year, were astonished.

words.definition: An observable fact or event, especially one that is notable or unusual.
examples: The aurora is a natural phenomenon caused by solar particles.

sat.passage: Bioluminescence, the production of light by living organisms, is a common phenomenon in the deep sea, where sunlight never reaches. A large share of the animals living there can generate their own glow.

words.definition: The desire to promote others' welfare, especially through donations.
examples: Her philanthropy funded dozens of schools.

sat.passage: Having made a fortune in shipping, the merchant devoted the last decades of her life to philanthropy. She funded free libraries, hospitals, and scholarships for children whose families could not afford school fees.

words.definition: Relating to the study of fundamental questions; calm in the face of difficulty.
examples: She was philosophical about the loss, calling it a lesson.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: When a hailstorm destroyed the season's entire crop, the old farmer was philosophical about the loss. Bad years come to every farm, he remarked, and next spring the fields would simply be planted again.

words.definition: A person among the first to explore or develop something.
examples: She pioneered the use of X-rays in medicine.

sat.passage: In the mid-nineteenth century, a few surgeons began to pioneer the practice of washing their hands between patients. Most of their colleagues ridiculed the habit at first, but it dramatically reduced deaths from infection.

words.definition: To make less angry.
examples: The manager offered a refund to placate the customer.

sat.passage: To placate customers angered by the delayed flight, the airline offered free meals and vouchers for future travel. The gesture worked: by the time the plane finally boarded, most passengers had stopped complaining.

words.definition: Seeming reasonable or probable.
examples: The detective's theory was plausible but unproven.

sat.passage: The detective's first theory, that the thief had slipped out through the study window, was hardly plausible, since the window had been painted shut for years. She soon settled on a more likely explanation involving the servants' staircase.

words.definition: A dangerous or difficult situation.
examples: The article described the plight of the flood victims.

sat.passage: The documentary drew national attention to the plight of families whose homes had been destroyed by the wildfire. Within a week, viewers had donated enough money to provide temporary housing for hundreds of people.

words.definition: Evoking a keen sense of sadness or regret.
examples: The film's final scene is especially poignant.

sat.passage: The film's most poignant scene shows the elderly musician, now too frail to play, running his fingers silently over the keys of the piano he once performed on in concert halls around the world. Many viewers leave the theater in tears.

words.definition: To divide into sharply opposing groups.
examples: The issue polarized the community.

sat.passage: Over the course of the debate, the proposal to build a highway through the old neighborhood began to polarize the city. Residents who once held mixed views increasingly lined up firmly for or against it, and the two camps stopped attending each other's meetings.

words.definition: To think about carefully.
examples: She pondered the offer for days.

sat.passage: Standing at the edge of the canyon, the young geologist paused to ponder how a narrow river could have carved such an enormous gorge. She turned the question over in her mind for several minutes before she began taking notes.

words.definition: To make something widely known or liked.
words.usage: Used for ideas, styles, and scientific concepts brought to the public.
examples: Her television series popularized astronomy for a generation of viewers.

sat.passage: Although scientists had studied black holes for decades, it was a series of best-selling books and television documentaries in the 1980s that helped popularize the idea among ordinary readers. Many of those readers had never taken a physics course.

words.definition: Claiming to represent ordinary people against elites.
examples: The populist candidate promised to fight corruption.

sat.passage: Campaigning on a populist platform, the candidate promised to break up powerful railroad companies and banks. He accused them of enriching a few wealthy elites at the expense of ordinary farmers and laborers.

words.definition: To depict or describe in a certain way.
words.usage: Used for art, acting, and characterization.
examples: The film portrays the scientist as a lonely genius.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Earlier novels about the mill towns of New England had treated factory workers as a faceless crowd. In her 1932 novel, the fictional author Ada Linwood portrayed them instead as distinct individuals, giving each chapter to a different worker's hopes, quarrels, and private jokes.

words.definition: To present a problem or question; to sit for a portrait.
words.usage: Pose a threat, pose a question.
examples: Rising seas pose a threat to coastal cities.

sat.passage: Since arriving in the Great Lakes in the 1980s, invasive zebra mussels have spread rapidly. By filtering huge amounts of plankton from the water, they leave little food for native fish and mussels, and ecologists warn that they pose a serious threat to the lakes' food webs.

words.definition: All future generations.
examples: The letters were saved for posterity.

sat.passage: When the town's oldest bakery closed, a local historian spent months recording interviews with its retired bakers. She hoped to preserve their recipes and stories for posterity, so that residents born decades later could still learn how the bakery had shaped the neighborhood.

words.definition: To suggest or assume something as a basis for reasoning.
words.usage: Academic; used for theories and assumptions.
examples: Einstein postulated that the speed of light is constant.

sat.passage: In the nineteenth century, the orbit of Uranus did not match astronomers' predictions. To explain the mismatch, some astronomers postulated that an unseen planet was tugging on it, and they used that assumption as the starting point for new calculations, which eventually led to the discovery of Neptune.

words.definition: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically; practical.
words.usage: Contrasts with idealistic or theoretical approaches.
examples: The mayor took a pragmatic approach, focusing on what could be done this year.

sat.passage: Faced with a small budget and a crumbling bridge, the city council took a pragmatic approach. Instead of commissioning an elaborate new design that might take a decade to fund, it repaired the existing structure so that traffic could keep moving.

words.definition: Not securely held; dangerously likely to fall or collapse.
examples: The vase sat in a precarious spot on the shelf's edge.

sat.passage: Built on a narrow ledge high above the river, the osprey nest looked precarious; a single strong gust seemed likely to send it tumbling into the water below. Even so, the birds returned to it every spring and raised their chicks there.

words.definition: To come before in time, order, or position.
examples: A loud crack preceded the avalanche.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Large earthquakes do not always strike without warning. In many cases, smaller tremors known as foreshocks precede the main shock by hours or even days, and seismologists study these earlier tremors in hopes of one day forecasting major quakes.

words.definition: An earlier event or decision used as an example.
examples: The ruling set a precedent for future cases.

sat.passage: The judge's decision was the first in the state to grant a river legal protection as if it were a person. Since then, lawyers in several similar cases have cited the ruling as a precedent, urging other judges to follow its example.

words.definition: (v.) To cause something to happen suddenly; (adj.) hasty.
words.usage: Also a chemistry term for a solid forming in a solution.
examples: The scandal precipitated the minister's resignation.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: For decades the textile mill had employed nearly half the town. Its sudden closure in 1974 precipitated a wave of departures: within two years, almost a third of the residents had packed up and moved to larger cities in search of work.

words.definition: Exact and accurate.
words.usage: The SAT's own question asks for the 'most logical and precise' word.
examples: The recipe calls for precise measurements.

sat.passage: Earlier maps of the coast showed its outline only roughly, often misplacing harbors by several kilometers. The new satellite survey, by contrast, was remarkably precise: its measurements located each lighthouse to within a single meter of its true position.

words.definition: To prevent something from happening; to make impossible.
words.usage: Formal; used for conditions that rule out possibilities.
examples: The injury precluded her from competing in the finals.

sat.passage: The research team had hoped to study the glacier year-round. However, the violent winter storms in the region precluded any fieldwork between November and March, so the scientists installed automated sensors that could collect data while they were away.

words.definition: Having developed abilities at an unusually early age.
examples: The precocious child read novels at age five.

sat.passage: Clara Venn, the young heroine of the novel, is remarkably precocious. By age six she is composing short pieces for piano, and by twelve she is correcting the mistakes of the adult musicians in her village orchestra.

words.definition: An animal that hunts others for food.
examples: Wolves are the main predator of elk in the park.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: On remote islands without foxes or cats, ground-nesting seabirds often have no instinct to flee danger. When rats arrived on one such island aboard a ship, they raided nests and ate eggs and chicks, and the birds had no defense against the new predator.

words.definition: Established or decided in advance.
words.usage: Describes outcomes, routes, or criteria set beforehand.
examples: The robots follow a predetermined path through the warehouse.

sat.passage: In the experiment, the robot did not choose its own route through the warehouse. Instead, it followed a predetermined path that engineers had programmed the night before, which allowed researchers to compare its speed with that of human workers on the same route.

words.definition: A difficult, unpleasant situation.
examples: Stranded without a phone, they faced a predicament.

sat.passage: When a rockslide blocked the only trail off the ridge, the hikers faced a serious predicament. Their water was running low, their phones had no signal, and the sun was already setting behind the mountains.

words.definition: Present as the strongest or main element.
examples: Pine is the predominant tree in the forest.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The forest contains more than forty species of trees, but oaks are by far the predominant type. They make up nearly 70 percent of all trunks in the survey plots, and their acorns feed most of the forest's deer and squirrels.

words.definition: An opinion not based on reason or experience, often unfair.
examples: The novel explores prejudice in a small town.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the novel, newcomers to the fishing village are treated with suspicion before anyone has even spoken to them. The villagers' prejudice against outsiders, based on old rumors rather than experience, fades only after a stranger risks his life to rescue a stranded boat.

words.definition: Coming before a more important action; initial.
examples: Preliminary results suggest the drug works.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Before committing money to a full excavation, the archaeologists sent a small underwater drone to examine the shipwreck. This preliminary survey revealed enough intact cargo to justify a larger expedition the following summer.

words.definition: A statement on which an argument is based.
examples: The argument rests on a false premise.

sat.passage: The novel's central premise is simple: a lighthouse keeper discovers that the ships passing her island are arriving from the future. Every later twist in the plot follows from this starting idea.

words.definition: To suppose something is true without proof; to be bold enough to.
examples: I presume you've already read the instructions.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Because the letter was found among the general's papers and bore his seal, archivists had long presumed that he wrote it himself. Only recently did handwriting analysis suggest that one of his aides had actually drafted it.

words.definition: Failing to observe limits; overconfident.
examples: It was presumptuous to assume she would agree.

sat.passage: Ellen had met the gallery owner only once, at a crowded reception. Her friends therefore thought it presumptuous of her to ask him to hang her paintings in his front window, a spot usually reserved for the city's best-known artists.

words.definition: Trying to seem more important or cultured than one is.
words.usage: Negative; describes people, writing, or style.
examples: Critics called the restaurant's menu pretentious.

sat.passage: Critics praised the restaurant's simple, hearty food but mocked its menu, which described a plain bowl of soup in elaborate French phrases. To many diners, the language seemed pretentious, an attempt to make the meal sound far more refined than it actually was.

words.definition: How widespread something is.
words.usage: Noun form of prevalent; common in health passages.
examples: The survey measured the prevalence of nearsightedness.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Public health researchers examined the eyes of 4,000 schoolchildren to determine the prevalence of nearsightedness. They found that the condition affected about one in three students, a much larger share than in their parents' generation.

words.definition: Widespread in a particular area or time.
examples: Malaria is prevalent in some tropical regions.

sat.passage: In the early nineteenth century, the belief that disease spread through foul-smelling air was prevalent among doctors in Europe. Because nearly everyone in the profession accepted the idea, few thought to look for other causes, such as contaminated water.

words.definition: Able to be stopped from happening.
words.usage: Common in health and safety contexts.
examples: Many of the injuries were preventable with proper equipment.

sat.passage: A review of the factory's accident records found that most injuries had been preventable. Workers who wore the required gloves and goggles were almost never hurt, while nearly every serious injury involved someone who had skipped that equipment.

words.definition: Relating to an early stage of development; simple or crude.
examples: Primitive mammals lived alongside dinosaurs.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Compared with modern computers, the earliest mechanical calculators were primitive machines. Built from hand-cranked gears and levers, they could add and subtract slowly but could do little else.

words.definition: Most important; (n.) the head of a school.
examples: The principal cause of the decline was overfishing.

sat.passage: Pollution and disease both harmed the bay's oysters, but researchers concluded that overharvesting was the principal cause of their decline. In every decade they studied, the oyster count fell fastest in the years when boats took the most oysters.

words.definition: Existing or coming before.
examples: No prior experience is required.

sat.passage: Applicants to the animal shelter's volunteer program need no prior experience with dogs. During their first week, staff members teach every newcomer how to feed, walk, and calm the animals, so even people who have never owned a pet can quickly help out.

words.definition: In original condition; clean and unspoiled.
examples: The beach was pristine and empty.

sat.passage: Because a rockfall had sealed the cave's entrance for thousands of years, the explorers who finally reopened it found it in pristine condition. The delicate crystal formations were unbroken, and no trash, soot, or footprints marked the floor.

words.definition: To investigate thoroughly; (n.) an investigation or device for exploring.
examples: The journalist probed the company's finances.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: After residents near the chemical plant complained of mysterious illnesses, a team of reporters spent a year probing the company's safety records. Their investigation uncovered dozens of leaks that the company had never disclosed to regulators.

words.definition: Presenting a problem or difficulty.
examples: Relying on a single source is problematic.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Historians studying the battle have only one eyewitness account to work with, which they find problematic. The writer may have misremembered events years later, and as an officer on the losing side, he had reasons to exaggerate the enemy's strength.

words.definition: Remarkably great in size or degree.
examples: She had a prodigious memory for names.

sat.passage: Arctic terns make a prodigious journey every year. Flying from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back, a single bird may travel roughly 70,000 kilometers, the longest annual migration of any animal known.

words.definition: Competent; skilled.
examples: He is proficient in three languages.

sat.passage: When the exchange student arrived in Osaka, she knew only a few phrases of Japanese. After two years of daily lessons and conversations with her host family, however, she had become proficient in the language and could follow university lectures and write essays with ease.

words.definition: Very great or intense; showing deep insight.
examples: The invention of the printing press had a profound effect on society.

sat.passage: The spread of the printing press in fifteenth-century Europe had a profound effect on society. Books, once copied slowly by hand, became affordable to ordinary people, literacy rose sharply, and new ideas traveled faster than ever before.

words.definition: Happening gradually; favoring social reform.
examples: The disease causes a progressive loss of vision.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The inherited disorder causes a progressive loss of hearing. Patients usually notice only slight difficulty in their teens, but their hearing worsens steadily over many years, and by middle age most rely on hearing aids.

words.definition: To forbid by law or rule.
examples: The park prohibits camping near the lake.

sat.passage: To protect shorebirds that nest in the sand, the park prohibits dogs on the beach from April through August. Rangers patrol the shoreline during those months and issue fines to visitors who ignore the rule.

words.definition: To increase rapidly in number.
examples: Coffee shops proliferated downtown.

sat.passage: As smartphones became common in the 2010s, food delivery apps proliferated. Within a few years, a city that had once been served by a single delivery company had dozens of them, each competing for the same restaurants and customers.

words.definition: Producing much.
examples: The prolific author wrote over 100 books.

sat.passage: The fictional painter Marguerite Osei, heroine of the novel, is remarkably prolific. Over a forty-year career she completes more than 3,000 canvases, many of them in a single afternoon, and her studio overflows with finished work.

words.definition: To extend the duration of.
words.usage: Used for lives, meetings, and conflicts.
examples: Proper storage can prolong the shelf life of vegetables.

sat.passage: Shipping companies often coat fresh apples with a thin layer of edible wax. The coating slows the loss of moisture from the fruit and can prolong its shelf life by several weeks, allowing the apples to reach distant markets still crisp.

words.definition: Important or famous; projecting or easily seen.
words.usage: Describes leading figures and noticeable features.
examples: She became a prominent voice in the environmental movement.

sat.passage: As a teenager, she organized small cleanups along the river near her home. By her forties, she had become a prominent voice in the national environmental movement, testifying before lawmakers and leading campaigns followed by millions.

words.definition: A natural inclination.
examples: Cats have a propensity to sleep in sunny spots.

sat.passage: Many retrievers have a strong propensity for swimming. Even puppies that have never seen a lake will often plunge into the water on their first visit, a trait that breeders selected for when the dogs were used to fetch ducks.

words.definition: A person who supports or advocates for an idea or cause.
words.usage: Often 'a proponent of'. Opposite of opponent or critic.
examples: He was a leading proponent of public parks in the city.

sat.passage: In the 1850s, as the city grew more crowded, one local newspaper editor became a leading proponent of a large public park. He wrote dozens of editorials urging officials to set aside land where workers and their families could escape the noise of the streets.

words.definition: A statement expressing an opinion or judgment; a proposal.
examples: Opening a store downtown was a risky proposition.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: To most of her neighbors, opening a bookstore in a town of only 800 people seemed a risky proposition. Yet by hosting weekly readings and selling coffee alongside the books, the owner turned a profit within two years.

words.definition: Lacking imagination; ordinary.
examples: The explanation was disappointingly prosaic.

sat.passage: For decades, villagers told tales of a ghost that moaned inside the abandoned mill on windy nights. When engineers finally inspected the building, the true explanation proved prosaic: air whistling through a cracked window frame.

words.definition: The possibility of a future event; a view.
examples: The prospect of rain worried the farmers.

sat.passage: For farmers in the drought-stricken valley, the prospect of spring rain brought both hope and worry. Rain would revive their wilting crops, but a storm that was too heavy could wash away the dry topsoil before it had time to absorb the water.

words.definition: The state of being successful, especially financially.
examples: The railroad brought prosperity to the town.

sat.passage: When the railroad reached the town in 1871, it brought new prosperity. Local farmers could suddenly ship grain to distant markets, merchants opened shops along the main street, and within a decade the population had tripled.

words.definition: An official procedure or set of rules.
words.usage: Used in science, diplomacy, and computing.
examples: The lab follows a strict safety protocol.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Before entering the clean room where computer chips are made, technicians must follow a strict protocol. They put on full-body suits, pass through a chamber that blasts away dust, and enter only after a supervisor checks each step.

words.definition: Arranged for the present, possibly to be changed later.
examples: The results are provisional until the full data are reviewed.

sat.passage: The election commission released provisional results on election night. Officials cautioned, however, that the totals could change once absentee ballots, which would not be counted until later in the week, were added.

words.definition: Causing a strong reaction, often deliberately.
examples: The essay makes a provocative argument.

sat.passage: The museum's new exhibit is deliberately provocative. One installation displays a mound of discarded clothing taller than a person, forcing visitors to confront how much they throw away, and the exhibit has drawn both angry letters and passionate praise.

words.definition: To stir up a reaction, especially an angry or strong one.
examples: The article provoked a heated debate among readers.

sat.passage: When the newspaper printed an essay arguing that the town's historic courthouse should be torn down, the editors expected some disagreement. They were surprised, however, when the essay managed to provoke more than four hundred angry letters in a single week.

words.definition: Acting with or showing care and thought for the future.
words.usage: Describes careful decisions, especially about money or risk; adverb 'prudently'.
examples: It would be prudent to save part of every paycheck.

sat.passage: With storms becoming more frequent along the coast, the town's planners decided it would be prudent to raise the new library a full meter above the ground. The extra height added to construction costs, but it protected the collection from future flooding.

words.definition: To follow or chase; to seek to achieve.
words.usage: Pursue a goal, a career, or a suspect.
examples: She pursued a career in medicine.

sat.passage: Although her parents hoped she would one day take over the family hardware store, Maya decided to pursue a career in marine biology. She enrolled in a university program on the coast and spent her summers tagging sea turtles.

words.definition: A state of uncertainty over what to do.
examples: She was in a quandary about which college to choose.

sat.passage: The editor found herself in a quandary. The article was ready to print, but a last-minute source had cast doubt on one of its central claims: publishing on schedule risked spreading an error, while delaying it risked losing the story to a rival paper.

words.definition: To put an end to; to suppress.
examples: The mayor tried to quell the residents' fears.

sat.passage: After a minor chemical spill near the reservoir, many residents worried that their tap water was unsafe. To quell those fears, city officials held a public meeting and released test results showing that the water met every safety standard.

words.definition: Doubtful as to truth, quality, or honesty.
words.usage: Describes claims, motives, and methods that invite doubt.
examples: The study's conclusions are questionable because its sample was so small.

sat.passage: The study claimed that a new diet sharply improved memory, but its conclusions were questionable. It included only twelve participants, lasted just one week, and was paid for by the company that sold the diet.

words.definition: Representing the most perfect example of a type.
examples: The diner is the quintessential small-town restaurant.

sat.passage: With its red vinyl booths, chrome counter, and waitress who knows every customer's usual order, the diner is the quintessential small-town restaurant. Filmmakers looking for a classic American setting have used it in more than a dozen movies.

words.definition: Far-reaching or thorough; favoring extreme change.
examples: The invention brought radical changes to farming.

sat.passage: The mechanical reaper brought radical changes to farming in the nineteenth century. Harvesting work that had once required a dozen laborers could now be done by one person and a team of horses, and many farm workers left the countryside for factory jobs.

words.definition: A close, harmonious relationship.
examples: The teacher quickly built a rapport with her students.

sat.passage: The new teacher worked quickly to build rapport with her students, learning every name on the first day and asking each of them about their interests. By October, even the shyest students felt comfortable sharing their ideas in class.

words.definition: To give formal approval to.
examples: The states ratified the amendment in 1920.

sat.passage: The treaty could not take effect until it had been ratified by at least two-thirds of the member nations. After months of debate, the last of the required parliaments voted its approval, and the agreement became binding the following spring.

words.definition: Based on reason or logic.
examples: She made a rational decision based on the facts.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: When stock prices suddenly plunged, many investors sold their shares in a panic. Lena, however, made a rational decision: she reviewed each company's finances, concluded that their long-term prospects were strong, and kept her investments.

words.definition: To try to justify behavior with logical-sounding reasons that may not be the true ones; also, to make more efficient.
words.usage: Often implies self-justification (rationalize a bad decision).
examples: He rationalized skipping practice by saying he needed rest.

sat.passage: After skipping his third practice in a row, Theo rationalized his absence by telling himself that rest was just as important as training. Deep down, though, he knew the real reason was that he dreaded the coach's grueling new drills.

words.definition: Without hesitation; easily.
examples: Fresh water was readily available at the camp.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Before the reservoir was built, fresh water was scarce in the valley, and families walked for miles to collect it. Today, clean water is readily available from taps in every home, and few residents remember the long walks of the past.

words.definition: A field or domain of activity; a kingdom.
examples: Space travel was once in the realm of science fiction.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: For centuries, travel to the Moon belonged to the realm of fiction, imagined by novelists but dismissed as impossible by engineers. That changed in the twentieth century, when rockets powerful enough to escape Earth's gravity were finally built.

words.definition: An act of resistance against authority or convention.
words.usage: Used for political uprisings and personal defiance.
examples: Her bright clothes were a small rebellion against the school's dull uniforms.

sat.passage: At the strict boarding school, students were required to wear the same gray uniform every day. Her bright red socks were a small rebellion, a quiet way of defying the dull rules, and although teachers frowned at them, no one ever forbade them.

words.definition: To express sharp disapproval.
examples: The coach rebuked the players for arriving late.

sat.passage: When the players arrived twenty minutes late for the bus to the championship game, the coach rebuked them sharply in front of the entire team. He warned that anyone who was late again would spend the next game on the bench.

words.definition: A refutation or contradiction.
examples: The senator delivered a sharp rebuttal.

sat.passage: During the debate, the first speaker argued that the town should ban cars from its main shopping street. Her opponent then delivered a forceful rebuttal, presenting survey data showing that most local shops depended on customers who arrived by car.

words.definition: Stubbornly uncooperative toward authority or control.
words.usage: Describes people, animals, or problems that resist being managed.
examples: The recalcitrant mule refused to cross the bridge.

sat.passage: The farmer's mule was famously recalcitrant. No matter how gently he coaxed it or how hard he tugged on its rope, it planted its hooves at the edge of the wooden bridge and refused to take another step.

words.definition: To move back; to diminish.
examples: The floodwaters slowly receded.

sat.passage: In the weeks after the flood, residents waited anxiously for the waters to recede. As the river slowly dropped back within its banks, families returned to find mud coating their floors and furniture.

words.definition: Willing to consider or accept new ideas.
examples: The manager was receptive to the team's suggestions.

sat.passage: The new manager was receptive to her team's suggestions. She held weekly meetings at which anyone could propose changes, and within her first month several employees' ideas had already been put into practice.

words.definition: Given or felt by each toward the other; mutual.
words.usage: Describes relationships, agreements, and effects that go both ways.
examples: The two countries signed a reciprocal trade agreement.

sat.passage: Under the new treaty between the two neighboring countries, the visa policy is reciprocal. Each nation allows the other's citizens to live and work within its borders without special permits, so travelers in both directions benefit equally.

words.definition: To respond to an action or feeling with a corresponding one.
words.usage: Used for returning favors, kindness, or affection.
examples: When neighbors helped her move, she reciprocated by cooking them dinner.

sat.passage: When her neighbors spent an entire weekend helping her repair her storm-damaged roof, Mrs. Alvarez was eager to reciprocate. The following Saturday, she cooked them a large dinner and offered to watch their children whenever they needed help.

words.definition: Exchange for mutual benefit.
examples: Trade agreements depend on reciprocity.

sat.passage: Trade agreements depend on reciprocity. A country that lowers its taxes on foreign goods expects its trading partners to lower their taxes in return, and if they refuse, the agreement usually collapses.

words.definition: Able to be identified from previous knowledge or features.
words.usage: Describes features or patterns that are easy to identify.
examples: The singer's voice is instantly recognizable.

sat.passage: Although the singer had not released an album in twenty years, her voice remained instantly recognizable. When her new song played on the radio, listeners across the country identified her within the first few notes.

words.definition: To remember something.
words.usage: Slightly formal; often used for memories from long ago.
examples: She could barely recollect the house she lived in as a child.

sat.passage: At ninety, the retired sailor sometimes forgot what he had eaten for breakfast. Yet he could still recollect the name of every ship he had served on and describe the storms each one had weathered decades earlier.

words.definition: To restore friendly relations; to make compatible.
examples: It's hard to reconcile his kindness with his harsh words.

sat.passage: Biographers have long struggled to reconcile the inventor's public generosity with his private cruelty. He donated fortunes to hospitals and schools, yet letters from his employees describe him as a harsh, even vindictive, boss.

words.definition: To build up again or reorganize in a different form; to restore dried food by adding water.
words.usage: Often 'reconstituted as' a new organization or form.
examples: After the war, the orchestra was reconstituted as a national ensemble.

sat.passage: After the war scattered its musicians, the city's orchestra stopped performing for several years. In 1950 it was reconstituted as a national ensemble, with new members recruited from across the country and a mission to tour every province.

words.definition: To build again; to piece together past events.
examples: Scientists reconstructed the dinosaur's skeleton from fragments.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: No one has ever seen the dinosaur move, but its footprints survive in hardened mud. By measuring the spacing and depth of those tracks, paleontologists reconstructed how the animal walked, estimating both its stride length and its top speed.

words.definition: To put right; to correct.
words.usage: Used for errors, injustices, and problems.
examples: The company promised to rectify the billing error.

sat.passage: When hundreds of customers discovered they had been charged twice for the same order, the company issued an apology. It promised to rectify the error within a week by refunding every extra charge.

words.definition: To define again or differently; to change the nature of.
words.usage: Used for terms, roles, and fields that change.
examples: Smartphones redefined how people access information.

sat.passage: For centuries, maps were printed on paper and updated only every few years. Satellite navigation redefined what a map could be, turning it into a constantly updated guide that could reroute drivers around traffic in seconds.

words.definition: To remedy or set right an unfair situation; (n.) compensation for a wrong.
words.usage: Formal; used for injustices and grievances.
examples: The law was designed to redress decades of unequal pay.

sat.passage: For decades, women at the company had earned less than men for the same work. The new policy was designed to redress that injustice: it required managers to review every salary and pay back wages to employees who had been underpaid.

words.definition: No longer needed; repetitive.
examples: 'Free gift' is redundant, since gifts are free.

sat.passage: The editor crossed out the phrase "past history" in the student's essay. She explained that the word "past" was redundant, since history is by definition about events that have already happened.

words.definition: To act out a past event again.
words.usage: Used for historical events and scenes.
examples: Volunteers reenacted the famous battle on its anniversary.

sat.passage: Every summer, hundreds of volunteers dressed in wool coats and tricorn hats gather to reenact a Revolutionary War battle on the field where it was fought. They march in the original formations and fire blank charges from muskets while spectators watch from the hillside.

words.definition: To remove impurities; to improve by small changes.
examples: Researchers refined their methods after the first trial.

sat.passage: The first trial of the new water filter produced inconsistent results. Rather than starting over, the engineers refined their design, adjusting the size of the filter's pores and slowing the flow of water, until every test met the safety standard.

words.definition: A change made to improve something; (v.) to make such changes.
words.usage: Common in history and civics passages.
examples: The reforms gave more citizens the right to vote.

sat.passage: In the 1880s, the city's police department was notorious for bribery and favoritism. A series of reforms, including hiring officers through written exams rather than political connections, gradually transformed it into one of the most respected departments in the country.

words.definition: To prove a statement or theory wrong.
examples: The experiment refuted the old assumption.

sat.passage: For decades, many doctors believed that stomach ulcers were caused mainly by stress. That belief was refuted when researchers demonstrated that most ulcers are caused by a bacterium and can be cured with antibiotics.

words.definition: A government, especially an authoritarian one; a system or routine.
examples: The regime restricted freedom of the press.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the novel, a military regime seizes power in a small island nation and immediately shuts down every independent newspaper. The story follows a young printer who secretly publishes pamphlets criticizing the generals who now rule the country.

words.definition: To control or maintain the rate, amount, or behavior of something by rules or adjustment.
words.usage: Used for laws governing industries and for body processes (regulate temperature).
examples: Sweating helps the body regulate its temperature.

sat.passage: Unlike mammals, desert lizards cannot produce much of their own body heat. Instead, they regulate their temperature through behavior, basking on sunny rocks in the cool morning and retreating into shady burrows during the midday heat.

words.definition: To strengthen or support.
words.usage: Used for structures, ideas, and behaviors.
examples: The new data reinforce the researchers' conclusion.

sat.passage: A team of biologists found that honeybees could learn to recognize photographs of particular human faces. A second study, using an entirely different set of photographs, reinforced that conclusion, since the bees once again picked out the faces they had been trained on.

words.definition: The act of refusing to accept or consider something.
words.usage: Used for ideas, proposals, and people.
examples: The scientist's rejection of the old model surprised her colleagues.

sat.passage: Most astronomers of her era accepted the idea that the universe was static and unchanging. The young astronomer's outright rejection of that model shocked her colleagues, but her measurements of distant galaxies eventually persuaded many of them that the universe is expanding.

words.definition: To assign to a lower position.
examples: The old furniture was relegated to the attic.

sat.passage: When the school opened its new science wing, the old wooden lab tables were relegated to a storage room in the basement. There they sat for years, collecting dust, while students worked at gleaming new benches upstairs.

words.definition: Persistent; never stopping.
examples: The relentless rain flooded the streets.

sat.passage: For eleven straight days, the relentless rain soaked the region. Not a single hour passed without a downpour, and rivers rose until they spilled over their banks and flooded the streets of several towns.

words.definition: The quality of being trustworthy or performing consistently well.
words.usage: Common in science for data and measurements.
examples: Researchers questioned the reliability of the self-reported data.

sat.passage: The researchers questioned the reliability of the survey's data. Adults had been asked to recall exactly how many hours they had slept each night as young children, and memories that old are often inaccurate.

words.definition: To give up willingly.
examples: The founder relinquished control of the company.
sources: ACT Practice Test (Preparing for the ACT booklet)

sat.passage: After leading the company for thirty years, the founder finally agreed to relinquish control to a younger board of directors. She kept an office in the building, but she no longer made decisions about the company's products or budget.

words.definition: Unwillingness or hesitation.
examples: Despite his reluctance, he agreed to speak.

sat.passage: Despite his reluctance to speak in public, the shy engineer agreed to present the team's findings at the conference. He rehearsed for weeks in front of a mirror, and his hands still trembled as he walked onto the stage.

words.definition: Careless in performing one's duty.
examples: I would be remiss not to thank the volunteers.

sat.passage: The museum director began her speech by saying that she would be remiss not to thank the volunteers. Over the past year, they had spent more than 2,000 unpaid hours cleaning and repairing the exhibit's fragile tapestries.

words.definition: A small remaining part of something larger.
words.usage: Often a leftover from the past.
examples: Only a remnant of the ancient wall still stands.

sat.passage: Only a small remnant of the ancient city wall still stands. The crumbling stretch of stone, about ten meters long, is now surrounded by apartment buildings, and few passersby realize that it once encircled the entire medieval town.

words.definition: Deep regret for a wrong committed.
examples: He showed no remorse for his actions.

sat.passage: In the novel's final chapter, the thief returns the stolen necklace and confesses to the family, weeping. His remorse is genuine: he spends the rest of his life working to repay the people he wronged.

words.definition: Far away in distance or time; slight.
words.usage: Remote places; a remote chance means a very small one.
examples: The chance of finding the ring in the sand was remote.

sat.passage: The searchers knew their chance of finding the lost ring on the beach was remote. The tide had come in twice since it was dropped, and the sand stretched for miles in both directions.

words.definition: To cause to become; to provide; to represent artistically.
examples: The flood rendered the road impassable.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The spring flood washed away a large section of the mountain road and rendered it impassable for weeks. Until repairs were finished, the village at the top of the pass could be reached only by helicopter.

words.definition: To restore something old to good condition.
examples: Volunteers renovated the old theater.

sat.passage: Instead of tearing down the century-old theater, a group of volunteers spent three years renovating it. They repaired the leaking roof, restored the painted ceiling, and replaced hundreds of torn velvet seats.

words.definition: Fame; high reputation.
examples: The chef won renown for her desserts.

sat.passage: Inés Calder, the chef at the center of the novel, begins her career in a tiny roadside café. Her desserts eventually win her international renown, and food lovers travel from across the world to taste them.

words.definition: An unintended consequence.
examples: The decision had serious repercussions.

sat.passage: The decision to drain the wetland and build a shopping center had repercussions that its planners never anticipated. Without the marsh to absorb rainwater, nearby neighborhoods began to flood during storms, and property values fell.

words.definition: The full range of skills or works a person or group can perform.
words.usage: Used for musicians, actors, and animals' behaviors.
examples: The mockingbird has a huge repertoire of songs.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The northern mockingbird has an enormous repertoire. A single male may imitate the songs of dozens of other bird species, along with sounds such as car alarms and creaking gates, and he keeps adding new songs throughout his life.

words.definition: Containing or characterized by repetition, often dully.
examples: The work was repetitive, so the factory added machines.

sat.passage: Workers on the assembly line spent eight hours a day tightening the same four bolts on identical parts. Because the work was so repetitive, many workers complained of boredom, and the factory eventually installed machines to do the task.

words.definition: To make an exact copy of; to reproduce results.
words.usage: Key science word: other labs replicate an experiment to confirm it. 'Replicable' means able to be reproduced.
examples: Other teams were unable to replicate the original findings.

sat.passage: The original study reported that a simple breathing exercise dramatically improved students' test scores. When three other laboratories tried to replicate the experiment using the same procedures, however, none of them found any effect, and many scientists began to doubt the result.

words.definition: To subdue by force; to restrain or hold back feelings.
words.usage: Used for governments controlling people and for suppressing emotions.
examples: She repressed a laugh during the serious ceremony.

sat.passage: During the solemn ceremony, the guest of honor tripped on the stage steps and sent his notes flying. The young usher had to repress a laugh, biting her lip and staring at the floor until the moment had passed.

words.definition: A temporary relief or cancellation of a punishment or hardship.
words.usage: Often 'a brief reprieve from' something unpleasant.
examples: The rain offered a brief reprieve from the heat wave.

sat.passage: After two weeks of scorching temperatures, a brief thunderstorm offered residents a reprieve from the heat wave. By the next afternoon, however, the thermometer had climbed past 100 degrees again.

words.definition: To produce offspring; to copy; to repeat results.
examples: Other labs could not reproduce the results.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: When a small lab announced that a common soil bacterium could break down plastic within days, other researchers rushed to test the claim. Following the original methods exactly, three independent teams tried to reproduce the result, but none observed any breakdown, leading many scientists to question the initial report.

words.definition: To refuse to accept; to reject.
examples: The scientist repudiated her earlier claims.

sat.passage: For years, the economist had argued that raising the minimum wage would inevitably cause widespread job losses. After reviewing a decade of data from cities that had raised wages without such losses, however, she publicly repudiated her earlier position and called for a new approach.

words.definition: To look like or be similar to.
examples: The orchid resembles a bee.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The bee orchid has evolved a remarkable disguise. Its flowers closely resemble female bees in color, shape, and even texture, so male bees attempt to mate with the blossoms and, in the process, carry pollen from plant to plant.

words.definition: A large natural or artificial lake for storing water; a supply.
words.usage: Literal and figurative (a reservoir of knowledge).
examples: The town's water comes from a mountain reservoir.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Some songbirds, a team of ecologists found, carry the virus without ever becoming ill. Because these birds can harbor the pathogen for months and pass it to mosquitoes each spring, the researchers describe them as a reservoir for the disease, a hidden source from which new outbreaks can arise.

words.definition: Remaining after the greater part has gone.
examples: Residual heat from the oven warmed the kitchen.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Even after a forest fire has been put out, residual heat in the soil can persist for days. Firefighters therefore patrol burned areas long after the flames are gone, checking for smoldering roots that could reignite and start the blaze all over again.

words.definition: A small amount of something that remains after a process.
examples: The pan was coated with a sticky residue.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: To learn what ancient potters stored in their jars, archaeologists scraped a thin, dark residue from the inner walls of vessels found at the site. Chemical analysis of this leftover material revealed traces of olive oil and honey, suggesting that the jars once held food.

words.definition: Able to recover quickly from difficulty; able to spring back into shape.
words.usage: Describes people, communities, ecosystems, and materials.
examples: The resilient forest regrew within a decade of the fire.

sat.passage: Coral reefs are often described as fragile, but some prove surprisingly resilient. After a severe bleaching event killed much of the coral on one Pacific reef, divers found that within a decade the reef had largely regrown, its colorful colonies once again crowding the shallow waters.

words.definition: Able to withstand something; opposed to something.
examples: Some bacteria have become resistant to antibiotics.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Farmers have long sprayed their fields with the same weed killer, and the practice has had an unintended effect. Over many generations, some weeds have developed genes that protect them from the chemical, making these plants resistant to treatments that once wiped them out easily.

words.definition: Determined; unwavering.
examples: She remained resolute in the face of criticism.

sat.passage: Throughout the long winter of the siege, the city's mayor remained resolute. Even as food supplies dwindled and some advisers urged surrender, she refused to open the gates, insisting each night in her radio addresses that the city would hold out until help arrived.

words.definition: (v.) To settle or find a solution; to decide firmly; (n.) determination.
words.usage: Resolve a dispute; strengthen one's resolve.
examples: The two sides resolved their differences.

sat.passage: For decades, two neighboring towns argued over who controlled a stream that ran along their shared border. The dispute was finally resolved in 1987, when both councils agreed to a plan that divided the water equally and created a joint committee to manage it.

words.definition: Reacting quickly and positively.
words.usage: Often 'responsive to' needs, changes, or stimuli.
examples: Plants are responsive to changes in light.

sat.passage: Sunflower seedlings are highly responsive to light. When researchers placed a lamp to one side of a tray of young plants, the stems bent toward it within hours, and when the lamp was moved, the seedlings shifted direction again to follow it.

words.definition: To hold back or keep under control.
examples: She restrained her excitement until the results were officially announced.

sat.passage: As the orchestra played the final notes of the premiere, the young composer struggled to restrain her emotions. She sat perfectly still in the back row, hands folded tightly in her lap, and allowed herself to smile only after the audience had filed out of the hall.

words.definition: Self-control; a measure that limits or restricts.
words.usage: Often praise for holding back (showed restraint).
examples: The judge showed restraint in her response to the outburst.

sat.passage: Reviewers praised the director for her restraint in depicting the battle. Rather than filling the screen with explosions and graphic injuries, she showed the fighting mostly through the soldiers' faces and the distant sound of guns, leaving the worst horrors to the audience's imagination.

words.definition: To limit the size, amount, or range of something.
examples: The city restricted parking on the street to residents only.

sat.passage: To protect nesting sea turtles, officials on one island restrict access to several beaches between May and October. During those months, visitors may enter the protected areas only with a licensed guide, and lights near the shore must be switched off after dark.

words.definition: Imposing limits on someone's freedom or activity.
examples: Residents complained that the parking rules were too restrictive.

sat.passage: Early in the twentieth century, many publishers imposed restrictive contracts on authors. Writers often could not sell their work to other publishers, change their manuscripts' titles, or keep rights to translations, conditions that left them with little control over their own books.

words.definition: An increase or revival after inactivity.
examples: Vinyl records have seen a resurgence.

sat.passage: After nearly disappearing in the 1990s, the art of hand-lettered shop signs has enjoyed a resurgence in recent years. Young painters are learning the craft from retired sign makers, and storefronts in many cities once again display gilded, brush-painted names.

words.definition: To keep possession of; to continue to have.
words.usage: Used for information, heat, water, and employees.
examples: Clay soil retains water longer than sandy soil.

sat.passage: Clay soils are dense, with tiny particles packed closely together. As a result, they retain water far longer than sandy soils do, which can help crops survive dry spells but can also leave roots waterlogged after heavy rain.

words.definition: To strike back.
examples: The country retaliated with tariffs.

sat.passage: When one nation placed heavy taxes on imported steel, its trading partners were quick to retaliate. Within weeks, they announced their own taxes on the first nation's farm products, a response designed to hurt its exporters as much as the steel tax had hurt theirs.

words.definition: Not revealing thoughts or feelings readily.
examples: She was reticent about her past.

sat.passage: Although the novelist gave many interviews, she was notably reticent about her childhood. Whenever a reporter asked about her early years, she changed the subject or offered only a brief, vague reply before returning to the topic of her latest book.

words.definition: To withdraw or move back; (n.) a quiet place to rest.
examples: Glaciers have retreated dramatically over the last century.
sources: ACT Practice Test (Preparing for the ACT booklet)

sat.passage: Over the past century, the glacier has retreated nearly three kilometers up its valley. Photographs from 1910 show ice reaching the edge of a village, while today hikers must walk for more than an hour from that spot to reach the glacier's melting front.

words.definition: To get back; to bring back.
words.usage: Used for objects, data, and memories.
examples: The dog retrieved the ball from the lake.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Some sea otters keep a favorite stone tucked in a pouch of loose skin under each forearm. After diving to retrieve clams and urchins from the seafloor, an otter floats on its back and uses the stone to crack open the shells.

words.definition: To regard with deep respect and admiration.
examples: Villagers revered the old teacher for her wisdom.

sat.passage: In many villages along the river, people revere the oldest fishermen, who are believed to understand the water better than anyone. Young people seek their advice before every season, and at festivals the elders are given the seats of honor.

words.definition: Deep respect.
examples: The villagers treated the old tree with reverence.

sat.passage: In the traditional tea ceremony, every movement carries meaning. The host cleans each utensil slowly and deliberately, and guests handle the tea bowl with reverence, turning it carefully and admiring its glaze before drinking. Even the simple act of pouring hot water is performed as though it were a gesture of honor.

words.definition: To move backward; to make the opposite of what it was.
words.usage: Reverse a decision, reverse a trend.
examples: The new policy reversed years of decline.

sat.passage: For much of the twentieth century, the population of the island's native parrots fell steadily as forests were cleared. A replanting program begun in 1990 has helped reverse that trend: surveys now count more parrots each year than the year before.

words.definition: To reconsider and change, often to improve.
words.usage: Used for writing, estimates, and theories.
examples: Astronomers revised their estimate of the galaxy's age.

sat.passage: When new telescope data suggested that the universe was expanding faster than expected, astronomers were forced to revise their estimate of its age. The updated figure is several hundred million years younger than the one published a decade earlier.

words.definition: Involving dramatic change; relating to a revolution.
examples: The printing press was a revolutionary invention.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Before the use of anesthesia began in the 1840s, surgeons had to work quickly on patients who were fully awake and in agony. The ability to keep patients unconscious was revolutionary: it allowed doctors to perform long, delicate operations that had previously been impossible.

words.definition: The art of persuasive speaking or writing; language that sounds impressive but may lack substance.
words.usage: Neutral (study of persuasion) or negative (empty rhetoric).
examples: The senator's speech was full of rhetoric but short on details.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The candidate's speech was full of stirring rhetoric about a bright future, but listeners noticed that it contained almost no specifics. She promised to fix the city's schools and roads without explaining how she would pay for the repairs or when they would begin.

words.definition: Unable to bend; strict and unchangeable.
examples: The school's rigid schedule left little free time.

sat.passage: The new bridge's designers deliberately avoided a rigid structure. Because the region experiences frequent earthquakes, they built the deck to sway slightly and absorb shaking, reasoning that a frame unable to bend would be more likely to crack under stress.

words.definition: Extremely thorough and careful.
examples: The drug passed rigorous safety tests.

sat.passage: Before the new vaccine was approved, it underwent rigorous testing. Over three years, researchers tracked tens of thousands of volunteers, checked every reported side effect, and had independent experts review each stage of the data.

words.definition: A ceremony or series of actions performed in a set order.
examples: Morning coffee is a ritual for many people.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: For the farming families of the valley, the first planting of spring was a ritual that rarely changed. Each year, the eldest member of the household threw the first handful of seed at dawn, the family shared a meal of bread and honey, and only then did the real work begin.

words.definition: (v.) To be equal or comparable to; (n.) a competitor.
words.usage: As a verb, means 'match in quality' (few cities rival Paris).
examples: The small bakery's bread rivals that of the city's best restaurants.

sat.passage: The small coastal town has only a few thousand residents, yet its annual film festival has grown remarkably influential. Critics now say that its lineup of premieres rivals those of festivals held in major international cities, and well-known directors compete for a spot on its program.

words.definition: Strong and healthy; able to withstand challenges.
words.usage: Common in science: a robust finding holds up under testing.
examples: The results were robust across different age groups.

sat.passage: The link between sleep and memory appears to be robust. Across dozens of studies using different age groups, different tasks, and different measurement methods, researchers have consistently found that people remember new information better after a full night's sleep.

words.definition: Basic; undeveloped.
examples: He had only a rudimentary knowledge of French.

sat.passage: Early mapmakers in the region had only rudimentary tools: a compass, a knotted rope for measuring distance, and their own observations of the stars. Despite these basic instruments, their charts of the coastline proved surprisingly accurate when compared with modern satellite images.

words.definition: Most noticeable or important.
examples: The summary covers the salient points.

sat.passage: The museum's guide to the painting focuses on its most salient features. Visitors are directed first to the enormous red sun dominating the upper half of the canvas and then to the lone figure standing in the foreground, details that immediately draw the viewer's eye.

words.definition: (v.) To give official permission or approval; also, to penalize; (n.) a penalty or an approval.
examples: The league sanctioned the new tournament.
The country faced trade sanctions.

sat.passage: When the new sport of indoor climbing first appeared, competitions were organized informally by local gyms. That changed when the national athletics federation agreed to sanction the events, giving the winners official titles and allowing their results to count toward international rankings.

words.definition: Optimistic or positive, especially in a difficult situation.
words.usage: Often in negative constructions (not sanguine about the outcome).
examples: Despite the setbacks, the coach remained sanguine about the season.

sat.passage: Although the drought had already cut the harvest in half, the farmer remained sanguine. She told her neighbors that the rains would come before autumn and that next year's crop, planted in rested soil, might be the best they had ever seen.

words.definition: Fulfilling expectations or needs; acceptable though not outstanding.
examples: The repairs were satisfactory, though not perfect.

sat.passage: The inspectors' report on the old school building was mixed. They rated the plumbing and electrical systems as satisfactory, noting that both met basic safety standards, but they recommended major improvements before the building could be considered truly modern.

words.definition: To soak thoroughly; to fill completely so no more can be added.
words.usage: Used for liquids, markets, and colors.
examples: Heavy rain saturated the soil.

sat.passage: During the week-long storm, rain fell so steadily that it saturated the hillside. Once the soil could absorb no more water, the excess began to run off in sheets, and several sections of the slope slid onto the road below.

words.definition: To throw or spread in different directions.
words.usage: Used for seeds, crowds, and light.
examples: The wind scatters the seeds across the field.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Many desert plants depend on the wind to scatter their seeds. Their fruits split open on dry, gusty days, releasing tiny seeds with feathery tufts that can drift for kilometers before settling, so new plants sprout far from the parent.

words.definition: A possible sequence of events.
examples: Engineers planned for the worst-case scenario.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: City planners preparing for rising sea levels studied several possibilities. In the most severe scenario, which assumed that global emissions would keep increasing, floodwaters would reach the downtown business district by 2080, so the planners designed seawalls tall enough to handle even that outcome.

words.definition: The extent of an area or subject that something deals with.
words.usage: The scope of a study, beyond the scope.
examples: That question is beyond the scope of this report.

sat.passage: The historian acknowledges that her book has a narrow scope. Rather than surveying the entire Industrial Revolution, it examines a single textile mill in one English town between 1820 and 1840, using that mill's records to explore how factory work changed daily life.

words.definition: The feeling that someone is worthless; contempt.
examples: The critics treated the novel with scorn.

sat.passage: When the young painter first exhibited her bold, brightly colored canvases, established critics treated them with scorn, calling them childish and unfinished. Decades later, the same works hang in major museums, and the critics' dismissive reviews are remembered mainly as examples of misjudgment.

words.definition: Diligent, thorough, and very concerned with doing right.
examples: The accountant was scrupulous about every receipt.

sat.passage: The archive's restoration team is scrupulous in its work. Before repairing a damaged letter, conservators photograph every page, record each tear and stain, and use only materials that can be removed later without harming the original paper.

words.definition: To examine closely and thoroughly.
words.usage: Often 'scrutinized by' experts or the public.
examples: The contract was scrutinized by lawyers before signing.

sat.passage: Before the new bridge design was accepted, independent engineers scrutinized every calculation. They rechecked the load estimates line by line, tested scale models in a wind tunnel, and flagged two minor errors that the original designers had missed.

words.definition: Inclined to hide feelings or information.
words.usage: Describes people, animals, or organizations that conceal things.
examples: The secretive owl is rarely seen during the day.

sat.passage: The snow leopard is so secretive that some researchers spend years in its mountain habitat without seeing one. Scientists studying the cat rely instead on hidden cameras and on the droppings and tracks it leaves on remote ridges.

words.definition: Choosing carefully; affecting only certain things.
examples: The college is highly selective.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Hummingbirds are surprisingly selective when feeding. In field experiments, birds offered dozens of artificial flowers repeatedly visited only those whose nectar had the highest sugar content, ignoring the rest even when they were closer. The researchers concluded that the birds remember which blossoms reward them most.

words.definition: A physical feeling; widespread excitement.
examples: The young singer became an overnight sensation.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The young pianist's first concert in the capital caused a sensation. Newspapers printed her photograph on their front pages, tickets for her next performance sold out within hours, and crowds gathered outside her hotel hoping to catch a glimpse of her.

words.definition: The ability to appreciate and respond to complex feelings or art; (plural) a person's feelings and tastes.
examples: The film's violence offended some viewers' sensibilities.
sources: ACT Practice Test (Preparing for the ACT booklet)

sat.passage: The poet's early verses, written while she worked in a busy factory, reveal a remarkable sensibility. Her lines dwell on the color of dust in the afternoon light and the tired kindness of coworkers, small details that most observers would have overlooked.

words.definition: Quick to detect or respond to slight changes; easily upset; requiring care.
words.usage: Several meanings: sensitive instruments, sensitive skin, a sensitive topic.
examples: The sensor is sensitive enough to detect tiny vibrations.

sat.passage: The new seismometer is so sensitive that it can detect the vibrations of ocean waves striking a coastline hundreds of kilometers away. Researchers hope instruments like it will help them notice the faint tremors that sometimes come before large earthquakes.

words.definition: Calm and peaceful.
examples: The garden was serene at dawn.

sat.passage: The painting shows a mountain lake at dawn, its surface perfectly still. A single heron stands motionless in the shallows, and pale mist drifts over the water, giving the whole scene a serene quality that many viewers find soothing after the noise of the city.

words.definition: Having sharp judgment; clever in a practical way.
examples: A shrewd investor, she bought the land before prices rose.

sat.passage: A shrewd trader, the merchant bought large quantities of wool in the summer, when prices were low, and stored it in her warehouses. By winter, when demand had risen sharply, she sold it at nearly twice the price, earning enough to expand her business to two new towns.

words.definition: The quality of being important; meaning.
words.usage: Similar to 'import' (the significance of a discovery).
examples: Historians debate the significance of the treaty.

sat.passage: At first, the small clay tablet seemed ordinary to the archaeologists who found it. Only after translating its inscription did they grasp its significance: it was the oldest known record of a loan with interest, revealing that complex financial practices existed far earlier than historians had assumed.

words.definition: To imitate the appearance or conditions of something.
examples: The program simulates the effects of an earthquake.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: To train for missions, astronauts spend weeks in a large pool designed to simulate the weightlessness of space. Floating in heavy suits underwater, they practice repairing models of spacecraft, learning to move slowly and carefully as they would in orbit.

words.definition: Occurring at the same time.
examples: The two explosions were nearly simultaneous.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the experiment, two lights flashed at opposite ends of a dark room. Most participants reported that the flashes were simultaneous, but precise measurements showed that one had occurred a few thousandths of a second before the other.

words.definition: The quality of being honest and genuine.
words.usage: Describes feelings, apologies, and speech that are truly meant.
examples: No one doubted the sincerity of his apology.

sat.passage: When the company's founder apologized for the factory accident, some listeners doubted her sincerity. Their doubts faded, however, when she personally visited each injured worker, paid their medical bills, and closed the factory until new safety equipment was installed.

words.definition: Exceptional; unique; (grammar) referring to one.
examples: She had a singular talent for languages.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The biologist had a singular gift for spotting camouflaged insects. Where her colleagues saw only bark and leaves, she could pick out a motionless stick insect from several meters away, an ability that led to the discovery of eleven new species.

words.definition: Located in a particular place or position.
words.usage: Describes where something is placed or how someone is positioned.
examples: The village is situated at the foot of the mountain.

sat.passage: The ancient city was situated at the point where two rivers met. This location allowed traders to move goods by boat in three directions, and historians believe it explains how the settlement grew from a small village into a regional capital.

words.definition: Not easily convinced; having doubts.
examples: Many scientists were skeptical of the claim until more data appeared.
