sat.passage: When a researcher first reported that a common houseplant could remove most pollutants from indoor air, many scientists were skeptical. They pointed out that the tests had been done in tiny sealed chambers, and later studies showed that a typical room would need hundreds of plants to achieve the same effect.

words.definition: A doubting attitude toward claims or ideas.
words.usage: Often 'skepticism about' a claim; noun form of 'skeptical'.
examples: The announcement was met with skepticism by other researchers.

sat.passage: The company's claim that its new battery would last ten years on a single charge was met with skepticism. Engineers at rival firms noted that no existing technology came close to that performance, and several asked to see independent test results before accepting the figure.

words.definition: Only; single.
examples: Her sole aim was to help others.

sat.passage: For nearly forty years, the lighthouse keeper was the island's sole resident. Supply boats visited once a month, and between those visits she saw no one else, spending her days tending the lamp and recording the weather in a thick leather notebook.

words.definition: Formal and serious.
examples: They made a solemn promise.

sat.passage: The ceremony honoring the miners who died in the collapse was deeply solemn. Family members stood in silence as each name was read aloud, a single bell tolled after every name, and even the youngest children seemed to sense that this was no time for chatter.

words.definition: Showing care or concern.
examples: The nurse was solicitous of the patient's comfort.

sat.passage: The innkeeper was unusually solicitous toward her guests. She asked each traveler about dietary needs before preparing meals, left extra blankets in rooms on cold nights, and checked on a sick visitor several times a day until he recovered.

words.definition: To a moderate extent.
words.usage: Softens a claim; SAT answers often hinge on such qualifiers.
examples: The results were somewhat surprising.

sat.passage: The new tutoring program improved students' test scores somewhat. Average scores rose by about four points over the year, a gain the researchers described as encouraging but too modest to justify expanding the program to every school in the district.

words.definition: Highly developed and complex; worldly and refined.
words.usage: Describes technology, methods, and people with refined tastes.
examples: The ancient city had a sophisticated system of canals.

sat.passage: The ancient city had a sophisticated system for managing water. Engineers carved channels that carried rainwater from the hills into underground cisterns, used clay pipes to deliver it to public fountains, and built drains that kept streets from flooding during storms.

words.definition: Having supreme power; independent; (n.) a monarch.
examples: The treaty recognized the island as a sovereign state.

sat.passage: After decades of colonial rule, the island became a sovereign nation in 1962. It adopted its own constitution, began electing its own leaders, and joined international organizations as an equal member rather than as a territory governed from abroad.

words.definition: Thinly scattered.
examples: Vegetation is sparse in the tundra.

sat.passage: Vegetation on the high plateau is sparse. Only a few tough grasses and low shrubs grow there, widely separated across the rocky ground, because strong winds and thin soil prevent most plants from taking root. Travelers crossing the region can walk for hours without finding any shade.

words.definition: An individual example used for study or display.
examples: The museum has a rare specimen of the extinct bird.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The museum's collection includes a rare specimen of the great auk, a flightless seabird that was hunted to extinction in the 1840s. Researchers recently extracted DNA from the preserved bird's feathers to learn more about why the species vanished so quickly.

words.definition: A range of different positions or values; the range of light colors.
examples: Opinions spanned the entire political spectrum.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The town meeting about the proposed highway drew residents from across the political spectrum. Longtime conservatives sat beside progressive activists, and many who rarely agreed on anything found themselves united in opposing the road. Organizers said they had never seen such a varied crowd at a single meeting.

words.definition: To form a theory without firm evidence.
words.usage: Signals uncertainty; researchers speculate when data are incomplete.
examples: Historians speculate that the letter was never sent.

sat.passage: Because no written records survive from the island's earliest settlers, historians can only speculate about why they abandoned their villages around 1200. Some suggest a long drought, while others point to conflict with newcomers, but no evidence has yet settled the question.

words.definition: Happening without planning or outside cause.
examples: The crowd broke into spontaneous applause.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: No one had planned the celebration. When word spread that the long-delayed bridge had finally opened, residents poured into the streets, strangers began dancing together, and a spontaneous parade wound its way across the new span.

words.definition: Occurring at irregular intervals.
examples: There was sporadic gunfire through the night.

sat.passage: The volcano has remained mostly quiet since its last major eruption, but it is not entirely inactive. Over the past decade, scientists have recorded sporadic bursts of steam and ash, sometimes months apart and sometimes several in a single week, with no predictable pattern.

words.definition: False or fake; based on faulty reasoning.
examples: The study found the link to be spurious.

sat.passage: Each year, ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise and fall together. The connection is spurious, however: neither causes the other, and both simply increase during hot summer months, when more people buy cold treats and go swimming.

words.definition: To waste in a reckless way.
examples: He squandered his inheritance.

sat.passage: The young inventor received a generous grant to develop her water filter, but some investors worried that she would squander it. Their fears proved unfounded: she spent the money carefully, built a working prototype within budget, and gave the unused portion back to the foundation.

words.definition: To make or become steady.
words.usage: Used for prices, patients, and structures.
examples: Roots stabilize the soil on the hillside.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: On the steep hillside above the highway, engineers planted deep-rooted grasses and shrubs. As the plants grew, their roots began to stabilize the loose soil, and the landslides that had once blocked the road after every heavy rain became far less common.

words.definition: Not flowing or developing.
examples: Wages remained stagnant for a decade.

sat.passage: During the long dry season, the river shrinks into a series of stagnant pools. With no current to carry in fresh water, the pools quickly warm up and lose oxygen, and only fish that can gulp air at the surface manage to survive until the rains return.

words.definition: A position or attitude on an issue; a way of standing.
examples: The author takes a firm stance against the policy.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In her essay, the critic takes a firm stance against the practice of colorizing old black-and-white films. She argues that adding color distorts the original artistic choices of the filmmakers and urges studios to preserve the movies as they were first shown.

words.definition: Not moving or changing.
examples: Population levels remained static for decades.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: For most of the twentieth century, the village's population remained static at about 300 people. Each generation, roughly as many residents moved away or died as were born, so the number on the sign at the edge of town never needed to be changed.

words.definition: Loyal and committed.
examples: She was a staunch defender of free speech.

sat.passage: The senator was a staunch supporter of public libraries throughout her career. She voted for every library funding bill that reached the floor, spoke at dozens of branch openings, and even donated her own book collection to a small rural library.

words.definition: An oversimplified idea about a type of person or thing.
examples: The film challenges the stereotype of the absent-minded scientist.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Many early films portrayed scientists as wild-haired, absent-minded men working alone in cluttered laboratories. A new documentary challenges this stereotype by following a diverse group of researchers who work in teams, keep careful schedules, and spend much of their time collaborating.

words.definition: To suppress or hold back; to smother.
words.usage: Applies to feelings, ideas, and growth.
examples: Rigid rules can stifle creativity in the classroom.

sat.passage: Some educators argue that overly strict rules can stifle creativity in the classroom. When students are told exactly how every assignment must look, they say, children stop experimenting and begin focusing only on avoiding mistakes. Others counter that clear rules give students a stable foundation for creative work.

words.definition: Something that causes a reaction or activity.
words.usage: Science (a stimulus and response) and economics.
examples: The plant responds to light as a stimulus.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In a classic experiment, researchers rang a bell each time they fed a group of dogs. Eventually, the dogs began to drool at the sound of the bell alone, showing that a previously neutral stimulus could come to trigger a response on its own.

words.definition: Enduring pain or hardship without complaint.
examples: He remained stoic through the long recovery.

sat.passage: Throughout the months of grueling physical therapy that followed her accident, the dancer remained stoic. She rarely mentioned the pain, even to her family, and quietly completed every exercise her therapists assigned, no matter how exhausting.

words.definition: Easy to understand; honest and direct.
examples: The instructions were straightforward.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Assembling the bookshelf turned out to be straightforward. The kit included only six pieces and a single type of screw, and the instructions, printed as a few clear diagrams, could be followed in about fifteen minutes without any special tools.

words.definition: Carefully planned to achieve a goal.
examples: The fort was built at a strategic point on the river.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The fort was built on a strategic bluff overlooking the narrowest bend in the river. From that height, soldiers could see approaching boats long before they arrived and could control all traffic moving upstream toward the interior.

words.definition: Requiring or using great effort or energy.
words.usage: Describes exercise, work, and objections (strenuously object).
examples: The senator strenuously objected to the proposal.

sat.passage: The new hiking trail to the summit is far more strenuous than the old one. It climbs nearly a thousand meters in just four kilometers, and rangers advise hikers to carry extra water and to allow a full day for the round trip.

words.definition: Strict; precise and exacting.
examples: The lab has stringent safety standards.

sat.passage: Laboratories that handle dangerous viruses must follow stringent safety rules. Workers wear full-body suits with their own air supply, pass through several sealed chambers when entering or leaving, and shower with disinfectant before going home each day.

words.definition: Strongly and solidly built.
words.usage: Describes objects, bodies, and structures; adverb 'sturdily'.
examples: The sturdy table survived three moves.

sat.passage: Early settlers on the windswept plains learned to build sturdy homes from blocks of thick prairie sod. The heavy walls, often nearly a meter wide, held firm through fierce storms and kept the interiors warm in winter and cool in summer.

words.definition: To prevent or hinder the progress of.
words.usage: Informal-sounding but common in writing; used for obstacles blocking efforts.
examples: A lack of funding stymied the research project.

sat.passage: The expedition's attempt to reach the remote valley was repeatedly stymied by the weather. Heavy snow closed the mountain passes for weeks, and whenever the skies cleared, avalanches forced the team back to its base camp.

words.definition: Based on personal feelings or opinions.
examples: Judging art is often subjective.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Judging a baking contest is often subjective. While judges can easily check whether a cake is fully baked, deciding whether its flavor is delightful or merely pleasant depends largely on each judge's personal taste. As a result, two judges can taste the same cake and reach very different verdicts.

words.definition: Lower in rank or importance.
examples: In the novel, personal desires are subordinate to duty.

sat.passage: In the novel, the heroine's personal desires are always subordinate to her sense of duty. Although she longs to study painting in Paris, she remains in her village to care for her younger siblings, setting aside her own dreams again and again.

words.definition: Coming after something in time; following.
examples: The first trial failed, but subsequent experiments succeeded.

sat.passage: The first attempt to grow the crystals failed when the laboratory's temperature fluctuated overnight. In subsequent trials, however, the researchers kept the samples in an insulated chamber, and the crystals formed perfectly within a week. The team later published its method so that other labs could use it.

words.definition: Money granted by the government to help an industry or keep prices low.
examples: Farm subsidies keep food prices stable.

sat.passage: To encourage farmers to plant trees along riverbanks, the regional government offers a subsidy that covers most of the cost of seedlings and labor. Since the program began, the number of protected riverbanks has more than doubled, because landowners no longer have to bear the expense themselves.

words.definition: Of considerable importance, size, or worth.
examples: The program led to a substantial increase in graduation rates.

sat.passage: The new after-school program produced a substantial improvement in reading scores. Students who attended for a full year read nearly two grade levels higher than similar students who did not, a gain far larger than researchers had expected.

words.definition: To provide evidence to support.
examples: No data substantiate the company's claims.

sat.passage: The explorer claimed to have reached the mountain's summit alone in 1923, but he was never able to substantiate the story. He had no photographs from the top, his diary skipped the days of the climb, and no one else saw him on the peak.

words.definition: A person or thing acting in place of another.
examples: Honey can substitute for sugar in many recipes.

sat.passage: Many bakers substitute applesauce for butter when making muffins. The fruit provides moisture and a slight sweetness, allowing the muffins to stay soft while containing far less fat than those made with the original recipe. The trick has become popular among home cooks looking for lighter desserts.

words.definition: So delicate or precise as to be hard to notice or analyze.
examples: There was a subtle change in her tone.

sat.passage: The difference between the two bird species is subtle. Both have brown backs and speckled chests, and even experienced birdwatchers often must listen to their songs or look closely at the faint stripe above the eye to tell them apart.

words.definition: A number of things following one after another; the act of inheriting a position.
words.usage: Often 'in quick succession'; also used in ecology for changes in a community.
examples: Three storms hit the coast in quick succession.

sat.passage: Three powerful storms struck the coast in quick succession last autumn. Because each arrived only a few days after the one before, crews had no time to repair damaged seawalls, and flooding grew worse with every storm.

words.definition: A person or thing that follows another.
examples: The king named his son as his successor.

sat.passage: When the museum's longtime director announced her retirement, the board spent nearly a year searching for her successor. They finally chose a curator from another city, who took over the position the following spring and soon launched a series of new exhibitions.

words.definition: Briefly and clearly expressed.
examples: His succinct summary saved everyone time.

sat.passage: The editor's notes on the manuscript were succinct. Instead of pages of commentary, she wrote a single paragraph identifying the novel's two main weaknesses and suggesting how to fix each one, which the author found far more useful than lengthy critiques.

words.definition: The right to vote.
examples: The suffrage movement fought for women's voting rights.

sat.passage: In the late nineteenth century, activists in several countries campaigned for women's suffrage. They organized marches, collected signatures on petitions, and lobbied lawmakers, arguing that women should have the same right as men to cast ballots in elections.

words.definition: Existing or occurring at the surface; not thorough or deep.
words.usage: Describes wounds, similarities, and analyses that lack depth.
examples: The two languages share only a superficial resemblance.

sat.passage: At first glance, the two languages seem closely related, since many of their words sound alike. Linguists point out, however, that this resemblance is superficial: the languages' grammar and core vocabulary are completely different, and the similar-sounding words were mostly borrowed from a third language.

words.definition: Unnecessary; more than enough.
examples: The editor cut the superfluous words.

sat.passage: In revising her essay, the student cut every superfluous sentence. She removed passages that repeated earlier points and deleted a long anecdote that had nothing to do with her argument, reducing the essay from five pages to three.

words.definition: Higher in rank, quality, or importance.
examples: The new material is superior to steel in strength.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Engineers tested a new carbon-fiber material alongside traditional steel. The new material proved superior to steel in strength, withstanding loads nearly twice as heavy, while weighing only about a quarter as much. The engineers believe it could eventually make bridges and aircraft both lighter and safer.

words.definition: Something added to complete or enhance something else; (v.) to add to.
words.usage: Often 'a supplement to'. Implies addition, not replacement.
examples: Field notes supplement the data collected by the sensors.

sat.passage: Weather stations on the mountain record temperature and wind speed every minute, but the instruments cannot capture everything. Researchers therefore supplement the automated data with field notes, recording observations such as the condition of the snow and the behavior of local birds.

words.definition: According to what is generally believed, though doubtful.
examples: The house is supposedly haunted.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The old inn on the hill is supposedly haunted by the ghost of a sea captain. Guests have reported strange noises and flickering lights, but investigators who spent a week there found only drafty windows and faulty wiring.

words.definition: To forcibly put an end to; to prevent from developing or being expressed.
words.usage: Used for rebellions, information, emotions, and biological processes.
examples: The medicine suppresses the immune response.

sat.passage: Some plants release chemicals into the soil that suppress the growth of nearby competitors. Black walnut trees, for instance, produce a compound that prevents many other species from germinating or thriving beneath their branches. Gardeners often notice that tomatoes planted near these trees wilt and die.

words.definition: To exceed; to be greater or better than.
examples: The student's skill soon surpassed her teacher's.

sat.passage: When the young chess player began lessons at age six, her teacher expected steady but ordinary progress. Within four years, however, the student's skill had begun to surpass her teacher's, and by twelve she was regularly defeating him in tournament games.

words.definition: An amount that is more than needed.
examples: The farm sold its surplus grain.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In years when rainfall was plentiful, farmers in the river valley harvested far more grain than their households could eat. Rather than letting the extra rot in storage, they traded the surplus to herders in the hills in exchange for wool and salt.

words.definition: Likely to be influenced or harmed by something.
examples: Young plants are especially susceptible to frost.

sat.passage: Young oak seedlings are especially susceptible to browsing deer: a single night of feeding can strip a sapling of all its leaves. Older trees, protected by bark too tough to chew and branches too high to reach, are rarely harmed.

words.definition: To halt temporarily; to hang.
words.usage: Suspend a game; suspended in water.
examples: Officials suspended the race because of lightning.

sat.passage: After heavy rains washed out part of the mountain road, the transit authority suspended bus service to the village for two weeks. Engineers rebuilt the damaged section, and buses resumed their regular route by the end of the month.

words.definition: Having or showing a feeling that something is wrong; causing such a feeling.
words.usage: Describes people who doubt and things that seem questionable.
examples: The guard grew suspicious of the unfamiliar truck.

sat.passage: When the curator examined the newly donated painting, she grew suspicious. The canvas was supposedly three hundred years old, yet its paint contained a pigment not invented until the twentieth century, so she asked a laboratory to test the work before putting it on display.

words.definition: To keep going over time; to endure or support.
words.usage: Can mean maintain, or suffer (sustain an injury).
examples: The small town could not sustain a large factory for long.

sat.passage: Hummingbirds have among the highest metabolic rates of any animal, so during the day they must feed every few minutes to sustain their energy. At night, many species enter a state of torpor, lowering their body temperature to conserve fuel until morning.

words.definition: Able to be maintained over time without depleting resources.
examples: The town switched to sustainable fishing practices.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: For decades, the fleet caught cod faster than the population could reproduce, and by the 1990s the stock had collapsed. The new management plan sets catch limits low enough that the fishery will be sustainable, allowing fish numbers to recover while still supporting local jobs for generations.

words.definition: Serving as a symbol; significant as a representation rather than in practice.
words.usage: A symbolic gesture has meaning but little practical effect.
examples: The ribbon cutting was a symbolic start to the project.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: When the new city council took office, its first act was to rename the central square after the town's founder. The change was largely symbolic: it cost almost nothing and altered no laws, but residents saw it as a sign that the council valued local history.

words.definition: The operation of things at the same time or rate.
words.usage: Used for clocks, signals, behaviors (fireflies flashing together).
examples: The synchronization of the fireflies' flashes amazed the visitors.

sat.passage: In some forests of Southeast Asia, thousands of male fireflies gather in a single tree and flash in near-perfect synchronization, lighting up and going dark at the same instant. Researchers think this coordinated display makes the males easier for females to spot from a distance.

words.definition: The combination of parts to form a whole.
examples: Her theory is a synthesis of earlier ideas.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The historian's new book does not present fresh archival discoveries. Instead, it offers a synthesis of decades of earlier research, weaving together studies of trade, religion, and climate into a single account of the empire's decline.

words.definition: Made by chemical processes; artificial.
examples: Nylon is a synthetic fiber.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Before the 1930s, most stockings were knitted from silk, which is spun by silkworms. Nylon changed that: because the fiber was synthetic, created in a laboratory from chemicals derived from coal and petroleum, it could be manufactured cheaply and in enormous quantities.

words.definition: Done according to a fixed plan or system; methodical.
examples: The team conducted a systematic search of the area.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Rather than sampling whichever streams were easiest to reach, the survey team took a systematic approach. They divided the watershed into a grid and collected water from the center of every square on the same day each month.

words.definition: Understood without being stated.
examples: Her silence was taken as tacit approval.

sat.passage: No one on the committee formally endorsed the director's plan, but no one objected to it either. Taking their silence as tacit approval, she began hiring staff for the project the next morning.

words.definition: Only slightly connected to the main topic; diverging.
words.usage: Describes remarks or issues that drift away from the point.
examples: His speech included several tangential stories about his childhood.

sat.passage: During the hearing, the senator repeatedly raised points that were tangential to the bill under discussion, such as the history of the building where the committee met. The chair finally reminded him to address the bill's actual provisions.

words.definition: Able to be touched or clearly perceived; real rather than abstract.
examples: The new program produced tangible improvements in reading scores.

sat.passage: Many of the tutoring program's benefits, such as students' growing confidence, are hard to measure. But it has also produced tangible results: the share of participants who graduated on time rose from 61 to 84 percent in three years.

words.definition: Too long, slow, or dull; tiresome.
words.usage: Describes tasks and processes that are boring and repetitive.
examples: Counting every seed by hand was tedious work.

sat.passage: Before computers, compiling a concordance of a long book was tedious work. Scholars copied every occurrence of every word onto a separate slip of paper and sorted the slips by hand, a repetitive process that could take decades.

words.definition: To moderate or soften; to harden metal.
examples: She tempered her criticism with praise.

sat.passage: The early test results were encouraging, but the lead researcher tempered her team's excitement by noting that the trial had involved only twenty patients. Larger studies, she cautioned, would be needed before anyone could call the treatment effective.

words.definition: Relating to time; worldly rather than spiritual.
examples: The study looked at temporal patterns in bird song.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: A fossil's position in rock layers reveals its temporal relationship to other fossils: specimens buried deeper generally lived earlier than those found above them. Combined with radiometric dating, this principle lets geologists arrange species in the order in which they appeared.

words.definition: Lasting for only a limited time.
examples: The bridge closure is only temporary.

sat.passage: After the earthquake damaged the city's main hospital, doctors treated patients in temporary tents set up in a nearby park. The tents were taken down eighteen months later, once the rebuilt hospital opened its doors.

words.definition: To attract or entice someone to do something, often unwise.
examples: The warm weather tempted us to skip work.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Grocery stores often place candy and magazines beside the checkout line, where shoppers waiting to pay may be tempted to buy items they had not planned to purchase. Marketers call these unplanned purchases impulse buys.

words.definition: Persistent; holding firmly.
examples: The tenacious reporter uncovered the truth.

sat.passage: The burdock plant spreads its seeds by attaching them to passing animals. Each seed head is covered with tiny hooks so tenacious that they cling to fur for miles, an observation that later inspired the invention of hook-and-loop fasteners.

words.definition: A principle or belief.
examples: Honesty is a central tenet of journalism.

sat.passage: One central tenet of the Arts and Crafts movement was that everyday objects should be both useful and beautiful. Guided by this principle, its members rejected cheap factory-made goods and promoted furniture, textiles, and books made by skilled hand workers.

words.definition: Not certain or fixed; hesitant.
words.usage: Describes plans, conclusions, and steps that may change.
examples: The researchers reached a tentative conclusion pending further tests.

sat.passage: The archaeologists' identification of the site as a royal burial ground is still tentative. They have found gold ornaments typical of elite graves, but they will not be confident until the inscriptions on the tomb walls are translated.

words.definition: Very weak or slight; thin.
words.usage: Describes connections, arguments, or holds that could easily fail.
examples: The link between the two events is tenuous at best.

sat.passage: The author claims that her novel's plot was inspired by her grandmother's wartime letters, but the connection is tenuous. The letters mention none of the novel's events, and only one minor character shares a name with a relative.

words.definition: To bring to an end.
words.usage: Formal; used for contracts and processes.
examples: The company terminated its contract with the supplier.

sat.passage: When inspectors discovered that the contractor had used substandard concrete in the bridge's foundation, the city terminated its agreement with the company. A different firm was hired to tear out the faulty work and finish the job.

words.definition: The special words used in a subject.
examples: The article explains medical terminology in plain language.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Medical terminology can bewilder patients: a doctor might describe a bruise as a contusion or a heart attack as a myocardial infarction. Some hospitals now train physicians to explain diagnoses in everyday language instead.

words.definition: Brief, sometimes rudely so.
examples: His terse reply ended the conversation.

sat.passage: Asked by reporters whether she would run for a second term, the mayor gave a terse reply of two words. Then, without offering any further explanation, she turned and walked back into city hall.

words.definition: By that means; as a result of that.
examples: The dam controls floods, thereby protecting the valley.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the 1850s, engineers raised the streets of Chicago by several feet and laid sewer pipes beneath them, thereby giving the city's waste a downhill path to the river. The project ended years of muddy, flooded roads.

words.definition: A main claim that a writer sets out to support; a long academic paper.
examples: The essay's thesis is that trade shaped the region's culture.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The essay's thesis appears in its first paragraph: that the printing press did more to spread everyday languages than to spread Latin. Each later section offers evidence supporting this claim, from booksellers' records to surviving pamphlets.

words.definition: Consideration for others; careful thinking.
words.usage: Describes kind behavior or reflective judgment.
examples: Her thoughtfulness showed in the handwritten notes she sent.

sat.passage: Guests at the inn often remarked on the owner's thoughtfulness. She remembered which visitors preferred tea to coffee, left extra blankets for those arriving on cold nights, and wrote each departing guest a short note.

words.definition: A level at which something starts to happen; a doorway.
words.usage: Pain threshold; on the threshold of discovery.
examples: Above a certain threshold, noise becomes harmful.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Some seeds will not germinate until soil temperatures pass a certain threshold. In one experiment, a species of desert wildflower stayed dormant at 10 degrees Celsius but sprouted readily once the soil warmed beyond 15 degrees.

words.definition: Willingness to accept views or behavior different from one's own; the ability to endure.
examples: Cacti have a high tolerance for drought.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Camels have a remarkable tolerance for dehydration. They can lose up to a quarter of their body water and keep walking across the desert, whereas a similar loss would be fatal for most other mammals.

words.definition: Poisonous; very harmful.
examples: Some mushrooms are highly toxic.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Monarch caterpillars feed only on milkweed, a plant containing chemicals that are toxic to most animals. By storing these chemicals in their bodies, monarchs make themselves dangerous to eat, and birds that swallow one often vomit and avoid the species afterward.

words.definition: (n.) A mark or very small amount left behind; (v.) to find the origin of.
words.usage: The SAT has tested 'trace' meaning 'a mark or sign left behind'.
examples: The hikers found no trace of the trail under the snow.

sat.passage: When archaeologists excavated the abandoned settlement, they found no trace of the violent conflict described in later legends. There were no burned buildings, no weapons, and no hastily buried remains anywhere on the site.

words.definition: A distinguishing quality or characteristic.
examples: Curiosity is a common trait among scientists.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Among Arctic foxes, a thick white winter coat is a trait passed from parents to offspring, helping the animals blend into snowy landscapes. Foxes born with darker fur are more easily spotted by prey and tend to catch less food.

words.definition: The path of a moving object; the course of development.
words.usage: Literal (a rocket's trajectory) and figurative (career trajectory).
examples: The company's growth followed a steady upward trajectory.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: By tracking the asteroid's position over several nights, astronomers calculated its trajectory. They determined that it would pass more than four million kilometers from Earth, posing no risk of impact.

words.definition: Free from disturbance; calm.
examples: The lake was tranquil in the early morning.

sat.passage: After weeks in the noisy city, Amara found the lake tranquil. No motorboats crossed its surface, and the only sounds were the occasional cry of a loon and the soft lapping of water against the dock.

words.definition: To make a thorough or dramatic change in form or character.
words.usage: Used for landscapes, industries, and people.
examples: The railroad transformed the small town into a busy city.
sources: ACT Practice Test (Preparing for the ACT booklet)

sat.passage: Over the past century, irrigation canals transformed the valley. What had been dry scrubland grazed by a few goats became a patchwork of orchards and vineyards supplying fruit to cities hundreds of miles away.

words.definition: Lasting only a short time.
examples: The pain was transient and soon passed.

sat.passage: Most of the town's summer residents are transient: tourists who rent cottages for a week or two before moving on, along with seasonal workers who leave once the hotels close in September. By October, the population shrinks to a few hundred year-round households.

words.definition: To send or pass from one person, place, or thing to another.
words.usage: Used for signals, diseases, and traditions.
examples: Mosquitoes can transmit malaria.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Some species of mosquito can transmit the virus that causes yellow fever. When an infected mosquito bites a person, it passes the virus into the bloodstream along with its saliva, and the disease may then reach the next mosquito that bites.

words.definition: Allowing light through so objects can be seen clearly; open and honest; easily understood.
words.usage: The SAT has tested the literal 'clear/see-through' meaning in a literary passage.
examples: The water was so transparent that we could see fish far below.

sat.passage: The water in the mountain pool was so transparent that Elena could count the pebbles on the bottom, six feet below. Small trout hovered above them, every fin visible, as if floating in air.

words.definition: Very great in amount, scale, or intensity.
examples: The project required a tremendous amount of work.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Building the railroad across the mountains required a tremendous amount of labor. Thousands of workers blasted tunnels through solid granite, hauled rails by hand, and toiled through winters in which snowdrifts buried entire camps.

words.definition: Fear or anxiety about what may happen.
examples: She approached the stage with trepidation.

sat.passage: Having never spoken in public before, Malik approached the podium with trepidation. His hands trembled as he unfolded his notes, and he paused twice to steady his voice before beginning.

words.definition: To cause an event or reaction.
examples: The earthquake triggered a tsunami.

sat.passage: Contrary to popular belief, a single loud noise is unlikely to trigger an avalanche. Far more often, slides are set off by the weight of a skier or by a sudden warming that weakens buried layers of snow.

words.definition: Of little value or importance.
examples: They argued over a trivial detail.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The editor dismissed most of the reader's complaints as trivial, such as a misplaced comma here and an inconsistent spelling there. She took seriously, however, the one error that misstated a key date in the war.

words.definition: Loud confusion; disorder.
examples: The announcement caused a tumult in the hall.

sat.passage: When the verdict was announced, the courtroom erupted in tumult. Spectators shouted and climbed onto benches, reporters shoved toward the exits, and the judge pounded her gavel for several minutes before order returned.

words.definition: Characterized by conflict, disorder, or unsteady movement.
examples: The 1960s were a turbulent decade.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The decade after the revolution was turbulent. Three governments rose and fell, rival factions battled in the streets, and the national currency lost nearly all its value.

words.definition: Cruel and oppressive government.
examples: The colonists rebelled against tyranny.

sat.passage: Under the king's tyranny, citizens could be imprisoned without trial, newspapers that criticized the crown were shut down, and taxes were raised at the monarch's whim. Many families fled across the border.

words.definition: Present, appearing, or found everywhere.
words.usage: Describes technologies, species, and trends that are everywhere.
examples: Smartphones have become ubiquitous in modern life.

sat.passage: Plastic microfibers have become ubiquitous in the environment. Researchers have found them in Arctic sea ice, in deep-ocean sediments, in tap water, and even in the air of remote mountain villages.

words.definition: Final; being the best or most extreme.
words.usage: The ultimate goal; the ultimate test.
examples: The ultimate goal is to cure the disease.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The engineers' ultimate goal is a fusion reactor that produces more energy than it consumes. For now, however, they are focused on an intermediate step: keeping the superheated plasma stable for longer than a few seconds.

words.definition: Fully in agreement.
examples: The jury reached a unanimous verdict.

sat.passage: The jury's decision was unanimous. All twelve members voted to acquit, and the foreperson announced the verdict knowing that not a single juror had dissented.

words.definition: Not pretentious or arrogant; modest.
words.usage: Describes people and places that are humble or plain.
examples: The unassuming café served the best soup in town.

sat.passage: Despite having won two national awards for her research, the chemist was unassuming. She rarely mentioned her prizes, ate lunch with the lab's students, and insisted that everyone call her by her first name.

words.definition: Unable to be denied or disputed.
words.usage: Describes facts, talent, and evidence that are clearly true.
examples: Her influence on modern dance is undeniable.

sat.passage: Critics disagreed about whether the young pianist's interpretations were too unconventional, but her technical skill was undeniable. She played the concerto's most difficult passages flawlessly, at a tempo few professionals attempt.

words.definition: To judge something to be smaller or less important than it really is.
words.usage: Used for costs, abilities, and risks.
examples: Many people underestimate how long a project will take.

sat.passage: The city's planners badly underestimated the cost of the subway extension. They budgeted two billion dollars, but tunneling through unexpectedly hard bedrock pushed the final price above five billion.

words.definition: To experience or be subjected to.
examples: Caterpillars undergo a dramatic transformation.

sat.passage: Before a new drug can be sold, it must undergo several rounds of clinical trials. Each round tests the drug's safety and effectiveness in a larger group of patients than the one before.

words.definition: To be the basis or cause of.
examples: Poverty underlies many health problems.

sat.passage: Neuroscientists have long sought to understand the brain processes that underlie memory. One leading theory holds that memories form when connections between certain neurons grow stronger with repeated use.

words.definition: To weaken or damage something, especially gradually or secretly.
words.usage: Often about undermining an argument, authority, or confidence.
examples: The new evidence undermines the original theory.

sat.passage: Repeated budget cuts gradually undermined the agency's ability to inspect factories. By the end of the decade, it had half as many inspectors as before and could visit each plant only once every seven years.

words.definition: To commit to and begin a task.
examples: The team will undertake a five-year study of the reef.

sat.passage: After years of planning, the small museum decided to undertake an ambitious project: cataloging and photographing all 40,000 objects in its collection. Once the work is complete, scholars around the world will be able to view the items online.

words.definition: Not showing someone or something in a favorable way.
examples: The biography offers an unflattering portrait of the inventor.

sat.passage: The new biography paints an unflattering portrait of the inventor. It describes him as a man who took credit for his assistants' work, broke promises to investors, and refused to share profits with his early partners.

words.definition: Remaining the same in all cases and at all times; consistent.
words.usage: Describes size, color, rules, and distribution.
examples: The tiles are uniform in size and color.

sat.passage: To ensure that the bricks fired evenly, the potters pressed the clay into wooden molds of uniform size. As a result, every brick in the kiln had the same thickness and heated at the same rate.

words.definition: To make or become united.
words.usage: Used for nations, theories, and groups.
examples: The leader worked to unify the divided country.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: In the nineteenth century, electricity and magnetism were treated as separate forces with separate laws. One physicist hoped to develop a single theory that would unify the two explanations, showing them to be aspects of the same phenomenon.

words.definition: Expressing oneself freely, without self-consciousness.
examples: The children danced in uninhibited joy.
sources: ACT Practice Test (Preparing for the ACT booklet)

sat.passage: At home the toddler was uninhibited, singing loudly and dancing around the kitchen in front of anyone who visited. At preschool, though, she hid behind her teacher and barely spoke.

words.definition: Impossible to understand.
examples: The message was garbled and unintelligible.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The radio message from the ship was unintelligible. Static garbled nearly every word, and operators on shore could make out only a few scattered syllables.

words.definition: Applicable to all cases or people.
words.usage: Describes truths, rights, and experiences shared by everyone.
examples: Music is sometimes called a universal language.

sat.passage: Linguists have long debated whether any grammatical features are universal. Every known language, for instance, appears to distinguish between nouns and verbs, which suggests that this distinction may be shared by all human languages.

words.definition: Not conspicuous or attracting attention.
words.usage: Describes design, behavior, and presence that blend in.
examples: The security cameras were small and unobtrusive.

sat.passage: The architects designed the new visitor center to be unobtrusive. It is built partly underground, its roof is covered with native grasses, and from the hiking trail it is nearly invisible against the hillside.

words.definition: Never done or known before.
words.usage: Describes events and levels beyond anything recorded.
examples: The city saw unprecedented rainfall last spring.

sat.passage: The heat wave of that July was unprecedented in the region. Temperatures exceeded 40 degrees Celsius on nine consecutive days, a streak that had never occurred in more than 150 years of weather records.

words.definition: Not able to be predicted; changeable.
examples: Mountain weather can be unpredictable.

sat.passage: Farmers in the region find the spring rains unpredictable. In some years the rains arrive in early March, in others not until May, and occasionally they fail to come at all.

words.definition: Having no moral principles.
examples: Unscrupulous dealers sold fake antiques.

sat.passage: During the gold rush, unscrupulous merchants often sold flour mixed with sawdust and charged miners ten times the usual price for basic tools. Many prospectors spent their earnings faster than they could find gold.

words.definition: Likely to change or fail; not steady.
words.usage: Used for structures, chemicals, and situations.
examples: The old bridge was declared unstable.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Nitroglycerin is so unstable that a slight jolt can cause it to explode. This made the liquid extremely dangerous to transport until chemists found a way to mix it with an absorbent clay in the 1860s.

words.definition: Not feeling or showing concern for others; not likable.
words.usage: Describes people, responses, and fictional characters.
examples: The novel's narrator is intentionally unsympathetic.

sat.passage: The novel's narrator is deliberately unsympathetic. He lies to his friends, mocks his sister's hardships, and never apologizes, yet readers keep turning the pages to see whether such a disagreeable figure will ever change.

words.definition: Honest and respectable.
examples: The mayor was known as an upstanding member of the community.

sat.passage: Neighbors described the shopkeeper as an upstanding member of the community. He paid his debts promptly, volunteered at the library, and once returned a lost wallet containing several hundred dollars.

words.definition: Usefulness; a public service like water or electricity.
examples: The tool's utility made it popular with farmers.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Naval engineers began to question the utility of the heavy armor plating. It slowed the ships so much that they could no longer outrun enemy vessels, and it offered little protection against newer shells.

words.definition: To make practical use of.
examples: The factory utilizes solar power.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: To survive the dry season, some desert frogs utilize the fat stored in their bodies, burning it slowly while they remain buried underground for months. When the rains return, they dig out to feed and breed.

words.definition: To waver between opinions.
examples: He vacillated between two job offers.

sat.passage: For weeks the council member vacillated on the proposed stadium, supporting it in one interview and opposing it in the next. Frustrated voters began calling her office to demand a clear answer.

words.definition: Not clearly expressed or defined.
examples: His answer was vague and unhelpful.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The instructions that came with the bookshelf were frustratingly vague. They said only to attach the sides securely, without specifying which screws to use or where the holes should go.

words.definition: Logically sound; legally acceptable.
examples: She raised a valid point about the cost.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The lawyer argued that the contract was not valid because one of the signatures had been forged. A document signed under false pretenses, she explained, cannot be enforced in court.

words.definition: To check or prove the accuracy of; to confirm.
words.usage: Common in science: results validated by later studies.
examples: The model's predictions were validated by real-world measurements.

sat.passage: Later observations validated the ecologists' prediction. When wolves disappeared from the island, the moose population tripled within five years, just as the team's model had forecast.

words.definition: The quality of being changeable or uneven.
examples: The data showed high variability between samples.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Weather on the high plateau shows great variability. A sunny morning can give way to hail by noon, and temperatures may swing by more than 25 degrees Celsius in a single day.

words.definition: A form that differs slightly from others of the same type.
words.usage: Used for genes, viruses, and spellings.
examples: 'Color' and 'colour' are spelling variants.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Folklorists have identified a regional variant of the old ballad. Its melody is the same as in the better-known version, but its final verse describes a flood rather than a fire.

words.definition: Truthfulness; accuracy.
examples: Historians questioned the veracity of the account.

sat.passage: Historians questioned the veracity of the explorer's journal after comparing it with ship records. The records showed that he had been hundreds of miles away on several of the dates when he claimed to have discovered new islands.

words.definition: To make sure something is true or accurate.
words.usage: Used for facts, identities, and results.
examples: Journalists must verify their sources before publishing.

sat.passage: Before publishing the leaked documents, the newspaper hired two independent experts to verify that they were genuine. Both concluded that the paper, ink, and signatures matched records from the period.

words.definition: A trace of something that no longer exists.
examples: The ruins are the last vestige of the empire.

sat.passage: The tiny hip bones found inside some whales are a vestige of their ancestors' hind legs. These small, useless bones are evidence that the ancestors of modern whales once walked on land.

words.definition: Capable of working successfully; able to live or grow.
examples: Solar power has become a viable alternative to coal.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Some lotus seeds remain viable for centuries. Researchers have successfully grown plants from seeds that were recovered from a dry lakebed and dated to more than a thousand years old.

words.definition: Keeping careful watch for danger.
examples: Lifeguards must stay vigilant.

sat.passage: Meerkats take turns standing guard while the rest of the group forages. The sentry remains vigilant, scanning the sky for hawks and giving a sharp alarm call the moment a predator appears.

words.definition: To clear of blame or show to be right.
words.usage: Often when later evidence proves someone right.
examples: The new fossil vindicated the scientist's controversial theory.

sat.passage: For years, other geologists dismissed her claim that the canyon had been carved by a single catastrophic flood. She was vindicated when later surveys uncovered giant ripple marks, each several meters high, that only an enormous flood could have produced.

words.definition: Having a strong desire for revenge.
examples: The vindictive king punished his critics.

sat.passage: In the novel, the dismissed steward grows vindictive. He spreads rumors about his former employer and secretly sabotages the estate's harvest, determined to repay what he sees as an unjust firing.

words.definition: To break a rule or agreement; to disrespect.
examples: The company violated safety regulations.

sat.passage: The factory was fined after inspectors found that it had violated environmental regulations by dumping untreated wastewater into the river at night. The company was also ordered to pay for the cleanup.

words.definition: Moral excellence; a good quality.
examples: Patience is a virtue.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: Many ancient philosophers regarded patience as a virtue. They described it as a moral strength that good people developed through practice and that allowed them to endure hardship without anger or complaint.

words.definition: (n.) A completely empty space; (adj.) not valid or legally binding.
words.usage: Literal (the void of space) or legal (the contract is void).
examples: Her departure left a void in the team.

sat.passage: Because the seller did not actually own the land, the court declared the sale void. The buyer was entitled to a full refund, and the property remained with its rightful owner.

words.definition: Liable to change rapidly and unpredictably.
examples: Oil prices have been volatile this year.

sat.passage: Prices for crude oil were especially volatile that year. They rose by 30 percent in a single month and then fell almost as sharply a few weeks later, making it hard for airlines to plan their budgets.

words.definition: The power of using one's own will; choice.
words.usage: 'Of one's own volition' means by choice.
examples: She left the job of her own volition.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: No one forced the young composer to leave the conservatory; she withdrew of her own volition. She had decided that she would learn more by touring with a band than by sitting in classrooms.

words.definition: Done by choice, not by force.
examples: Participation in the survey was voluntary.

sat.passage: Participation in the workplace survey was voluntary. Employees could decline to answer any question, and those who chose not to take part at all faced no penalty.

words.definition: To decrease in strength or extent.
examples: Interest in the fad waned quickly.

sat.passage: Public interest in the space program began to wane after the first moon landings. Television networks stopped broadcasting launches live, and lawmakers steadily cut the agency's budget.

words.definition: Justified or necessary.
words.usage: Describes concerns, actions, and conclusions that are reasonable given the evidence.
examples: Given the storm forecast, closing the schools was warranted.

sat.passage: The bridge had developed new cracks after each of the last three storms. Given this evidence, the engineers concluded that closing it to heavy trucks was warranted until repairs could be made.

words.definition: Feeling or showing caution about possible dangers or problems.
examples: Deer are wary of humans.

sat.passage: Having been cheated once by a traveling salesman, the farmer was wary of strangers who offered bargains. Now he insisted on inspecting every tool carefully before he paid a cent.

words.definition: The health, happiness, and well-being of a person or group.
examples: The inspector checked that the welfare of the workers was protected.

sat.passage: The new regulations focus on the welfare of farm animals. They require that hens have room to spread their wings and that pigs have access to straw bedding and outdoor space.

words.definition: In contrast to the fact that.
examples: Frogs have smooth skin, whereas toads have bumpy skin.

sat.passage: Desert tortoises can go months without drinking, obtaining most of their water from the plants they eat, whereas many lizards in the same habitat must find water every few days. This difference shapes where each species can live.

words.definition: By which.
words.usage: Formal; introduces a method or process.
examples: They devised a system whereby members could vote online.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: The researchers devised a system whereby volunteers could report bird sightings through a smartphone app. The thousands of reports that poured in allowed the team to map migration routes across the entire continent.

words.definition: Playfully quaint or fanciful.
examples: The book has whimsical illustrations.

sat.passage: The children's library is decorated in a whimsical style. Bookshelves are shaped like tree trunks, a reading nook sits inside a giant teacup, and painted foxes peek out from behind the doors.

words.definition: Found or distributed over a large area or number of people.
words.usage: Describes beliefs, damage, and species distributions.
examples: The belief that bats are blind is widespread but false.

sat.passage: Once confined to a few valleys in the Alps, the plant has become widespread across Europe. It now appears along roadsides and riverbanks from Spain to Finland.

words.definition: To hold and use a weapon or tool; to have and use power.
words.usage: Figurative use is common: wield influence or power.
examples: The committee wields great influence over the budget.

sat.passage: As the governor's closest adviser, Hale wielded enormous influence. No bill reached the governor's desk without his review, and legislators sought his support before introducing new proposals.

words.definition: The quality of having experience, knowledge, and good judgment.
words.usage: 'Conventional wisdom' means a commonly held belief.
examples: Conventional wisdom held that the disease was incurable.
sources: New Academic Word List (Browne, Culligan & Phillips, CC BY-SA 4.0)

sat.passage: For most of the twentieth century, conventional wisdom held that dinosaurs were sluggish, cold-blooded reptiles. Fossil evidence of feathers and rapid growth, however, has led many paleontologists to reject that view.

words.definition: Having a feeling of vague, regretful longing.
examples: She gave a wistful look at her childhood home.

sat.passage: Looking through photographs of her childhood summers at the lake, my grandmother grew wistful. She sighed softly and said she wished she could return, just once, to the cabin her family had sold decades ago.

words.definition: To refuse to give something that is due or wanted.
words.usage: Used for information, payment, and approval.
examples: The company chose to withhold the test results from the public.

sat.passage: The company chose to withhold the safety report from regulators for nearly a year. It released the document only after a journalist obtained a copy and published its findings.

words.definition: Having great energy or enthusiasm for a cause.
words.usage: Can be positive or suggest excess.
examples: The zealous volunteers worked through the night.

sat.passage: The young lawyer was zealous in her defense of the tenants. She worked late into the night researching housing law, filed appeal after appeal, and refused every settlement that would have left families without homes.
